# HPLC: Separating mixtures in time

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/c01/en/
Language: en

Separate a mixture into distinguishable time signals, then turn peak area into concentration and mass with a clear experimental meaning.

## How do we count only the caffeine in coffee?

Coffee contains many dissolved substances as well as color and aroma. A direct ultraviolet measurement records their combined optical response, while the caffeine we want to measure is only one contributor. Materials research encounters the same difficulty: water exposed to a polymer may contain released drug, residual small molecules and degradation products. Cell-culture medium contains nutrients, metabolites and additives. Measuring one target reliably often begins by separating it from the surrounding mixture and then selecting an appropriate detector.

High-performance liquid chromatography, abbreviated HPLC, passes a liquid mixture through a column containing a stationary separation medium. Different molecules interact with that medium for different average lengths of time. Substances introduced together consequently arrive at the outlet at different times. A detector continuously records what passes it, producing a chromatogram with time on the horizontal axis and a response such as ultraviolet absorbance on the vertical axis. The column separates, and the detector translates passing material into a signal. Their combination creates an analytical measurement.

Imagine people crossing a shopping district from the same starting point. Some keep walking; others stop repeatedly, so their arrival times differ. Molecules have no intentions: thermal motion and interactions determine their exchanges between the moving liquid and stationary environment. Even molecules of the same compound follow somewhat different histories, producing a distribution of arrival times rather than a perfectly synchronized group. Good separation therefore requires both different average arrival times for different compounds and sufficiently narrow arrival distributions for each compound.

This chapter follows a complete quantitative experiment: understand the column, separate a target from its neighbors, convert peak area to concentration, and return that concentration to the original research question. Caffeine provides a familiar motivation, while explicitly constructed data make the calculations inspectable. The same reasoning applies to residual monomer, additives in material extracts and drug release. Suitability begins with whether the target remains stable in the chosen liquid, can be separated under useful conditions and gives a measurable detector response.

## Turning a molecular preference into minutes of separation

The moving liquid is the mobile phase. The environment retained within the column is the stationary phase, which may include chemical groups on particles or a retained liquid-like environment. Molecules move forward readily while carried by the mobile phase and advance more slowly on average while associated with the stationary phase. Repeated exchange along the column accumulates small differences into measurable time differences. The important question is how the two environments treat different molecules. An ordinary reversed-phase column is therefore not simply a filter that sorts everything by molecular size.

This repeated-distribution idea also illuminates the history. In his 1952 Nobel lecture, Archer Martin described partition chromatography as a connection between chromatography and countercurrent extraction. Martin and Richard Synge developed separation methods in a setting where understanding protein composition required distinguishable components from complex mixtures. The original column illustration shows two bands separating as differences accumulate. Modern pumps, refined packing and continuous detection make this process more reproducible and measurable. The scientific need encouraged a separation method, and improved separation enabled more demanding biochemical questions.

Common reversed-phase methods use relatively hydrophobic stationary surfaces, such as C18 groups, with mobile phases containing water and a miscible organic solvent. Many hydrophobic compounds remain longer under these conditions; increasing organic solvent often helps elute them. These comparisons apply within specified conditions. Charge, hydrogen bonding, aromatic interactions and details of the surface all influence retention, and two columns labeled C18 can have different selectivities. Very polar compounds, charged molecules and macromolecules may benefit from other mechanisms, including hydrophilic interaction, ion exchange or size exclusion.

Charge state deserves an early explanation. Some molecules accept or release protons, so pH changes the proportions of charged and neutral forms. Those forms interact differently with water and the stationary surface, changing retention. A buffer helps maintain the desired acidity, while its concentration and ion identity can also influence separation. Conditions must suit the analyte, the column and the detector. For example, nonvolatile salts have different practical consequences when the column is connected to mass spectrometry than when the detector simply measures ultraviolet absorbance.

![Original partition and flow-path diagrams. Two bands represent different average retention, illustrating the idea behind Martin and Synge’s partition chromatography. The right panel places pumping, injection, separation and detection in flow order; dimensions are schematic.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/9177064aa8cf9073e3111225.svg?v=9177064aa8cf)

Figure 1Original partition and flow-path diagrams. Two bands represent different average retention, illustrating the idea behind Martin and Synge’s partition chromatography. The right panel places pumping, injection, separation and detection in flow order; dimensions are schematic.

Follow a modern instrument in the direction of flow. Solvents are degassed, mixed and pumped; an injection system introduces a defined sample volume; the column separates; a detector measures the effluent before it reaches collection or waste. Pressure drives liquid through a bed of fine particles, but pressure itself does not identify compounds. Smaller particles can shorten some transport paths while increasing resistance to flow. Understanding these distinct functions prevents a common misconception: a higher-pressure instrument does not automatically separate two molecules with nearly identical interactions.

## Peak width matters as much as arrival time

Retention time runs from injection to the target peak maximum. It includes transit with the mobile phase and the additional delay caused by retention. A suitably detectable marker that is essentially unretained under the selected conditions can estimate the hold-up time, t₀. Subtracting t₀ from retention time and dividing by t₀ gives the retention factor, k. This separates ordinary passage time from additional retention. The marker and measurement geometry must suit the column-volume question; the first small feature in a chromatogram is not automatically a trustworthy hold-up marker.

$$
k=\frac{t_R-t_0}{t_0},\qquad t_R=t_0(1+k)
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/8dc6f7e80ecaac9fa07890ce.svg) | Retention factor under isocratic conditions, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/0dfa193aee7778fd0c1a71af.svg) | Target retention time, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a15f4e949d9181049b209fc5.svg) | Hold-up time from an appropriate unretained marker, min. |

Normalize additional retention by unretained transit. tR=4 min and t₀=1 min give k=3. Changing gradient composition requires more than a single constant k.

If t₀ is 1 min and a compound arrives at 4 min, its retention factor is 3. Total passage takes four times the unretained transit time, with three times that interval added through retention. A second compound with k=3.36 arrives at 4.36 min. The ratio of the larger to smaller retention factor is 1.12, called the selectivity for this pair. Selectivity expresses how differently the phases treat the compounds. If their retention factors are equal, making both wait longer does not create a difference between their mean arrival times. A change in discriminating interactions is needed.

Molecules of one compound arrive over a range of times because they experience different flow paths, diffusion and exchange histories. Two peak centers separated by 0.3 min can be easy to distinguish when peaks are narrow, but strongly overlap when both are broad. Resolution compares the center separation with their widths. State whether widths are measured at the baseline or at half maximum, because the corresponding formula coefficients differ. A numerical resolution value is meaningful only with a defined width convention.

$$
R_s=\frac{2(t_{R,2}-t_{R,1})}{w_1+w_2},\qquad \alpha=\frac{k_2}{k_1}\quad(k_2\geq k_1>0)
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/c29ea71c312c1c2bf08acd27.svg) | Resolution of the two peaks, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/43bdb088cbae6d3907fc9e8b.svg) | Earlier and later retention times, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/8959dc68ce37371df41f244e.svg) | Baseline peak widths, min; 4σ in the Gaussian model here. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7995b2daef1650484d2fa651.svg) | Selectivity, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/d62ad609310d0b90a08f3cae.svg) | Isocratic retention factors of the two compounds, dimensionless. |

Center separation relative to mean baseline width quantifies separation. Times 4 and 4.36 min and widths 0.32 and 0.3488 min give Rs≈1.07656. k values 3 and 3.36 give α=1.12. Tailing or unequal areas require inspection of the relevant integration interference.

The theoretical plate number, N, describes relative peak narrowness. It does not count physical shelves inside the column. For an approximately Gaussian peak, dividing retention time by its time standard deviation and squaring gives N. The standard deviation describes the spread of arrival times around their mean. If retention time stays fixed while width is halved, N increases fourfold. Under otherwise matched conditions, resolution then increases approximately twofold. Improving efficiency helps, but it acts differently from changing chemical selectivity.

$$
N=\left(\frac{t_R}{\sigma_t}\right)^2=16\left(\frac{t_R}{w}\right)^2
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/256531b7f0ddb14dd11a59a3.svg) | Theoretical plate count, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/0dfa193aee7778fd0c1a71af.svg) | Retention time, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/87de164e10556b3dda44460d.svg) | Standard deviation of Gaussian arrival-time distribution, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/5f85a26e5089def254fee2b9.svg) | Gaussian baseline width, taken as 4σt, min. |

For an approximately Gaussian peak under suitable isocratic conditions, relative width describes efficiency. tR=4 min and σt=0.08 min give N=2500; halving width at fixed retention gives N=10000. Extra-column dispersion also contributes to observed width.

![Constructed isocratic Gaussian peaks have unit area, t₀=1 min and k₁=3. A versus B changes only N; A versus C changes only selectivity. Resolution uses baseline widths of 4σ; the heatmap contour marks Rs=1.5.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/2f78881c5e500308f7f0648d.svg?v=2f78881c5e50)

Figure 2Constructed isocratic Gaussian peaks have unit area, t₀=1 min and k₁=3. A versus B changes only N; A versus C changes only selectivity. Resolution uses baseline widths of 4σ; the heatmap contour marks Rs=1.5.

The three chromatograms compare these routes. Initial conditions use N=2500 and selectivity 1.12. Increasing N to 10000 leaves centers unchanged but narrows the peaks. Keeping N=2500 while increasing selectivity to 1.30 moves the centers apart. The heatmap extends these combinations across a continuous range, with a white contour at model resolution 1.5. For similar-area, nearly symmetric Gaussian peaks, that is associated with good separation. A much smaller peak next to a large one, or a strongly tailing peak, calls for direct inspection of the interference relevant to its integration.

Flow also influences width. At slow flow, molecules have more time to diffuse along the column; at fast flow, exchange between environments may lag behind the moving liquid. Differences in paths contribute as well. These effects create a useful range of flow conditions. Doubling flow commonly shortens retention times, but also changes pressure, dispersion and detector sampling, so resolution need not improve. The interactive experiment first isolates efficiency and selectivity. Method development then connects those concepts to column length, particles, solvent, pH and temperature.

## Narrow the peaks or move them apart

Hold the first retention factor at 3 and compare efficiency, selectivity and time scale. Hold-up time only rescales this model; it does not predict how real flow affects efficiency.

[Figure: Interactive two-component chromatogram](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/c01/en/#C01-plot)

## Introducing the specimen in a suitable state

The chromatogram begins at injection, but the quantitative story starts earlier. Sampling uniformity, complete dissolution, adsorption to containers or filters, and decomposition during storage all affect how much target reaches the instrument. Turbid specimens generally need appropriate clarification to keep particles out of narrow flow paths. Centrifugation, filtration and extraction must also suit the analyte. A hydrophobic molecule may be retained by a filter, while a drug can be lost with precipitated protein. Preparation should protect the separation system and bring the target into a solution whose history can be followed.

Sample solvent can alter the chromatogram. A large injection dissolved in a strong reversed-phase eluent may begin moving before the analyte focuses into a narrow band at the column head. Broadening, splitting or fronting can follow. Raising concentration while keeping injection volume small is therefore not always equivalent to injecting a large volume of dilute solution. Excess sample mass can also exceed the linear capacity of the stationary phase, changing retention and shape with concentration. Comparing several injection amounts helps establish whether position, shape and area behave as expected.

Isocratic elution keeps mobile-phase composition constant during a run. It suits mixtures with a manageable retention range and supports the simple k and N relationships used here. Gradient elution changes composition with time, often increasing organic solvent in reversed-phase work to release strongly retained components. The retention behavior of a molecule then changes during its passage, so the run is not equivalent to an isocratic experiment with one fixed k. After the gradient, the column must return to and equilibrate at its initial conditions before the next comparable injection.

A changed pump composition does not instantly reach the column. Mixer, tubing and injection-system volume must first be traversed. With a gradient delay volume of 0.75 mL and flow of 0.50 mL/min, the delay is 1.5 min. Two instruments running the same programmed gradient can consequently deliver different composition histories at their column entrances. Method transfer should compare actual gradient arrival and system volume. The figure shows two curves with the same slope but different arrival times, distinguishing this system effect from separation within the column.

The detector must respond appropriately to the analyte. Ultraviolet detection suits compounds absorbing at the selected wavelength; a diode-array detector records a range of wavelengths. Fluorescence detection suits intrinsically fluorescent or suitably labeled targets. Refractive-index and other detectors can help with compounds lacking strong ultraviolet absorption, but have their own mobile-phase requirements. Mass spectrometry adds mass and fragmentation information. Choosing a convenient wavelength is only one decision: solvent background, analyte response, neighboring components and the working concentration together determine whether detection is adequate.

Sampling speed also matters for narrow peaks. If the detector records too few points while a component passes, a peak may look angular and its measured height or area may depend on timing. Extra tubing and a large detector cell can broaden a band after it has left an efficient column. A short, fast separation therefore requires the whole flow path and detector configuration to preserve the resolution achieved inside the column. This explains why transferring a method involves more than copying the column name and solvent ratio.

## From one peak to the amount in the original specimen

Measure an authentic standard under matched conditions to compare retention time. Adding a small amount of the standard to the sample and observing the corresponding increase can further help locate the target. Different compounds can coelute, producing one visually tidy peak. Comparing spectra across the front, apex and tail, changing separation conditions or adding mass-spectral information provides additional evidence. Retention time is a condition-dependent identity clue, and coordinated observations strengthen the assignment.

Area measurement begins with the baseline, the signal expected when the target is absent. A slowly varying background can be estimated from nearby intervals free of other components, then subtracted before integration. A narrow window loses the peak wings; an excessively wide window can include neighboring components and baseline error. The window experiment demonstrates that enclosing the tallest part still misses considerable area. Tailing and overlapping peaks require a defined integration rule applied consistently and checked across the intended concentration range.

External calibration measures known concentrations of the same analyte with matched injection and detection conditions. The example uses six concentrations with three constructed repeats per level and fits a straight line. Its slope gives the mean area increase per concentration unit; its intercept represents the near-zero offset. Blank behavior, residuals and error structure guide whether to retain an intercept or use weighting. Forcing a line through zero simply because that looks convenient can change an unknown result. Samples should fall within the verified calibration range, with accurate dilution used when necessary.

$$
A=mc+b,\qquad c_{\mathrm{original}}=D\frac{A_{\mathrm{unknown}}-b}{m}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/88c650b4e9eb956a41e222a9.svg) | Target peak area for calibration or unknown, mAU min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/528857d51fe0ca9fb1f0a19e.svg) | Calibration slope, (mAU min)/(micrograms/mL). |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/b332ba26d1b8a3e4b8f817ed.svg) | Analyte concentration in the injected vial, micrograms/mL. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a77a353782459b753313d802.svg) | Calibration intercept, mAU min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75.svg) | Total dilution factor from original solution to injected vial, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/994c7009d659d06ee37650ec.svg) | Original solution concentration, micrograms/mL. |

Invert the response within a verified linear range, then apply dilution. m=6, b=0.8, A=78.8 and D=4 give 13 micrograms/mL in the vial and 52 micrograms/mL originally. The program computes nearby results from noisy calibration and integration.

![Constructed quantitative experiment with a fixed seed. The true unknown concentration is 13 micrograms/mL; calibration uses three repeats per level. Shading marks the target integration interval. Residuals are measured calibration areas minus fitted areas. The final panel varies the integration window to show the contribution of peak wings.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/d06234bc7b39e67a85b99ad8.svg?v=d06234bc7b39)

Figure 3Constructed quantitative experiment with a fixed seed. The true unknown concentration is 13 micrograms/mL; calibration uses three repeats per level. Shading marks the target integration interval. Residuals are measured calibration areas minus fitted areas. The final panel varies the integration window to show the contribution of peak wings.

The teaching relationship is approximately area equals six times concentration plus 0.8. Concentration is in micrograms per milliliter, and area is in mAU min, where mAU means one thousandth of an absorbance unit. The constructed unknown contains 13 micrograms per milliliter; integration and calibration recover a nearby value. If that solution came from a fourfold dilution, the original concentration is approximately 52 micrograms per milliliter. Fourfold means final volume divided by the volume of original solution taken, not added-solvent volume divided by original volume. Recording aliquots, final volumes and subsequent dilutions keeps the conversion connected to the specimen.

Reporting content within a material requires further accounting. Multiply extract concentration by total extract volume, then divide by extracted material mass. An original extract at 52 micrograms per milliliter in 10 mL contains 520 micrograms. If it came from 0.20 g of material, the content is 2600 micrograms per gram, or 2.6 milligrams per gram. Units cancel or remain in meaningful ways at each step, making dimensional checks part of the reasoning. A peak representing 90% of total detector area is a detector-area fraction; compounds with unequal responses prevent automatic interpretation as 90% mass purity.

Internal calibration adds a known amount of another suitable compound to standards and samples and uses the ratio of analyte to internal-standard areas. A globally larger or smaller injection changes both signals, so their ratio reduces that source of variation. The internal standard should be stable, absent from the specimen or distinguishable, and separated from target and matrix peaks. Tracking extraction loss additionally requires adding it before the relevant preparation step and demonstrating comparable recovery behavior. Adding it after extraction helps only with subsequent steps. A spike-recovery experiment adds the analyte itself to investigate measured recovery; it answers a different question.

## What should accompany a convincing calibration line?

A straight calibration line indicates that the selected model describes the measured standards over that range. Extraction loss, coelution and degradation while samples wait for injection require additional observations. Place checks where the relevant errors arise: solvent blanks examine system background, preparation blanks examine reagents and containers, blanks after concentrated samples examine carryover, and independently prepared check samples evaluate measurement after calibration. These controls have distinct purposes and make a changed result easier to diagnose.

Recovery provides an intuitive preparation check. Compare two equivalent specimens, adding a known amount of analyte to one before extraction. Subtract the unspiked result from the spiked result and divide by the added amount. If a 10 microgram addition produces an 8.5 microgram increase, the recovery is 85%. This characterizes how much of the added analyte becomes measurable under the tested concentration, matrix and processing conditions. Repeating the comparison after changing a container, extraction condition or filter turns an observed loss into an experimentally addressable step.

$$
\mathrm{Recovery}=\frac{q_{\mathrm{spiked}}-q_{\mathrm{unspiked}}}{q_{\mathrm{added}}}\times100\%
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/da2911810e849da2f484a127.svg) | Spike recovery percentage, %. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/340607043a312e60188e2839.svg) | Measured analyte amount in the spiked specimen, micrograms. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/17a361682607930130ab2ca5.svg) | Measured amount in the corresponding unspiked specimen, micrograms. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/2ed64c2d28a6fe11e9f25433.svg) | Known amount added before the relevant processing step, micrograms. |

Subtract the original contribution and compare the increment with the added amount. An 8.5 microgram increase from a 10 microgram spike gives 85%. Specimens and final volumes must be comparable, with spike timing defined.

Precision and recovery answer related but different questions. Three values close to 85% describe a relatively stable loss; values of 60%, 85% and 105% point to variation or interference. A stable bias and a variable process affect research differently. Analyte originally embedded in a complex material may not behave exactly like a freely added spike. Different addition times, repeated extraction or suitable reference materials can bring validation closer to the behavior of the original specimen. A correction becomes useful when its physical basis matches the preparation being corrected.

The calibration residual plot preserves each repeat's deviation from the fitted line. Residuals on one side at low concentration and the other at high concentration can reveal an unsuitable linear range or model. Increasing error with concentration motivates examination of weighting. For a real sample sequence, retention time, check-sample concentration and pressure plotted against injection order can reveal trends or abrupt changes. Such plots help distinguish gradual column changes, solvent problems and isolated injection events.

Replicate structure should also match the claim. Reinjecting one vial measures injection and short-term instrument variation. Preparing several aliquots examines preparation variation. Sampling independent specimens addresses variation in the material or biological process. Keeping those levels separate helps explain whether a small difference between formulations reflects repeatable material behavior or simply a repeatable measurement on one prepared solution. The useful outcome is an uncertainty statement tied to the actual experimental unit.

Before an analytical sequence, a standard mixture can test whether the system still separates the important pair, gives the expected retention behavior and produces repeatable areas. Define those checks around the task. A method for a trace impurity beside a dominant main component places different demands on separation from a method measuring two similarly abundant compounds. If the check changes, examine solvent preparation, leaks, temperature, column condition and injection settings in a controlled order. Changing several settings at once can produce a better-looking chromatogram while obscuring the reason for improvement. A short sequence containing a blank, standards, a check sample, unknowns and periodic checks turns the run into a coherent comparison rather than a collection of unrelated traces.

A fixed seed generates labeled teaching data and saves all figures, calibration repeats, the unknown chromatogram and release-sampling table.

## When concentration becomes a materials result

Drug-release measurements show why a reliable concentration still needs an experiment-specific mass balance. Suppose a material sits in 10 mL of liquid. At each sampling time, 1 mL is removed for analysis and replaced with 1 mL of drug-free liquid. Before the third withdrawal, the mass remaining in the vessel is the current concentration multiplied by 10 mL. Drug removed during the first two withdrawals has already left the vessel and must be added back when calculating cumulative release. Ignoring it particularly underestimates experiments with early release or frequent sampling.

$$
M_n=Vc_n+v\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}c_i
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4f3c9d3ab8208b50c9e81e73.svg) | Cumulative released mass before sampling event n, micrograms. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/bef27a67f1f86637c8224c0d.svg) | Total vessel volume restored after each replacement, mL. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/31eea81269f83b010cbeea2c.svg) | Concentrations in the mixed liquid before the corresponding withdrawals, micrograms/mL. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/6ea26af94b3e02fd7aa1d744.svg) | Fixed withdrawn volume at each event, mL. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/532fd9de01c5518cbb6ef73b.svg) | Sampling indices, dimensionless; the sum covers earlier withdrawals only. |

Cumulative mass equals current vessel mass plus previously removed mass. V=10 mL, v=1 mL and c₁/c₂/c₃=2/5/8 micrograms/mL give M₃=80+2+5=87 micrograms. Assumes mixing, equal analyte-free replacement and appropriate treatment of degradation or other losses.

If the first three concentrations are 2, 5 and 8 micrograms per milliliter, the vessel contains 80 micrograms just before the third sample. Earlier withdrawals removed 2+5=7 micrograms, giving 87 micrograms cumulative release. The arithmetic assumes thorough mixing, known withdrawal volume, analyte-free replacement liquid, restoration of the 10 mL total volume and no substantial degradation or other consumption of the counted analyte. If degradation occurs, measuring the parent compound and degradation products can establish a fuller account of material fate.

![Three defined teaching calculations. Gradient delay is 0.75 mL / 0.50 mL/min=1.5 min; spike recovery is modeled at 85%; a 10 mL release vessel is sampled by 1 mL withdrawals with analyte-free replacement, giving 87 micrograms cumulative release before the third withdrawal.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/4f484d06cdaecffd647bc61e.svg?v=4f484d06cdae)

Figure 4Three defined teaching calculations. Gradient delay is 0.75 mL / 0.50 mL/min=1.5 min; spike recovery is modeled at 85%; a 10 mL release vessel is sampled by 1 mL withdrawals with analyte-free replacement, giving 87 micrograms cumulative release before the third withdrawal.

Extraction experiments similarly distinguish the amount released into a defined medium from the total amount originally present in the material. Temperature, medium, exposure duration, surface area and liquid volume affect the result. Comparing formulations requires matching these conditions to the same research question. Residual-monomer content calls for sufficiently complete extraction with appropriate recovery validation. Migration during use calls for a contact experiment representing that use. The same chromatographic signal can serve different questions, and the reported quantity should follow the experimental definition.

Analytical measurement and preparative collection use the same separation idea with different priorities. An analytical injection uses a small amount to estimate composition or concentration. A preparative run collects a useful quantity of the desired material, so loading capacity, collection boundaries, recovery and solvent removal become central. Collecting only the middle of a peak can improve purity while reducing recovered amount; collecting the full band may recover more material together with neighboring impurities. If the purpose is to purify a peptide or additive for later experiments, examine the collected fraction again under an appropriate analytical method and relate recovered mass to the amount initially loaded. The chromatogram then guides a physical separation rather than merely reporting a number.

The final description connects preparation, separation, detection wavelength, calibration range, integration and quality checks into a reproducible account. Retain raw chromatograms alongside processed area tables so each concentration has an inspectable basis. When improving the experiment, locate the issue before injection, during separation, at detection or in conversion back to the original specimen. HPLC earns its place by turning a complicated mixture into temporally distinguishable components and reconnecting those components to a defined chemical, biological or materials question.

# 体积排阻色谱：聚合物分子有多大

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/c02/
Language: zh-CN

让溶解的链通过多孔空间，读懂尺寸分离、质量加权和一整群分子的分布。

## 同样叫聚合物，为什么一瓶很稠，另一瓶很稀

把两份透明质酸粉末各称取相同质量，加入同样多的水，得到的溶液可能有不同的黏稠程度。化学名称相同，只说明构成链的基本单元相同，并没有告诉我们每条链包含多少个单元。可以把它们想成由相同珠子串成的项链：一盒以短项链为主，另一盒混有少量很长的项链，盒子的总质量相同，拿起和缠绕时的表现仍会不同。真实溶液还受浓度、盐、温度和链间作用影响；要追问链长是否发生了变化，就需要一种能把不同大小的溶解分子逐渐分开的测量。体积排阻色谱，简称 SEC，正适合承担这个环节。

这个问题在生物实验里也很常见。一瓶蛋白质可能同时含有单个蛋白、两个蛋白结合形成的二聚体，以及更大的聚集体；凝胶过滤可以帮助分开这些组分，并收集后续实验需要的部分。在材料研究中，可降解聚合物经过一段时间后，外观可能依旧完整，链却已经断成较短片段。测量降解前后的 SEC 分布，能够把“外观看起来差不多”推进到“可溶部分的链群体怎样变化”。这里的可溶部分是一个实验对象：如果样品中还有未溶解网络或沉淀，就应同时称量、观察和记录它们，才能把色谱结果放回完整材料的质量平衡中。

SEC 的中文名称是体积排阻色谱。凝胶渗透色谱 GPC 常用于有机溶剂中的聚合物分析，凝胶过滤色谱 GFC 常用于水溶液中的生物大分子分离；三个名称背后共享同一种核心机制。柱内装满带有孔道的颗粒，不同大小的溶解分子能够访问不同数量的孔内空间，因此流出柱子的平均位置不同。仪器首先给出的是信号随洗脱时间或洗脱体积的变化。把这个位置转换成摩尔质量，还需要校准或联用检测器。理解这两步的分工，之后看到一个标有“分子量”的横坐标，就会自然追问它是怎样建立起来的。

本章沿着一份样品进入色谱柱的过程展开：先理解为什么大分子反而先出来，再认识校准曲线，接着区分按分子个数和按质量得到的平均值。我们会一起读一组公开发表的聚乙烯累计分布，并用完整程序把孔道机制、标准曲线、原始形式的色谱信号和积分选择连起来。学完以后，应能解释一条曲线的横纵坐标，判断一次峰位移动可能意味着什么，并为下一次实验选择有用的对照。

## 大分子先出来：多孔小球里的“侧边房间”

想象一条走廊，两侧有许多小房间。两组参观者从同一个入口出发：一组只能沿走廊前进，另一组还会进入沿途房间停留。即使两组在走廊里的移动方式相同，第二组平均也会更晚到达出口。SEC 中，颗粒之间的液体类似走廊，颗粒内部的孔道类似房间。较大的溶解分子能进入的孔内空间较少，较小的分子能进入较多空间，于是前者通常更早洗脱。这里并不是把大分子强行压过一个筛孔，也不是小分子被堵在出口；分离来自分子在可访问溶剂空间之间的分配。

这段历史很能帮助人摆脱“筛子总让小东西先通过”的直觉。耶克·波拉特在回顾早期研究时提到，即使没有施加电泳所用的电流，淀粉柱中不同分子仍出现分离。后来，波拉特与佩尔·弗洛丁研究交联葡聚糖凝胶，相关工作发表于 1959 年。孔道能够把大分子和小分子盐分开，成为蛋白质脱盐的重要工具。图中的柱和信号是围绕这个机制绘制的示意：大分子先形成一个流出带，盐随后出现。它表现的是脱盐的物理思路，曲线数值由本章构造，并非早期实验的复刻。

为了给“能够进入多少空间”一个量化尺度，先测两个参照体积。完全不能进入孔道、且不与填料发生额外作用的标记，提供排阻体积 V₀；足够小、能够访问全部相关孔内液体的标记，提供总可达体积 Vₜ。这里的 Vₜ 是由合适标记测得的色谱体积，不是拿直尺量柱子外壳之后算出的圆柱体积。目标分子的洗脱体积 Vₑ 落在两者之间时，可把它多访问的体积除以可供访问的孔体积，得到无量纲的 Kₐᵥ。下式把类比中的“进入了一部分房间”变成一个可比较的测量。

$$
K_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{V_e-V_0}{V_t-V_0}
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/17929f84b05c9c9ee6b7954d.svg) | 表观孔体积可达比例，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/daa1e83231d13f3a99351353.svg) | 目标分子的洗脱体积，mL。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/454606841ec20ef0f43cd9f6.svg) | 完全排阻的合适标记测得的体积，mL。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/ad460123890fe451611439a3.svg) | 完全进入相关孔空间的合适标记测得的总可达体积，mL。 |

在大小排阻主导且参照标记适合时，以多访问的体积除以孔内可达体积。Vₑ=9、V₀=3、Vₜ=18 mL，Kav=6/15=0.4。0 与 1 对应两端参照；额外吸附或排斥会改变这个解释。

![原创孔道与脱盐机制示意。颗粒间与孔内空间不按真实尺度绘制；B 为构造脱盐曲线，连接 1959 年凝胶过滤的机制。C 用 V₀=3、Vₜ=18 mL 展示可达比例。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/332d0565684a77299bb67fb8.svg?v=332d0565684a)

图 1原创孔道与脱盐机制示意。颗粒间与孔内空间不按真实尺度绘制；B 为构造脱盐曲线，连接 1959 年凝胶过滤的机制。C 用 V₀=3、Vₜ=18 mL 展示可达比例。

当目标大到几乎所有孔都进不去时，不同的大分子可能一起在 V₀ 附近流出；当目标小到能够访问几乎所有孔时，不同的小分子也可能一起靠近 Vₜ。真正适合按大小区分的区域在两端之间，这就是选择填料孔径范围的原因。把一根适合分离盐与蛋白质的脱盐柱，直接拿来精细区分两个大小相近的蛋白质，往往得不到同样的分离效果。前者要求把两大组分开，后者要求在很窄的大小差别上获得足够的位置差异，还需要较小的进样体积和更高的柱效。

真实分子还会与孔壁发生静电、疏水或其他相互作用。例如，带电的多糖在盐浓度很低时，链可能伸展得更开，也可能受到填料表面电荷影响。两种效应都能改变峰位，因此增加盐后峰位变化并不自动等于链断了。建立方法时，可以通过合适的缓冲液、离子强度和填料化学，尽量让大小分配成为主要保留机制，再用浓度系列和已知样品检查这一判断。类比帮助我们理解机制，实验对照则负责检查真实体系是否满足它。

## 从流出位置到摩尔质量，中间要搭一把尺子

检测器看到某个峰出现在 10 mL，并不会直接知道它是一万还是十万克每摩尔。常规校准的做法，是让一组摩尔质量已知、分布较窄的标准聚合物分别通过同一套系统，记录每个标准的峰位。在适当的工作范围内，摩尔质量的十进对数往往与洗脱体积近似呈线性关系。对数在这里相当于把“乘十倍”变成相同的刻度间隔，使几千、几万、几十万能够放在一张图里清楚比较。图中的标准点从小质量到大质量依次向较小的洗脱体积移动，正与前面的孔道机制一致。

1964 年，约翰·摩尔发表了以交联聚苯乙烯凝胶进行聚合物分离的工作，GPC 随后把聚合物分布测量变成更连续的仪器过程。这个发展也把校准问题推到了中心：记录一条流出曲线只是第一步，必须知道曲线上每个位置对应什么样的分子。我们用一条教学标准曲线说明计算，斜率表示洗脱体积每变化 1 mL，对数摩尔质量变化多少；截距则决定整把尺子在纵向的位置。实际方法应使用标准样覆盖目标分布，观察残差和两端弯曲，而不是为了让公式简单，强行把整个柱范围拟合成直线。

$$
\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{M}{1\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}\right)=a-bV_e
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/34058a2a5d1de088feed7d98.svg) | 校准赋予的摩尔质量，g/mol。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/349015631ec44ef653936c85.svg) | 线性校准截距，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a77a353782459b753313d802.svg) | 校准下降斜率的大小，mL⁻¹。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/daa1e83231d13f3a99351353.svg) | 洗脱体积，mL。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/be8ebdecd039424afe275a60.svg) | 十进对数；括号内先除以单位量，使其无量纲。 |

在标准覆盖、近似线性的分离范围内，以对数连接大小位置与标准质量。a=7、b=0.25 mL⁻¹、Vₑ=10 mL，log₁₀ M=4.5，对应约 31,623 g/mol；Vₑ=12 mL 对应 10,000 g/mol。同一化学系列与溶液条件支持该转换。

![构造标准与链群体：log₁₀ M 的数量分布均值 4.2、标准差 0.35，质量分布随权重改变。色谱额外展宽 σV=0.25 mL，面积归一化为 1。D 按流出顺序累计，从大分子到小分子。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/da13b991941f2f714ab8cc5b.svg?v=da13b991941f)

图 2构造标准与链群体：log₁₀ M 的数量分布均值 4.2、标准差 0.35，质量分布随权重改变。色谱额外展宽 σV=0.25 mL，面积归一化为 1。D 按流出顺序累计，从大分子到小分子。

标准的化学结构很重要。两条质量相同的链，如果一种在溶剂里伸展较开，另一种较紧凑，就会访问不同的孔内空间。一个支化聚合物与同质量的线性聚合物也可能表现出不同的溶液尺寸。因此，用聚苯乙烯标准校准未知聚合物时，直接得到的是该条件下的聚苯乙烯等效摩尔质量。把“等效”写清楚，相当于告诉读者尺子的刻度依据；它也让不同实验室的结果更容易比较。若研究的重点是链支化前后真实质量是否改变，单靠同一把尺寸尺还需要补上其他测量。

差示折光检测器常与 SEC 配合。它比较流出溶液与纯流动相的折射率差；在给定聚合物、溶剂和温度下，稀溶液的响应可与浓度联系起来。于是每一个小体积切片下面的信号面积可以表示该切片携带的质量。紫外检测器则只对能吸收所选波长的组分产生相应信号，同一混合物里不同组分的吸收能力可能不同。一个蛋白质与一个几乎没有该波长吸收的多糖即使同时流出，在紫外图上也不会自动按质量公平显示。解释峰面积之前，要先回答检测器对什么敏感，以及这种敏感度在各组分之间是否一致。

联用多角度光散射与浓度检测器，可以进一步从散射强度、角度和浓度推求各切片的摩尔质量，减少对同类标准校准的依赖。浓度测量所需的折射率增量、检测器之间的时间对齐、峰展宽以及尘埃或聚集体的贡献，都仍是数据链的一部分。把它称为不依赖常规分子量标准的测量，比把“绝对分子量”理解成完全不需要假设更有帮助。对于初次分析，先学会常规校准和质量响应，之后再加入联用检测器，推理会连贯得多。

## 一群长短不同的链，为什么需要两个平均值

假设一份样品只有两种链：九十条链的摩尔质量都是 10,000 g/mol，十条链都是 100,000 g/mol。按链数看，短链占九成；按质量看，十条长链贡献的质量反而略多于九十条短链。这里使用摩尔质量，是指一摩尔这类链的质量；g/mol 是单位，数值随链长增加。描述这群链时，我们可以让每条链各投一票，得到数均摩尔质量 Mₙ；也可以让每份质量各投一票，得到重均摩尔质量 M𝑤。两种平均都正确，差别在于研究问题选择了怎样的权重。

数均值的计算最接近日常的平均数：把各类链的数量乘以相应摩尔质量，全部加起来，再除以总链数。上面的例子得到 19,000 g/mol。它不是“有一半链比它轻、另一半比它重”的分界；那个分界叫中位数。在这组离散例子里，按链数的中位数是 10,000 g/mol，因为九成的链都在这里。把平均数与中位数区分开，对阅读宽分布尤其重要：少量长链能够推高平均数，而多数链仍可能较短。

$$
M_n=\frac{\sum_i N_iM_i}{\sum_i N_i}=\left(\sum_i\frac{w_i}{M_i}\right)^{-1},\qquad w_i=\frac{N_iM_i}{\sum_j N_jM_j}
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4f3c9d3ab8208b50c9e81e73.svg) | 数均摩尔质量，g/mol。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/2e48d6441cb55e92796c4f28.svg) | 对应类别中的链数，无量纲计数。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/80f8ce36f42008dae6d1d510.svg) | 对应类别的摩尔质量，g/mol。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/cec5f0994a4bad5c3ac4a9a4.svg) | 类别 i 的质量分数，无量纲，各类之和为 1。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/1f848077b31e64f57fc97f4b.svg) | 对所有相关链类别或质量切片求和的索引。 |

每条链等权平均；从质量切片出发，质量除以摩尔质量得到与链数成比例的权重。90 条 10,000 和 10 条 100,000 g/mol 的链给出 Mn=19,000 g/mol。质量分数分别为 9/19 与 10/19。

重均值则先问每一类链贡献多少质量，再用这些质量比例去平均摩尔质量。长链既有较大的摩尔质量，又贡献较大的质量权重，因此高质量尾部对 M𝑤 的影响更显著。同一个例子得到约 57,368 g/mol，明显高于 Mₙ。把两者相除得到分散系数 Đ，描述这两种加权平均相差多少。所有链完全相同时，两种平均相等，Đ 为 1；存在链长差异时，重均值通常更大。本例的 Đ 约为 3.019。这个数字概括了分布宽度的一个方面，但两条形状不同的分布仍可能具有相同的比值。

$$
M_w=\sum_i w_iM_i=\frac{\sum_iN_iM_i^2}{\sum_iN_iM_i},\qquad \mathit{Đ}=\frac{M_w}{M_n}
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/584328b60ee68abee6861462.svg) | 重均摩尔质量，g/mol。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/cec5f0994a4bad5c3ac4a9a4.svg) | 类别 i 的质量分数，无量纲，总和为 1。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/b26e60e55288c9229968cad0.svg) | 类别 i 的链数。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9b5817fb0c0bac5188945802.svg) | 类别 i 的摩尔质量，g/mol。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4f3c9d3ab8208b50c9e81e73.svg) | 数均摩尔质量，g/mol。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/40bf2c4da5241a580e5118bc.svg) | 分散系数，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/33f73a318016d781b6ae1aa9.svg) | 链类别或质量切片索引。 |

每份质量等权平均，长链的权重更大。同一 90:10 例得到 Mw≈57,368.42 g/mol，Đ≈3.01939。比较同一完整群体、非负权重时 Đ≥1；仪器展宽和截断积分会改变表观值。

SEC 的浓度型检测器通常先提供质量信息，而不是直接数出链的条数。要由质量切片求 Mₙ，就需要先用切片质量除以该处的摩尔质量，得到与链数成比例的量，再进行总质量除以总链数的计算。因此低摩尔质量尾部虽然质量不大，却可能代表很多条链，对 Mₙ 很有影响。图中同一构造群体的按数目分布和按质量分布，峰位并不重合；这不是画错，而是权重改变后自然产生的结果。软件导出“distribution”时，应读清它究竟按数量、质量、线性质量轴还是对数质量轴归一化。

现在看真实数据。罗斯与弗洛伦在 1972 年发表的 NBS 聚乙烯 SRM 1475 研究，给出了累计质量百分数随对数摩尔质量的表格。图中点直接对应公开表格的数字，纵轴回答“低于这个摩尔质量的聚合物，占总质量的百分之几”。本章用相邻点在对数轴上作线性插值，读出质量中位数；它与论文报告的 Mₙ 和 M𝑤 是不同的统计量。累计曲线从低质量向高质量累加，也与色谱图中从先流出的大分子向后累加的方向不同。读懂轴的方向，才能把一张真实的旧表格准确地转换成新的图。

![A 重绘 Ross 与 Frolen（NBS，1972）表 4 的真实累计质量数据；质量中位数由对数轴线性插值得到，原表印刷数值全部保留。B 是独立构造例：90 条 10,000 g/mol 短链和 10 条 100,000 g/mol 长链，比较链数与质量百分比。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/6f9862f4014067ff892935bf.svg?v=6f9862f40140)

图 3A 重绘 Ross 与 Frolen（NBS，1972）表 4 的真实累计质量数据；质量中位数由对数轴线性插值得到，原表印刷数值全部保留。B 是独立构造例：90 条 10,000 g/mol 短链和 10 条 100,000 g/mol 长链，比较链数与质量百分比。

## 真正进入色谱柱的，是经过制备的一份样品

一个聚合物粉末消失在液体里，并不一定意味着所有链都已经达到稳定、均匀的溶解状态。高摩尔质量组分可能溶解较慢，交联微凝胶可能只吸液膨胀，蛋白质可能在等待期间发生聚集。制备时要选择能够溶解目标、又与填料和检测器相容的流动相，并给出温度、时间和混合方式。对于容易受到机械剪切影响的大分子，过强的处理本身就可能改变分布；对于不稳定蛋白质，温度和缓冲条件又关系到构象与聚集状态。样品准备因此属于测量定义，而不是进样之前可以省略描述的杂务。

过滤可以去除堵柱颗粒，也可能改变我们准备测量的群体。若聚集体或高质量组分被滤膜截留，后面的色谱就只代表通过滤膜的部分；若目标吸附在膜上，回收量还会下降。可以将过滤前后浓度、可见沉淀、过滤器材质与样品回收联系起来检查。对于要研究可溶聚集体的蛋白质，选用合适的澄清步骤，并比较回收和尺寸分布，比把所有大颗粒统一移除后再宣称样品完全单一更有解释力。对难溶网络材料，记录可溶分数同样关键，因为柱子只接收溶液里的组分。

进样体积决定初始样品带有多宽。若一开始就注入很长的一段样品，即使孔道能够让不同组分产生位置差，最后也可能互相重叠。浓度过高还会改变溶液黏度、链间相互作用或局部流动，使峰形和位置出现浓度依赖。一个有用的小实验，是在其他条件不变时，改变进样浓度或体积并比较归一化曲线。若位置和形状稳定，浓度型检测器的面积又按加入量增加，就为所选条件提供了支持。若稀释后早出峰减少，则应同时考虑聚集平衡变化，而不仅是仪器负荷降低。

空白、窄分布标准和稳定参考样分别回答不同问题。溶剂空白帮助识别流动相或进样溶剂引起的系统峰；窄分布标准检查峰位与仪器展宽；稳定参考样监测整套方法的长期一致性。差示折光检测对温度与流动相差异敏感，充分平衡和稳定基线对积分尤其重要。用不同于流动相的溶剂配样，会把一个溶剂扰动与样品一起送进检测器。若它刚好落在低质量尾部，自动积分可能把它当成很多短链。比较空白图、样品图和标准图，能让这个问题在计算平均值之前就显现出来。

保存完整原始时间信号和实际流量，还有一个很实用的理由：时间与体积不是同一个量。流量稳定时，流过体积可由流量乘经过时间得到；比较不同流量下的峰位，宜先在统一的体积坐标上检查。过高流量可能增加某些展宽贡献，也可能使很大的链受到剪切作用。选择条件应围绕所需分辨率、样品稳定性和可用分析时间，而不是单纯把出峰越快当成越好。

## 峰变宽、峰移动，各自怎样影响结论

仪器会把一群到达时间非常接近的分子摊开。流动路径差异、孔内外交换、连接管路和检测池都可以贡献展宽。因此测得的宽度包含样品本来的分布，也包含系统增加的宽度。对于一个很窄的标准样，这个问题格外显眼；对于一个很宽的真实样品，仪器增加的部分可能相对较小。图中的模型让同一个链群体通过三种额外展宽条件，保持总面积和平均流出位置不变，只改变信号的宽度。把所有宽度都当成链长差异，计算出的分散系数就会升高。

另一种容易混淆的变化是整体峰位移动。设同质量的链因构象更紧凑而向后移动 0.5 mL，仍用原来的标准曲线换算，所有表观摩尔质量都会乘上约 0.750 的因子。图中的这一步没有让任何化学键断裂，却产生了约四分之一的表观质量下降。这说明研究链降解时，溶剂、盐、温度和标准校准应尽量保持可比，并结合反应化学、端基信息或其他检测结果来建立解释。若研究本来关注构象变化，峰位移动本身又成为有价值的信号，只是应把它放在尺寸变化的问题里。

积分范围也会悄悄改变答案。色谱后段对应较小的分子，删去这段信号会删掉相当数量的短链，使 Mₙ 升高。早段的高质量尾部即使面积较小，也可能对 M𝑤 产生明显影响。一个可复查的分析应同时展示原始信号、所选基线、积分起止点和换算曲线，再比较合理范围内改变这些选择后结果的变化。图中的积分终点扫描保留前段不变，只逐渐纳入低质量尾部，清楚显示两个平均值并不同步收敛。这样便能把“软件显示一个数字”变成“知道这个数字受哪些选择影响”。

![同一构造链群体的四种诊断。A、B 只增加高斯仪器展宽；C 只平移峰位，按原标准换算；D 只改变积分终点。各曲线揭示不同计算选择如何影响表观分布，未把这些变化当作实测降解。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/44c18f54d8175d084d7a5ad9.svg?v=44c18f54d817)

图 4同一构造链群体的四种诊断。A、B 只增加高斯仪器展宽；C 只平移峰位，按原标准换算；D 只改变积分终点。各曲线揭示不同计算选择如何影响表观分布，未把这些变化当作实测降解。

下面的交互实验保留两种真实链质量，分别为 10,000 和 100,000 g/mol。先改变长链的数量比例，观察数量很少的长链何时已经占据显著质量；再增加仪器展宽，比较真实与表观平均值；最后移动整个流出位置，模拟尺寸与标准不匹配造成的统一换算偏差。三个控制量回答不同问题，图上可以出现相似的变化，真实链群体却并不总是相同。先只动一个控制量并预测方向，再看计算结果，会比同时拖动所有滑块更容易建立因果关系。

## 同一群链怎样变成不同的表观分布

两种链为 10,000 和 100,000 g/mol。只改变一个控制量，比较真实与表观平均值。高斯展宽与统一峰位移动是这里明确定义的测量模型。

[Figure: 质量加权双峰色谱交互图](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/c02/#C02-plot)

若一个新样品出现很早的肩峰，可以据此设计下一步：检查它是否接近排阻边界，降低进样量确认峰形，改变适当的溶液条件观察聚集是否可逆，再收集该组分进行其他分析。若整个主峰稳定向后移动，首先核对标准和流动条件，然后围绕降解或构象改变选择补充测量。每一种后续动作都对应一个具体解释，SEC 就成为研究路径中的分流点，而不只是最后附上一张曲线。

## 把一条曲线变成能重新检查的完整分析

完整例子同时包含构造模型和公开数据，两者在图注与文件中分别标明。构造模型从一群对数摩尔质量呈正态分布的链出发，计算按质量加权后的色谱，再人为加入可控的仪器展宽。因此可以比较输入的真实平均值与测量模型输出的表观平均值，检查偏差究竟从哪里产生。公开数据部分读取 NBS 表格的累计质量百分数，保留原表的非均匀横坐标和舍入数字，不把它伪装成原始检测器信号。程序会把标准、色谱、展宽扫描和积分范围扫描保存为表格，便于逐项核对。

阅读代码时，建议先找到体积坐标和校准函数，再找到信号面积如何归一化，最后看两个平均值的积分。每个小切片都先有一个质量权重，除以该位置的摩尔质量才能得到与数量有关的权重。这里用数值积分近似连续曲线下面积，坐标间隔已经包含在计算中；若换成间距不均匀的真实采样数据，仍应让积分函数接收实际横坐标。把所有点的高度直接相加，只在间距相同且比例因子能够抵消时才有相应含义。

### 完整 SEC 分布、校准和诊断例子

构造模型与真实公开累计数据分别处理；输出四幅图及可复查的标准、色谱、展宽和积分表。

```
"""SEC/GPC: porous exclusion, calibration, mass weighting and real NBS data.

# Original mechanism drawing. Side pores hold solvent; macromolecules exchange
# with accessible pore volume. They are not forced through a sieve membrane.

# Constructed narrow-standard calibration and lognormal molecular population.
a,b=7.,.25;standards=np.array([1e3,3e3,1e4,3e4,1e5,3e5,1e6]);ve=(a-np.log10(standards))/b
mu,s=4.2,.35;ln10=np.log(10);mass_mu=mu+ln10*s*s
V=np.linspace(2,20,6001);M=10**(a-b*V);ideal=gauss(V,(a-mass_mu)/b,s/b)
def moments(signal):
    area=np.trapezoid(signal,V)
    return float(area/np.trapezoid(signal/M,V)),float(np.trapezoid(signal*M,V)/area)
Mn=10**mu*np.exp(.5*(ln10*s)**2);Mw=10**mu*np.exp(1.5*(ln10*s)**2);disp=Mw/Mn
sig=.25;observed=gauss(V,(a-mass_mu)/b,np.sqrt((s/b)**2+sig**2));mn_obs,mw_obs=moments(observed)

ax=axs[1,1];ax.plot(V,np.cumsum(observed)/np.sum(observed)*100,color=blue);ax.set(xlim=(4,17),xlabel=t('洗脱体积 / mL','Elution volume / mL'),ylabel=t('已流出质量 / %','Eluted mass / %'),title=t('D  先流出的是大分子','D  Larger molecules elute first'));ax.text(.03,.84,t('此累计方向：大 → 小','This cumulative direction: large → small'),transform=ax.transAxes)
save(fig,'calibration')
csvsave('calibration.csv',['elution_volume_mL','molar_mass_g_per_mol'],np.c_[ve,standards])
csvsave('constructed_chromatogram.csv',['elution_volume_mL','assigned_molar_mass_g_per_mol','ideal_mass_response_per_mL','broadened_mass_response_per_mL'],np.c_[V,M,ideal,observed])

raw=np.genfromtxt(Path(__file__).parent/'data/srm1475_table4.csv',delimiter=',',names=True)
logm=raw['log10_molar_mass_g_per_mol'];cdf=raw['cumulative_mass_percent'];median=10**np.interp(50,cdf,logm)
assert np.all(np.diff(logm)>0) and np.all(np.diff(cdf)>=0) and cdf[0]==0 and cdf[-1]==100

for p in ax.patches:ax.text(p.get_x()+p.get_width()/2,p.get_height()+2,f'{p.get_height():.1f}',ha='center',fontsize=10)
save(fig,'mass-distribution')

widths=np.linspace(0,1.2,61);factor=np.exp((ln10*b*widths)**2);rows=[]
fig,axs=plt.subplots(2,2,figsize=(12.8,8),layout='constrained')
ax=axs[0,0]
for w,c in zip([0,.6,1.2],[blue,gold,red]):
    y=gauss(V,(a-mass_mu)/b,np.sqrt((s/b)**2+w*w));ax.plot(V,y,color=c,label=f'σV = {w:.1f} mL')
ax.set(xlim=(4,17),xlabel=t('洗脱体积 / mL','Elution volume / mL'),ylabel=t('质量响应 / mL⁻¹','Mass response / mL⁻¹'),title=t('A  仪器把同一分布展宽','A  Instrument broadening'));ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9)
ax=axs[0,1];ax.plot(widths,disp*factor,color=red);ax.axhline(disp,color=green,ls='--',label=t('真实分散系数','True dispersity'));ax.set(xlabel=t('额外展宽 σV / mL','Extra broadening σV / mL'),ylabel=t('表观分散系数','Apparent dispersity'),title=t('B  展宽被误读为链长差异','B  Width becomes apparent heterogeneity'));ax.legend(frameon=False)
shifts=np.linspace(0,1.2,100);ax=axs[1,0];ax.plot(shifts,100*10**(-b*shifts),color=blue);ax.set(xlabel=t('向后移动的峰位 / mL','Later elution shift / mL'),ylabel=t('表观质量 / 真值 × 100%','Apparent / true mass × 100%'),title=t('C  同一质量，构象变紧凑','C  Same mass, more compact conformation'),ylim=(45,105))
ax=axs[1,1];cuts=np.linspace(12,18,70);mns=[];mws=[]
for cut in cuts:
    keep=V<=cut;ar=np.trapezoid(ideal[keep],V[keep]);mns.append(ar/np.trapezoid((ideal/M)[keep],V[keep]));mws.append(np.trapezoid((ideal*M)[keep],V[keep])/ar)
ax.plot(cuts,np.array(mns)/Mn,color=green,label='Mn');ax.plot(cuts,np.array(mws)/Mw,color=red,label='Mw');ax.axhline(1,color=dark,lw=.8,ls='--');ax.set(xlabel=t('积分终点 / mL','Integration endpoint / mL'),ylabel=t('截取值 / 完整值','Truncated / full value'),title=t('D  删掉小分子尾部的代价','D  Cost of deleting the low-mass tail'));ax.legend(frameon=False)
save(fig,'diagnostics')
csvsave('broadening.csv',['extra_sigma_mL','apparent_dispersity_analytic'],np.c_[widths,disp*factor])
csvsave('integration_sensitivity.csv',['integration_endpoint_mL','Mn_g_per_mol','Mw_g_per_mol'],np.c_[cuts,mns,mws])
toy_mn=.9*1e4+.1*1e5;toy_mw=(.9*1e8+.1*1e10)/toy_mn
summary={'Kav_example':.4,'toy_Mn_g_per_mol':toy_mn,'toy_Mw_g_per_mol':toy_mw,'toy_dispersity':toy_mw/toy_mn,'lognormal_true_Mn':float(Mn),'lognormal_true_Mw':float(Mw),'lognormal_true_dispersity':float(disp),'broadened_Mn':mn_obs,'broadened_Mw':mw_obs,'broadened_dispersity':mw_obs/mn_obs,'NBS_table_rows':len(raw),'NBS_mass_median_log_interpolation_g_per_mol':float(median),'NBS_reported_Mn_g_per_mol':17900,'NBS_reported_Mw_g_per_mol':52900,'NBS_reported_dispersity':52900/17900,'half_mL_shift_mass_ratio':10**(-.25*.5)}
assert abs(toy_mn-19000)<1e-8 and abs(toy_mw-57368.42105263158)<1e-7
assert abs(mn_obs/(Mn*np.exp(-.5*(ln10*b*sig)**2))-1)<1e-5
assert abs(mw_obs/(Mw*np.exp(.5*(ln10*b*sig)**2))-1)<1e-5
(O/'summary.json').write_text(json.dumps(summary,ensure_ascii=False,indent=2),encoding='utf8');print(json.dumps(summary,indent=2))
```

最后，把结论写成一个明确的实验回答。例如，在相同溶剂、温度、标准体系和积分规则下，两批可溶聚合物的表观分布是否变化，变化主要发生在主峰、短链尾部还是高质量肩峰；对于蛋白质，收集的峰是否对应后续实验需要的主要尺寸组分，以及回收的质量是否足够。保存分布本身、两个平均值和测量条件，比只保存一个“分子量”更能支撑之后的讨论。下一章的质谱将从另一种信号进入分子世界：它按离子的质荷比分开物种，与本章按溶液尺寸分配的机制形成清楚的互补。

# SEC/GPC: How large are polymer molecules

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/c02/en/
Language: en

Follow dissolved chains through porous spaces to understand size separation, mass weighting and molecular distributions.

## The same polymer name can hide very different chains

Dissolve equal masses of two hyaluronic acid powders in equal volumes of water. One solution may feel considerably thicker than the other. The chemical name identifies the repeating building blocks, but it does not tell us how many blocks are connected in each chain. Think of necklaces made from identical beads: a box of short necklaces and a box containing some very long ones can have the same total mass while tangling and flowing differently. Real solutions also respond to concentration, salt, temperature and interactions between chains. To investigate whether chain length contributes to a change, we need a measurement that separates dissolved molecules according to their size. Size-exclusion chromatography, abbreviated SEC, provides that part of the investigation.

A related question appears in protein research. A vial may contain individual proteins, pairs of associated proteins and larger aggregates. Gel filtration can separate these populations and allow useful fractions to be collected. In a degradable polymer, chains may have broken into shorter pieces while the material still looks intact. Comparing SEC distributions before and after treatment connects the visible object to changes in its soluble molecular population. The word soluble defines the population that enters the measurement. A network that only swells, or a fraction that precipitates during preparation, needs its own observation and mass accounting so that the chromatogram can be interpreted within the complete material.

The names gel permeation chromatography, or GPC, and gel filtration chromatography, or GFC, reflect historical applications of the same size-exclusion mechanism. GPC is commonly used for polymer analysis in organic solvents; GFC is common in aqueous biomolecular separation. A column contains porous particles. Dissolved molecules of different sizes can access different amounts of solvent inside those particles, so they leave the column at different average positions. The first output is detector response against elution time or volume. Converting that position to molar mass is a further step requiring calibration or additional detectors. Keeping these two steps distinct makes a molecular-mass axis much easier to understand.

We will follow a specimen through that sequence: why large molecules emerge first, how standards establish a scale, why a population requires more than one average, and how specimen preparation changes what reaches the column. A published polyethylene distribution provides a real example of a cumulative mass curve. A complete computational experiment then connects pore accessibility, calibration, detector-like signals and integration decisions. The aim is to read both axes of a chromatogram, explain plausible causes of a shift or shoulder, and choose a control that makes the next experiment more informative.

## Large molecules emerge first because they visit fewer side rooms

Imagine a corridor with many small rooms along its sides. One group of visitors stays in the corridor, while another also enters the rooms. Even if they move similarly in the corridor, the second group takes longer, on average, to reach the exit. In SEC, solvent between the packing particles resembles the corridor, and solvent inside their pores resembles the side rooms. Large dissolved molecules can access less of the internal space. Smaller molecules can explore more of it and therefore elute later. The mechanism does not require forcing a large molecule through a membrane pore. Nor are small molecules blocked at the outlet. Separation follows from their distribution between accessible solvent regions.

The history helps correct the familiar intuition that a sieve always lets small objects through first. In his retrospective account, Jerker Porath described separation in starch columns even without the electrical current used for electrophoresis. Work with Per Flodin on crosslinked dextran gels led to a 1959 publication and an influential approach to separating macromolecules from small solutes. Our original diagram connects that idea to desalting: a macromolecular band emerges before the salt band, allowing the first fraction to be collected. The plotted curves are teaching constructions representing this mechanism, rather than reconstructed measurements from the historical experiments.

Two measured reference volumes make the side-room analogy quantitative. An appropriate noninteracting marker that is completely excluded from the pores provides the exclusion volume, V₀. A small marker that accesses the relevant internal solvent provides the total accessible volume, Vₜ. This latter quantity is a chromatographic reference, not the external cylindrical volume calculated from the column casing. A target eluting at Vₑ has accessed an additional volume above V₀. Dividing that increment by the available pore volume gives the dimensionless accessibility measure Kₐᵥ. With V₀=3 mL, Vₜ=18 mL and Vₑ=9 mL, the increment is 6 mL out of 15 mL, giving 0.4.

$$
K_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{V_e-V_0}{V_t-V_0}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/17929f84b05c9c9ee6b7954d.svg) | Apparent accessible pore-volume fraction, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/daa1e83231d13f3a99351353.svg) | Target elution volume, mL. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/454606841ec20ef0f43cd9f6.svg) | Volume measured by a suitable fully excluded marker, mL. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/ad460123890fe451611439a3.svg) | Total accessible volume from a suitable fully included marker, mL. |

When size exclusion dominates and markers are appropriate, divide extra accessed volume by accessible pore volume. Vₑ=9, V₀=3 and Vₜ=18 mL give 6/15=0.4. Zero and one describe reference limits; additional adsorption or repulsion changes this interpretation.

![Original pore-access and desalting diagrams; dimensions are schematic. B uses constructed desalting bands to illustrate the mechanism associated with 1959 gel filtration. C uses V₀=3 and Vₜ=18 mL.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/cc78e80d8339979b32c57812.svg?v=cc78e80d8339)

Figure 1Original pore-access and desalting diagrams; dimensions are schematic. B uses constructed desalting bands to illustrate the mechanism associated with 1959 gel filtration. C uses V₀=3 and Vₜ=18 mL.

At either end of the useful range, size discrimination becomes weak. Several very large molecules may all be excluded and emerge near V₀. Several very small molecules may all access essentially the same internal space and emerge near Vₜ. The fractionation range lies between those limits. This explains why a column that works well for separating protein from salt is not automatically suitable for resolving two similarly sized proteins. Desalting requires group separation across a large size difference. Resolving nearby molecular populations requires enough position difference within a narrower range, together with a suitably narrow injected band and adequate column efficiency.

Real molecules may also interact with pore surfaces through charge, hydrophobicity or other chemistry. A charged polysaccharide at low salt concentration may adopt an extended conformation and experience electrostatic interactions with the packing. Both effects can move a peak. Changing salt and observing a different elution volume therefore calls for interpretation of the solution conditions. Buffer composition, ionic strength and packing chemistry are chosen to make size exclusion the principal retention mechanism. Concentration series and known reference specimens then help test that choice. The analogy explains the intended physical mechanism; controls establish whether the actual system follows it closely enough for the research question.

## Calibration builds a bridge from elution position to molar mass

A detector cannot know whether a peak at 10 mL contains chains of ten thousand or one hundred thousand grams per mole. Conventional calibration passes a series of known, relatively narrow polymer standards through the same system and records their peak positions. Within a useful working range, the base-ten logarithm of molar mass often changes approximately linearly with elution volume. A logarithmic scale puts successive factors of ten at equal distances, allowing thousands, tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands to share a readable graph. Larger standards appear at smaller elution volumes, consistent with their reduced pore accessibility.

John Moore's 1964 work with crosslinked polystyrene gels helped establish GPC as a continuous instrumental approach to polymer distributions. This development made calibration central: recording the effluent curve was valuable only when its positions could be related to molecular properties. Our teaching calibration uses a straight line whose slope describes the change in logarithmic molar mass per milliliter. Its intercept locates the scale vertically. In an experimental method, standards should span the distribution of interest, and residuals and end-region curvature should be inspected. A convenient straight equation is useful within the region supported by those measurements; a broad column range may require a different calibration form.

$$
\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{M}{1\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}\right)=a-bV_e
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/34058a2a5d1de088feed7d98.svg) | Calibration-assigned molar mass, g/mol. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/349015631ec44ef653936c85.svg) | Linear calibration intercept, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a77a353782459b753313d802.svg) | Magnitude of the decreasing calibration slope, mL⁻¹. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/daa1e83231d13f3a99351353.svg) | Elution volume, mL. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/be8ebdecd039424afe275a60.svg) | Base-ten logarithm; division by the unit quantity makes its argument dimensionless. |

Within the standards-covered approximately linear fractionation range, logarithms connect position to standard mass. a=7, b=0.25 mL⁻¹ and Vₑ=10 mL give log₁₀ M=4.5, or approximately 31,623 g/mol; 12 mL gives 10,000 g/mol. The conversion depends on chemical series and solution conditions.

![Constructed standards and population: the number distribution of log₁₀ M has mean 4.2 and SD 0.35; mass weighting changes its center. Extra chromatographic broadening is σV=0.25 mL and area is normalized to one. D accumulates in elution order, from large to small.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/6692e4e6e3bfe98fd37317af.svg?v=6692e4e6e3bf)

Figure 2Constructed standards and population: the number distribution of log₁₀ M has mean 4.2 and SD 0.35; mass weighting changes its center. Extra chromatographic broadening is σV=0.25 mL and area is normalized to one. D accumulates in elution order, from large to small.

The identity and conformation of the standards matter. Two chains with the same mass can occupy different effective sizes in a solvent. Branching may make a chain more compact than a linear chain of equal mass, while a change in solvent can alter expansion. An unknown polymer calibrated against polystyrene therefore receives a polystyrene-equivalent molar mass under the stated conditions. The term equivalent tells the reader how the ruler was constructed. It also helps comparisons between laboratories. If the research question asks whether a branching reaction changed actual mass, a size-based calibration benefits from an additional measurement that addresses that distinction.

A differential refractive-index detector is a common companion to SEC. It compares the refractive index of the eluting solution with that of the mobile phase. For a given polymer, solvent and temperature in an appropriate dilute range, response can be related to concentration. The area in a small elution-volume slice then represents mass in that slice. A UV detector instead responds to absorption at its selected wavelength. Different components can have very different absorptivities: a protein and a weakly absorbing polysaccharide do not automatically contribute equal signal per unit mass. Before interpreting peak areas as composition, establish what the detector senses and whether its response factor is comparable across the relevant populations.

Adding multi-angle light scattering and concentration detection allows molar mass to be inferred from scattering and concentration in successive slices, reducing dependence on conventional polymer standards. Refractive-index increment, detector alignment, band broadening and contributions from dust or aggregates remain part of that inference. Understanding this as a calibration-standard-independent mass measurement is more useful than treating the word absolute as the disappearance of experimental assumptions. Conventional calibration and concentration weighting provide a clear foundation; additional detectors then extend the information available from the same separation.

## One population, two averages and two different voting rules

Consider a deliberately simple population: ninety chains each have a molar mass of 10,000 g/mol, and ten chains each have a molar mass of 100,000 g/mol. Short chains account for ninety percent of the number, but the ten long chains contribute slightly more mass than all ninety short chains. Molar mass is the mass of a mole of the specified chains, expressed here in grams per mole. We can give every chain one vote and calculate number-average molar mass, Mₙ. Alternatively, we can let each unit of mass carry equal weight and calculate weight-average molar mass, M𝑤. Both calculations describe the same population, using different weighting rules.

The number average resembles an ordinary arithmetic mean. Multiply the count of each type by its molar mass, add those contributions and divide by the total chain count. Our example gives 19,000 g/mol. This is not the threshold with half the chains on each side; that threshold is a median. In the discrete example, the number median is 10,000 g/mol because ninety percent of the chains have that value. The distinction matters for broad distributions: a relatively small number of long chains can increase a mean while most individual chains remain shorter.

$$
M_n=\frac{\sum_i N_iM_i}{\sum_i N_i}=\left(\sum_i\frac{w_i}{M_i}\right)^{-1},\qquad w_i=\frac{N_iM_i}{\sum_j N_jM_j}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4f3c9d3ab8208b50c9e81e73.svg) | Number-average molar mass, g/mol. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/2e48d6441cb55e92796c4f28.svg) | Counts of chains in the corresponding classes, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/80f8ce36f42008dae6d1d510.svg) | Molar masses of the corresponding classes, g/mol. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/cec5f0994a4bad5c3ac4a9a4.svg) | Mass fraction of class i, dimensionless; fractions sum to one. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/1f848077b31e64f57fc97f4b.svg) | Indices covering all relevant chain classes or mass slices. |

Average with equal weight per chain. For mass slices, mass divided by molar mass gives a count-proportional weight. Ninety chains at 10,000 and ten at 100,000 g/mol give Mn=19,000 g/mol; mass fractions are 9/19 and 10/19.

The weight average first asks how much mass each class contributes, then uses those mass fractions to average molar mass. Long chains contribute both a larger molar mass and a larger mass-based weight. Consequently, the high-mass tail has a stronger influence on M𝑤. The same ninety-to-ten example gives approximately 57,368 g/mol. Dividing M𝑤 by Mₙ gives dispersity, written Đ, which compares these two weighted averages. Identical chains give a value of one. Heterogeneity generally raises the weight average above the number average; here the ratio is approximately 3.019. Different distribution shapes can share that ratio, so the full curve still contains useful information.

$$
M_w=\sum_i w_iM_i=\frac{\sum_iN_iM_i^2}{\sum_iN_iM_i},\qquad \mathit{Đ}=\frac{M_w}{M_n}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/584328b60ee68abee6861462.svg) | Weight-average molar mass, g/mol. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/cec5f0994a4bad5c3ac4a9a4.svg) | Mass fraction of class i, dimensionless, summing to one. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/b26e60e55288c9229968cad0.svg) | Count of chains in class i. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9b5817fb0c0bac5188945802.svg) | Molar mass of class i, g/mol. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4f3c9d3ab8208b50c9e81e73.svg) | Number-average molar mass, g/mol. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/40bf2c4da5241a580e5118bc.svg) | Dispersity, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/33f73a318016d781b6ae1aa9.svg) | Chain-class or mass-slice index. |

Average with equal weight per unit mass, giving long chains greater influence. The same 90:10 example gives Mw≈57,368.42 g/mol and Đ≈3.01939. For the same complete population with nonnegative weights, Đ≥1; broadening and integration truncation affect apparent values.

A concentration-sensitive SEC detector normally provides mass information before it provides anything related to molecule count. To calculate Mₙ from mass slices, divide each slice's mass by its assigned molar mass, obtaining a quantity proportional to the number of molecules. The total mass can then be divided by that total count-related quantity. A low-mass tail may contain little mass but many chains, making it influential for Mₙ. The constructed number and mass distributions in the figure therefore have different peak positions. This is a consequence of weighting. When software exports a distribution, check whether it is normalized by number or mass and whether the density is expressed per linear or logarithmic mass interval.

The real dataset comes from Ross and Frolen's 1972 NBS study of polyethylene SRM 1475. Points in the figure reproduce the published cumulative mass table: the vertical coordinate gives the percentage of mass below the indicated molar mass. Interpolation between neighboring entries on the logarithmic axis estimates a mass median. That statistic differs from the paper's reported Mₙ and M𝑤. The cumulative direction also differs from adding detector signal in elution order, where large molecules arrive first. Reading the axis direction is what makes a new plot of the historical table scientifically faithful.

![A replots published cumulative mass data from Ross and Frolen, NBS (1972), Table 4; the mass median uses linear interpolation in log M, preserving all printed values. B is a separate constructed population of 90 chains at 10,000 g/mol and 10 at 100,000 g/mol, compared by number and mass.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/b5b7cc9e6accd00e2e731172.svg?v=b5b7cc9e6acc)

Figure 3A replots published cumulative mass data from Ross and Frolen, NBS (1972), Table 4; the mass median uses linear interpolation in log M, preserving all printed values. B is a separate constructed population of 90 chains at 10,000 g/mol and 10 at 100,000 g/mol, compared by number and mass.

The complete example retains the table's printed values and rounding. It quotes the paper's moments for the aggregate distribution rather than deriving exact moments from a sparse cumulative table. The table answers a particularly intuitive question: what fraction of the material lies below a chosen mass threshold? Such thresholds can be useful when comparing release fragments or selecting fractions for another experiment. Number averages, weight averages, medians and threshold fractions each summarize a different feature. Choosing among them follows the research question, rather than a rule that one summary is universally the best.

## The column receives a prepared specimen, not an abstract material

A powder disappearing into liquid does not guarantee that every chain has reached a stable, uniformly dissolved state. High-mass material may dissolve slowly; crosslinked microgels may swell rather than dissolve; a protein may aggregate during the waiting period. Preparation therefore requires a solvent that dissolves the intended population while remaining compatible with the packing and detector. Temperature, dissolution time and mixing method help define that population. Strong mechanical treatment can change particularly vulnerable macromolecules, while temperature and buffer conditions can alter protein conformation and association. Preparation belongs within the measurement description because it determines what is actually measured.

Filtration removes particles that might obstruct a column, but it can also select the molecular population. An aggregate retained by a membrane will be absent from the subsequent chromatogram. Adsorption to the membrane can reduce recovery. Comparing concentration before and after preparation, inspecting sediment, and recording filter material help connect cleanliness with mass recovery. If soluble aggregates are the research target, choose a clarification procedure appropriate to that target and examine what it removes. For partially soluble network materials, the soluble mass fraction is similarly important: a clean SEC trace describes what entered the liquid phase, while the remaining network carries additional structural information.

Injection volume sets the initial width of the sample band. A long plug can make nearby populations overlap even when their mean retention differs. Excess concentration can also change viscosity, intermolecular interactions or local flow. A useful preliminary experiment changes concentration or injection volume while holding the other conditions fixed. Compare normalized profiles as well as total areas. Stable position and shape, together with a concentration-sensitive area that scales with loading, support the selected conditions. If an early peak decreases upon dilution, consider a shifting association equilibrium alongside reduced instrumental loading. Dilution is both a measurement adjustment and a possible change to the specimen.

A solvent blank, a narrow standard and a stable reference specimen answer different questions. The blank reveals disturbances associated with solvent and injection. A narrow standard checks position and system broadening. A stable reference monitors the method over time. Refractive-index detection responds to temperature and solvent differences, making equilibration and baseline stability especially valuable. Preparing a sample in a solvent unlike the mobile phase can introduce a disturbance near the low-mass tail. Automated integration may treat that disturbance as polymer. Comparing blank, standard and specimen traces exposes the problem before it is amplified by the calculation of a number average.

Keep the original time signal and the measured flow conditions. Time and volume are related but are not interchangeable labels: at stable flow, elapsed volume follows from flow rate multiplied by elapsed time. Comparing runs performed at different flows is clearer after expressing position on a consistent volume axis. Higher flow can change broadening and, for susceptible very large chains, introduce shear-related effects. Method selection balances separation, specimen stability and useful analysis time. A shorter run is valuable when it preserves the distinctions that the experiment is meant to measure.

## Broadening and shifting a peak tell different stories

The instrument spreads molecules that would otherwise arrive at nearly the same position. Different flow paths, exchange with pores, connecting tubes and the detector cell can all contribute. Observed width therefore includes both the specimen's distribution and the system's broadening. This is conspicuous for a narrow standard and may be a smaller relative contribution for a broad specimen. Our diagnostic model passes the same underlying population through three extra-broadening conditions, preserving total area and mean elution position. Interpreting all the added width as chain-length variation raises the apparent dispersity even though the molecular population has not changed.

A whole-peak shift creates a different effect. Suppose equal-mass chains become more compact and elute 0.5 mL later, while analysis continues to use the original calibration. The assigned masses are then multiplied by approximately 0.750. No bond is broken in this constructed operation, yet the apparent mass falls by about a quarter. When investigating degradation, comparable solvent, salt, temperature and calibration help separate this possibility from actual chain scission. Reaction chemistry, end-group information or additional detectors can then address the mechanism. When conformation itself is the research target, the position shift is useful information about size under the stated solution conditions.

Integration boundaries affect the answer as well. The late-eluting region corresponds to smaller molecules. Removing it discards many short chains and raises Mₙ. A relatively small early high-mass tail can strongly influence M𝑤. A reviewable analysis therefore shows the detector signal, baseline, integration boundaries and calibration, then examines reasonable changes to those choices. The endpoint scan in the figure holds the early boundary fixed and progressively includes the low-mass tail. The two averages converge at different rates. This transforms an isolated software result into a number whose sensitivity can be understood and discussed.

![Four diagnostics for the same constructed population. A and B add Gaussian instrumental broadening; C shifts elution while retaining the original calibration; D changes only the integration endpoint. The curves show how measurement choices change apparent distributions.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/28e37efc29d98b8dab05034b.svg?v=28e37efc29d9)

Figure 4Four diagnostics for the same constructed population. A and B add Gaussian instrumental broadening; C shifts elution while retaining the original calibration; D changes only the integration endpoint. The curves show how measurement choices change apparent distributions.

The interactive experiment retains two actual chain masses, 10,000 and 100,000 g/mol. First change the number fraction of long chains and observe when a small minority already contributes substantial mass. Next add system broadening and compare actual and apparent averages. Finally move the whole elution pattern to simulate a uniform mismatch between size and the calibration standard. These controls affect different parts of the measurement. Similar-looking changes in a curve do not always imply the same underlying population. Changing one control at a time and predicting the direction before reading the result develops a more useful understanding than moving every slider together.

## How the same chains acquire different apparent distributions

Chains have molar masses of 10,000 and 100,000 g/mol. Change one control at a time and compare actual and apparent averages. Gaussian broadening and a uniform position shift define this measurement model.

[Figure: Interactive mass-weighted chromatogram](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/c02/en/#C02-plot)

An early shoulder in a new specimen suggests concrete follow-up work. Check whether it approaches the exclusion boundary, reduce loading to inspect peak shape, vary appropriate solution conditions to investigate reversible association, and collect the fraction for another method. A stable shift of the entire main peak suggests checking standards and flow conditions before testing degradation or conformational explanations. Each action distinguishes a particular hypothesis. SEC then becomes a decision point within a research sequence, linking preparation and fraction collection to structural and functional measurements.

## A complete analysis keeps the reasoning available for inspection

The example contains both constructed models and a published dataset, identified separately in the captions and data documentation. The constructed population has a normally distributed logarithmic molar mass. From that population, the program calculates a mass-weighted chromatogram and adds a controllable amount of instrument broadening. Known input averages can then be compared with apparent output averages to locate the bias. The published-data branch reads the NBS cumulative mass table, preserving nonuniform positions and printed rounding. It treats the table as a reported cumulative distribution. Standard points, chromatograms, broadening scans and integration scans are exported so that each step can be examined independently.

When reading the code, begin with the volume coordinate and calibration function, then locate normalization and the two moment calculations. Each small slice first has a mass weight. Dividing by the assigned molar mass produces the corresponding count-related weight. Numerical integration approximates the area under a continuous curve and includes coordinate spacing. If you replace the constructed grid with irregularly sampled measurements, provide the actual coordinates to the integration function. Adding heights alone has the appropriate meaning only when sampling intervals are equal and the omitted proportional factor cancels in the intended ratio.
