# 表面张力：液滴、液面与界面能

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/p04/
Language: zh-CN

用薄板的力与悬滴的形状测量界面张力，再看表面年龄和浓度怎样改变读数。

## 一滴清洁剂，为什么能改变一大片水面

把清水滴到一片洁净塑料上，水往往聚成珠；加入少量表面活性剂后，同样体积的液体可能铺得更开。配制蛋白质药物时，研究者又会遇到另一个问题：摇晃产生的新鲜气液界面可能吸附蛋白质，影响它的构象与聚集。涂层能否均匀覆盖、乳液能否形成细小液滴、泡沫能否长期存在，都与界面有关。表面张力测量把这些看似不同的问题连接起来：在规定温度、组成和界面形成时间下，扩大一块液体表面，需要付出多少自由能？也可以换一种实验语言问：液体沿着接触线，给探针施加了多大的力？

液体内部的分子周围大多是同类邻居，界面附近的分子面对的环境不同。因此，让更多分子处于界面通常需要做功，液滴便倾向于减少表面积。固定体积的球体具有最小表面积，这解释了小水滴为什么接近球形。把表面想成一张会收缩的薄膜，有助于理解力的方向；但真实液面能够流动，界面上的分子也会持续交换，它与具有固定材料点的橡皮膜不同。表面张力的单位是牛顿每米，常写为毫牛顿每米；从能量角度看，它也等于每平方米需要的焦耳数。单位之间的等价来自做功等于力乘距离，而面积增加量等于边长乘移动距离。

日常说的表面张力通常指液体与气体之间的界面张力。油和水之间同样存在界面张力，只是两边都是液体，计算悬滴形状时必须使用两相密度之差。黏度则描述流动时内部摩擦的强弱：蜂蜜流得慢主要与黏度有关，液滴边界愿不愿意扩大与界面张力有关。两者能够同时影响液滴形成，却对应不同的测量量。一个液体具有较低表面张力，也并不自动意味着它能在任何固体上完全铺展；固液界面与固气界面的能量仍参与接触角的形成。本章用力和轮廓两条实验路线测量张力，再把时间与浓度放入同一张实验地图。

## 把水面的“干净程度”变成可以控制的变量

十九世纪末，Agnes Pockels在日常条件下研究水面。她在1891年发表于《Nature》的信中描述了一个长约70厘米、宽约5厘米、深约2厘米的长方形水槽：水加到槽口，一块可移动的横向薄片把水面分成不同区域。移动薄片时，受限区域的面积改变，表面污染物的拥挤程度也随之改变。她还利用轻巧的天平与小圆片研究水面作用力。这个设计的巧妙之处，是把“这盆水似乎不一样”拆成可以逐项改变的量：表面面积、表面物质和测力条件。图中的装置是根据这一实验思想绘制的原理示意，帮助理解变量之间的关系。

这段历史与今天的实验仍然相通。清洁过的容器、空气中的有机物、吸头上残留的清洗剂，都可能改变真正参与测量的表面。Pockels后续的讨论也重新检查了器具清洁与早期解释的关系。一个平滑、稳定的数字并不替代对界面状态的控制；如果痕量物质持续吸附，测到的表面张力就会随时间变化。对于蛋白质、脂质和聚合物溶液，界面本身还可能发生结构重排。研究者需要同时规定溶液怎样配制、界面何时生成、等待了多久，以及探针或液滴经历过怎样的接触过程。

![左：依据Pockels 1891年水槽与移动隔板实验思想绘制的原创示意，圆点代表表面物质。右：完全润湿薄板的弯月面与向下毛细力、向上浮力；几何与箭头不按比例。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/01c584f9b6060b3a365b1462.svg?v=01c584f9b606)

图 1左：依据Pockels 1891年水槽与移动隔板实验思想绘制的原创示意，圆点代表表面物质。右：完全润湿薄板的弯月面与向下毛细力、向上浮力；几何与箭头不按比例。

现代张力仪把这种变量控制与更灵敏的传感器结合起来。Wilhelmy板法将一片薄板悬挂在微量天平下，使板的下端接触并进入液体。液体沿着板的四周形成弯月面，表面张力在竖直方向上的分量会改变天平读数。悬滴法则从相机图像读取另一种结果：重力把液滴拉长，界面张力使轮廓保持紧凑，二者竞争决定外形。两种方法分别把界面性质编码进力和形状，因此它们的关键准备也不同。前者尤其关注探针周长、润湿状态与浮力，后者尤其关注图像尺度、密度差与轮廓质量。

## 从天平读数中分离毛细力和浮力

先在空气中称量干板，再把这个重量从后续读数中扣除，称为去皮。去皮后的读数仍然包含两项：接触线处的毛细力，以及浸入液体的板体受到的浮力。本例把向下的力规定为正，完全润湿时毛细力向下，浮力向上。假设薄板宽10毫米、厚0.1毫米，接触线绕板一周，其周长是两个宽度加两个厚度，等于20.2毫米。不能只取板的宽度，因为前后两个宽面和两条窄边都与液体相接。板越薄，窄边贡献越小，但它仍然有清楚的几何含义。

$$
F_{\mathrm{tare}}=\gamma P\cos\theta-\Delta\rho\,gwtz,\qquad P=2(w+t)
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/b01fb8392b6a8aa7cb7333fd.svg) | 扣除干板重量后的竖直力，N；向下为正。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7db9474e1e95a533a1714618.svg) | 液体界面张力，N/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600.svg) | 润湿周长，m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/06e47e2878930095abe73547.svg) | 板与液体的接触角，从液体内读取。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/988fbc7bbcda53116494bdef.svg) | 液体与空气密度差，kg/m³，本例近似1000。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/439e3cc8d431c550923e0870.svg) | 重力加速度，9.81 m/s²。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/5f85a26e5089def254fee2b9.svg) | 板宽，m；本例0.010。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/707bb132def3690d81bf1f0c.svg) | 板厚，m；本例0.0001。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9032cb23a878659e74b670d3.svg) | 浸入深度，m。 |

静态、规则截面和固定接触角条件下，竖直毛细力减去浮力。γ=0.050 N/m、θ=0、z=0给出F=0.00101 N；z=0.005 m时为0.00096095 N。

如果表面张力为50毫牛顿每米，接触角为零，刚接触水面时的毛细力是1.01毫牛顿。把板再浸入5毫米，排开的液体体积等于宽、厚、深度三者相乘，浮力达到0.04905毫牛顿，去皮后的向下读数便降为0.96095毫牛顿。将后一数字直接除以周长，会得到偏低的张力。更清楚的处理是记录多个浸入深度，画出力随深度的直线，再把直线外推到零深度。斜率主要反映浮力，截距给出毛细力。示例加入小幅测量噪声，得到约1.01048毫牛顿截距，对应50.02385毫牛顿每米。

![构造观测：A以零深度截距分离浮力；B固定真实张力为50 mN/m，显示误用零接触角带来的系统变化。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/226dd950f0d9ab8c29e821f2.svg?v=226dd950f0d9)

图 2构造观测：A以零深度截距分离浮力；B固定真实张力为50 mN/m，显示误用零接触角带来的系统变化。

接触角决定毛细力有多少投影到竖直方向。图中的板表面若具有30度接触角，而计算时仍假定完全润湿，原本50毫牛顿每米的张力会被读成约43.30毫牛顿每米。仪器测量的是力，接触角假设来自探针与液体的实际相互作用，二者需要配合。铂板常用于形成良好润湿的测量条件，但使用之前仍应按照材料与仪器要求清洁、检查并稳定温度。若蛋白质吸附改变了板面，连续测量中的接触角也可能改变。此时，随时间漂移的力既可能来自液面吸附，也可能包含探针表面变化，换用独立探针或轮廓法对照能够帮助分辨。

实验记录应保存原始力、浸入深度、时间和温度，而不只保存最终张力。气泡附着会改变排液体积，容器壁太近可能影响弯月面，液位漂移会改变实际浸入深度。测量低浓度表面活性剂时，容器、探针与空气接触处的吸附还可能消耗一部分溶质。保持相同容器尺寸、液体体积和等待程序，能够让样品之间的比较对应同一实验问题。检查线性残差也有具体作用：若力随深度明显弯曲，简单的固定接触角与固定周长模型就需要重新检查。

## 让液滴轮廓告诉我们界面的力量

从针头缓慢悬挂一滴液体，相机得到的首先是一条明暗边界。要把边界变成张力，需要理解弯曲界面两侧为什么存在压力差。界面张力沿表面拉拽，而曲面上不同位置的拉力方向并不平行；它们合起来形成指向曲率中心的作用。液滴内部必须具有相应压力，才能与这一作用平衡。Young–Laplace关系把这种平衡写成两个相互垂直方向曲率的贡献。球面两个方向的曲率半径相同，圆柱面则有一个方向近似平直，因此仅凭一个横截面的弯曲程度判断全部压力会遗漏信息。

$$
\Delta p=\gamma\left(\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}\right)
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/388b34d468326c8df9f49910.svg) | 界面两侧压力差，Pa；球滴内压减外压。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7db9474e1e95a533a1714618.svg) | 界面张力，N/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9cac43c0b77042679a064ee0.svg) | 第一主曲率半径，m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/99a0a123eddd37514ed7e5ce.svg) | 与第一方向垂直的第二主曲率半径，m。 |

机械平衡的曲面上，两方向曲率贡献相加。单个球形界面γ=0.050 N/m、R1=R2=0.001 m时，压力差100 Pa。悬滴沿高度还满足静水压变化。

当球形界面的半径为1毫米、张力为50毫牛顿每米时，内外压力差为100帕。这里讨论的是一个液体–气体界面；肥皂泡薄膜具有内外两个界面，需要分别考虑，不能把两种对象混用。悬滴从下端向上，液体静压逐渐降低，局部曲率也随之改变。程序沿界面弧长逐点积分，把顶点附近近似圆形的轮廓延伸到更高位置，再调整张力和顶点曲率半径，使计算边界贴近观测边界。图中展示液滴下段，因为这一区域直接体现曲率与重力竞争，而针头附近还涉及具体的附着几何。

![轴对称Young–Laplace模型的悬滴下段，规定张力50 mN/m与3 μm标准差径向噪声。左为轮廓和拟合；右为径向残差。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/fc217f57883ac2f46bb1f3c3.svg?v=fc217f57883a)

图 3轴对称Young–Laplace模型的悬滴下段，规定张力50 mN/m与3 μm标准差径向噪声。左为轮廓和拟合；右为径向残差。

示例规定真实张力为50毫牛顿每米、底端顶点半径为1毫米，并给轮廓坐标加入3微米量级的噪声。拟合得到张力约50.955毫牛顿每米，顶点半径约1.00059毫米，径向残差的均方根约2.56微米。两个参数对轮廓的影响并不完全独立：顶点半径控制局部曲率，张力控制重力沿高度造成多大形变。若液滴很小、几乎是球形，重力造成的变化很弱，许多张力值都可能与近似圆形轮廓相容。选择具有适当重力变形的稳定液滴，通常比单纯追求更小、更圆的液滴更有利于参数识别。

图像中的毫米尺度是计算的一部分。像素尺寸设置错误，会同时改变曲率与重力长度尺度；相机未水平放置、液滴轴线倾斜或液滴仍在振荡，也会破坏轴对称静态模型。实验时可用已知尺寸校准图像尺度，检查左右轮廓的一致性，等待运动衰减，并测定实验温度下两相密度。油中水滴使用水与油的密度差，空气中水滴常近似使用水的密度。分析结果连同残差随高度的分布一起观察：随机小幅波动与一侧持续偏离所指向的问题不同，后者更值得检查照明、边缘提取和轴线定位。

形状拟合还可以用一个简单的数量级检查来理解。曲率压力大约随张力除以液滴半径变化，而沿液滴高度的重力压力大约随密度差、重力加速度和高度的乘积变化。液滴尺寸增大时，重力相对于曲率作用增强，因此形状逐渐偏离球面。这个尺度关系也说明，知道图像中液滴有多少像素还不够，必须知道每个像素对应多长。液滴尺寸过大又可能接近脱落，轮廓在拍摄期间变化，所以应在可识别形变与稳定悬挂之间选择适合的范围。左右边界都能清晰辨认、底端顶点完整入镜、针头附近没有遮挡，是轮廓进入拟合前应直接检查的图像条件。

## 同一瓶溶液，也会有不同年龄的表面

表面活性剂分子往往包含亲水部分与疏水部分，在气液界面或油水界面上排列能够降低自由能。新鲜界面刚形成时，界面上的分子分布与长时间放置后的分布不同。分子需要从体相移动到界面，随后吸附、重新取向，某些大分子还会缓慢展开或形成相互作用网络。于是，表面张力不仅取决于配方，也取决于表面年龄。这里的年龄从这块界面生成时开始计时，与整瓶溶液放置了多久是两个变量。把一瓶放置一夜的溶液吹成新气泡，新气泡仍然只有刚形成的年龄。

$$
\gamma(a)=\gamma_{\infty}+(\gamma_0-\gamma_{\infty})e^{-a/\tau_r}
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/349015631ec44ef653936c85.svg) | 表面年龄，s。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/326221aa7409b4a62fda0814.svg) | 该年龄的张力，mN/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/97e4157d29a2b15aac854b6c.svg) | 初始张力，72 mN/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/dd2b4bb24d7b7e6ed71658d9.svg) | 长期极限，35 mN/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7f4562fee555940b00253509.svg) | 规定的弛豫时间，2 s。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/0be950b3e59846bc80f7e4ca.svg) | 自然对数的底，无量纲。 |

指定指数弛豫教学模型，差值每经过τr缩小至原来的1/e。a=2 s时γ=48.61154 mN/m；具体吸附体系需由其动力学确定时间规律。

为清楚分离时间因素，示例指定一条由72逐渐降到35毫牛顿每米的指数曲线，时间尺度为2秒。2秒时张力约48.61毫牛顿每米，因为初始与长期值之间的差还剩约36.8%。这条曲线是演示用的弛豫模型，参数并未代表某一种指定蛋白质或清洁剂的实测吸附常数。实际吸附可受扩散、能垒、界面占据和分子构象共同控制，因而可能出现多个时间阶段。理解示例时应关注可检验的关系：在相同配方与温度下，改变观察年龄可以改变所读取的力，也可以改变形成液滴时的界面形状。

最大气泡压力法适合观察不断生成的新界面。气体从浸没的毛细管中鼓出，气泡曲率先增加到一个特征状态，再继续长大；当界面近似半球、曲率半径等于管口半径时，曲率压力达到相应最大值。总压力还包括毛细管浸入深度造成的液柱压力，因此必须扣除该项后才能与表面张力联系。改变气泡形成速度，可以访问不同表面年龄。其时间定义通常与气泡形成到达到最大压力的阶段有关，不能直接用整次气泡脱落周期替代。把动态曲线与板法、悬滴法比较时，应先匹配各自真正观察的界面年龄。

时间曲线还影响取样方式。若每次测量都把同一表面反复拉起或压缩，上一轮操作可能已经改变界面面积和分子排列；下一轮读数便不再具有相同初始条件。需要比较新鲜界面时，应规定如何重新形成界面；需要研究老化时，则应尽量减少观察过程对界面的扰动。蛋白质体系尤其值得同时记录缓冲液、盐浓度和温度，因为这些条件会改变分子的电荷状态、分子间作用与构象稳定性。重复实验的对象应是经过完整制备和等待程序的独立界面，连续读取同一表面的多个时间点则描述这一界面的演化过程。

## 浓度曲线的转折，怎样联系到分子聚集

逐步增加表面活性剂浓度，界面吸附往往使表面张力下降。达到一定范围后，继续加入的分子更容易形成胶束等聚集体，张力曲线的下降趋势可能转为较平缓的平台。胶束可想象成把疏水部分藏在内部、亲水部分朝向水的动态聚集体；分子仍在聚集体与溶液之间交换。临界胶束浓度常通过性质随浓度变化的转折估计，表面张力只是其中一种性质。温度、盐浓度、表面活性剂组成都会影响这一转折，因此一个数值必须与配方和条件一起阅读。

$$
\gamma(c)=\gamma_p+k\min\!\left[\log_{10}(c/c_*),0\right]
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/482cc0189b34e0e766508729.svg) | 浓度c处的张力，mN/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/b332ba26d1b8a3e4b8f817ed.svg) | 表面活性剂浓度，mmol/L。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/71a1a028a21bc2c5b0e55c55.svg) | 转折浓度，mmol/L；本例1。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4ea68d49e66db4eeec415924.svg) | 平台张力，35 mN/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/8dc6f7e80ecaac9fa07890ce.svg) | 低浓度段每十倍浓度的斜率，本例−18.5 mN/m。 |

仅对无量纲比值c/c*取对数。浓度低于转折时下降，高于转折时为平台。c=0.1 mmol/L得到53.5 mN/m；构造含噪数据拟合c*≈0.98855 mmol/L。

横轴采用浓度的对数，是因为实验常跨越多个数量级。0.01、0.1、1和10毫摩尔每升在对数轴上等距，而在线性轴上前两个点几乎挤在一起。示例规定平台为35毫牛顿每米，转折浓度为1毫摩尔每升，转折之前每增加十倍浓度，张力下降18.5毫牛顿每米。因此0.1毫摩尔每升对应53.5毫牛顿每米，0.01毫摩尔每升对应72。程序在一系列候选转折位置上拟合下降段与平台，比较残差平方和，含噪数据得到约0.98855毫摩尔每升。转折位置附近的代价曲线展示哪些候选与数据更相容，避免只看到一个精确到很多位的小数。

![A为指定指数时间曲线；B与C为构造浓度系列及转折搜索；D根据IAPWS参考关系计算纯水温度曲线。前三图是教学模型，D是公开物性参考计算。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/b3e6243fe5ddc35ba044662d.svg?v=b3e6243fe5dd)

图 4A为指定指数时间曲线；B与C为构造浓度系列及转折搜索；D根据IAPWS参考关系计算纯水温度曲线。前三图是教学模型，D是公开物性参考计算。

测量浓度系列时，低浓度样品尤其容易受到痕量杂质与容器吸附影响。配液顺序、体积误差和母液浓度都可能移动横轴；等待时间不一致又会移动纵轴。如果浓度越高的样品恰好等待越久，就把两个变量混在了一起。对于混合表面活性剂或蛋白质体系，曲线可能具有宽转变、多个过程或持续的界面重排，分段直线适合描述清晰转折的数据，不应把每一个平台都自动命名为某种单一聚集机制。增加独立的散射、荧光探针或其他聚集信息，可以把经验转折与分子结构更紧密地联系。

$$
\gamma=B\Theta^{\mu}(1+b\Theta),\qquad\Theta=1-T/T_c
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7db9474e1e95a533a1714618.svg) | 纯水–水蒸气平衡参考张力，mN/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7533ad047439b7d799dd7afe.svg) | IAPWS系数，235.8 mN/m。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4098ceb27149a2b9e1dfa022.svg) | 由临界温度定义的无量纲温度变量。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/75d2faaecd7646e08d872763.svg) | 指数1.256，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a77a353782459b753313d802.svg) | 系数−0.625，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/c15eeb9e7a3ff525fbdcd2f1.svg) | 绝对温度，K。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/588edc03ab9f438e1d5b1f2e.svg) | 水的临界温度，647.096 K。 |

IAPWS参考关系适用于三相点至临界点间的水–水蒸气平衡。20°C换成293.15 K，得到72.73614 mN/m。图示采用1至90°C范围。

纯水参考也需要规定温度。图中的水曲线按照IAPWS给出的水–水蒸气平衡参考关系计算，20摄氏度约为72.736毫牛顿每米。它是公开参考公式的计算结果，用来理解温度趋势与检验单位换算；实验中的水样还受到纯度、气氛、界面年龄和仪器状态影响。公式中的温度必须换成开尔文，20摄氏度对应293.15开尔文，不能把20直接代入绝对温度比值。参考曲线随升温下降，也说明比较两份只差少量张力的样品时，温度稳定和记录十分重要。

## 交互实验：把三个误差来源分开

下面的薄板使用与计算示例相同的宽度、厚度和液体密度。表面张力按照给定的时间曲线变化，三个控制量分别是表面年龄、浸入深度与接触角。先保持完全润湿和零浸入深度，改变年龄，观察张力下降怎样变成测力读数下降。再固定年龄，把板浸得更深：液体本身的指定张力没有改变，但浮力抵消了一部分向下作用。最后改变接触角，比较“直接用力除以周长”的结果与按已知条件校正后的结果。三个操作分别对应界面演化、体积排液和几何投影。

## 交互：年龄、浮力与润湿

改变一个变量，观察真实张力、测力值与直接除周长的结果。模型采用10 mm宽、0.1 mm厚的板。

[Figure: 力与深度关系](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/p04/#P04-plot)

把年龄设为2秒、深度设为零、角度设为零时，张力约48.61毫牛顿每米，读数约0.982毫牛顿。增加深度到5毫米后，读数降低0.04905毫牛顿，但校正后的张力不变。再把接触角设为30度，毛细力还会乘上约0.866，说明两种几何因素可以同时存在。交互图中能够显示校正值，是因为模型明确知道这些输入；真实实验需要通过探针润湿、几何测量或独立实验建立相应条件。这个区别也给出了准备实验的顺序：先确定哪些变量能够控制和测量，再决定用哪条公式从信号反推出材料性质。

还可以把实验改成一个判断题：如果两个样品在零深度时读数不同，但深度曲线的斜率相同，哪些原因仍然可能存在？表面张力差和接触角差都能改变截距，因此需要控制润湿状态来分开。如果斜率也改变，应检查密度、板的实际截面、附着气泡和深度标定。把曲线的不同特征与不同物理因素对应起来，能够避免对每一次读数变化都给出同一个分子解释。对于新配方，先观察空白溶剂，再测加入单一组分的样品，最后比较完整配方，有助于找出哪一步真正改变了界面行为。

## 完整分析：让力、轮廓和浓度结果互相解释

完整程序生成三组构造观测：薄板随浸入深度变化的力、悬滴下段轮廓，以及表面张力随浓度变化的数据。它分别采用直线外推、Young–Laplace轮廓拟合和转折搜索，再把原始数据、拟合值与结果保存为表格。固定随机种子使相同环境下重复执行能够得到一致的教学结果，而输入数据中的噪声仍然保留在图里。读程序时，可以沿着“物理模型产生预测—观测与预测相减—调整参数减小差异”的顺序理解，不需要先掌握优化算法的全部数学推导。

### 完整Python：测力、液滴与浓度转折

执行三个独立拟合，保存观测和结果，并计算IAPWS水参考。

```
"""Surface-tension measurements: plate forces, pendant shape and surface age.
All measured-looking points are constructed teaching observations.
Water reference: IAPWS R1-76(2014), https://iapws.org/technical-guidance/release/Surf-H2O
Run: python main.py --output results --language en
"""
from pathlib import Path
import argparse,json
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
from scipy.optimize import least_squares
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle,Circle

def water_tension(temperature_c):
    tau=1-(np.asarray(temperature_c)+273.15)/647.096
    return 235.8*tau**1.256*(1-.625*tau)

def plate(gamma_mNm,theta_deg,depth_mm):
    width=.010;thickness=.0001;perimeter=2*(width+thickness)
    capillary=(gamma_mNm/1000)*perimeter*np.cos(np.deg2rad(theta_deg))
    buoyancy=1000*9.81*width*thickness*(np.asarray(depth_mm)/1000)
    return (capillary-buoyancy)*1000

def pendant(z_mm,gamma_mNm=50.,apex_radius_mm=1.):
    """Axisymmetric pendant interface: z upward from bottom apex, arc length s.
    dr/ds=cos(phi), dz/ds=sin(phi). Pressure decreases upward, giving
    dphi/ds=2/b-(Delta_rho*g/gamma)*z-sin(phi)/r.
    All numerical lengths here are mm; coefficient converts SI to mm^-2.
    """
    b=apex_radius_mm;k=1000*9.81/(gamma_mNm/1000)*1e-6;eps=1e-5
    def fun(s,y):
        r,z,phi=y
        return [np.cos(phi),np.sin(phi),2/b-k*z-np.sin(phi)/max(r,1e-10)]
    zmax=float(np.max(z_mm))+.01
    def stop(s,y):return y[1]-zmax
    stop.terminal=True;stop.direction=1
    sol=solve_ivp(fun,[eps,6*b],[eps,eps*eps/(2*b),eps/b],events=stop,max_step=.01,rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-10)
    return np.interp(z_mm,sol.y[1],sol.y[0])

def dynamic(age_s):return 35+37*np.exp(-np.asarray(age_s)/2)

def breakpoint_fit(logc,y):
    knots=np.linspace(-.5,.5,401);loss=[];coeffs=[]
    for k in knots:
        X=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(logc)),np.minimum(logc-k,0)])
        coeff=np.linalg.lstsq(X,y,rcond=None)[0];loss.append(np.sum((X@coeff-y)**2));coeffs.append(coeff)
    j=int(np.argmin(loss));return knots[j],coeffs[j],knots,np.asarray(loss)

def main():
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser();p.add_argument('--output',type=Path,required=True);p.add_argument('--language',choices=['zh','en'],default='en');args=p.parse_args()
    out=args.output;out.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True);tr=lambda z,e:z if args.language=='zh' else e
    plt.rcParams.update({'font.family':['Microsoft YaHei','DejaVu Sans'],'font.size':11,'axes.spines.top':False,'axes.spines.right':False,'svg.fonttype':'none','figure.facecolor':'#fbfcfc','savefig.facecolor':'#fbfcfc','text.color':'#18344a'})
    blue='#186c94';green='#188777';orange='#d27839'
    def save(f,n):f.savefig(out/f'{n}-{args.language}.svg',bbox_inches='tight');f.savefig(out/f'{n}-{args.language}.png',bbox_inches='tight',dpi=150);plt.close(f)
    rng=np.random.default_rng(1804);depth=np.linspace(0,5,31);forces=plate(50,0,depth)+rng.normal(0,.003,len(depth));coeff=np.polyfit(depth,forces,1)
    fitted_gamma=coeff[1]/.0202
    z=np.linspace(.08,1.6,70);r=pendant(z);r_obs=r+rng.normal(0,.003,len(z))
    fit=least_squares(lambda p:pendant(z,p[0],p[1])-r_obs,[48,1.02],bounds=([20,.8],[90,1.2]),xtol=1e-10,ftol=1e-10,gtol=1e-10)
    gamma_fit,b_fit=fit.x;pred=pendant(z,gamma_fit,b_fit)
    logc=np.linspace(-2,1,45);c=10**logc;gamma_true=35-18.5*np.minimum(logc,0);gamma_obs=gamma_true+rng.normal(0,.3,len(c));k,bc,knots,loss=breakpoint_fit(logc,gamma_obs)
    noiseless_k,*_=breakpoint_fit(logc,gamma_true)
    summary={'plate_gamma_fit_mNm':float(fitted_gamma),'plate_intercept_mN':float(coeff[1]),'plate_slope_mN_per_mm':float(coeff[0]),
       'plate_force_50_zero_mN':float(plate(50,0,0)),'plate_force_50_5mm_mN':float(plate(50,0,5)),
       'plate_30deg_naive_mNm':float(50*np.cos(np.pi/6)),
       'pendant_gamma_fit_mNm':float(gamma_fit),'pendant_apex_radius_fit_mm':float(b_fit),
       'pendant_residual_rms_um':float(np.sqrt(np.mean((r_obs-pred)**2))*1000),
       'cmc_fit_mM':float(10**k),'cmc_noiseless_mM':float(10**noiseless_k),
       'surface_age_2s_mNm':float(dynamic(2)),'water20_mNm':float(water_tension(20)),
       'data_kind':'Constructed plate/drop/surfactant observations; IAPWS water reference calculation'}
    (out/'summary.json').write_text(json.dumps(summary,indent=2),encoding='utf8')
    np.savetxt(out/'data.csv',np.column_stack([depth,forces,np.polyval(coeff,depth)]),delimiter=',',header='depth_mm,force_mN,fit_mN',comments='')
    np.savetxt(out/'pendant.csv',np.column_stack([z,r_obs,pred]),delimiter=',',header='height_above_bottom_mm,observed_radius_mm,fitted_radius_mm',comments='')
    np.savetxt(out/'concentration.csv',np.column_stack([c,gamma_obs,gamma_true]),delimiter=',',header='concentration_mM,observed_tension_mNm,specified_tension_mNm',comments='')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,4.7));a,b=axs
    a.set_xlim(0,10);a.set_ylim(0,5);a.axis('off');a.add_patch(Rectangle((.5,.8),9,3,facecolor='#d2e9eb',edgecolor=blue,lw=2));a.add_patch(Rectangle((6,.8),.22,3,color=orange))
    for x in np.linspace(1,5.5,9):a.scatter(x,2.2+.45*np.sin(x*2),s=35,color=green)
    a.annotate('',xy=(4.8,4.2),xytext=(6.1,4.2),arrowprops={'arrowstyle':'->','color':orange,'lw':2});a.text(5,4.65,tr('移动隔板，压缩受限表面','Move a barrier; compress a confined surface'),ha='center',fontsize=10)
    a.plot([2.5,2.5],[2.5,4.1],color='#455b6b');a.add_patch(Circle((2.5,2.5),.25,facecolor='white',edgecolor=blue));a.text(5,.3,tr('Pockels：控制面积与表面污染','Pockels: area and surface contamination'),ha='center',fontsize=10);a.set_title(tr('A  1891年的表面研究思想','A  Surface experiments reported in 1891'),loc='left')
    b.set_xlim(-3,3);b.set_ylim(-2.4,2.3);b.axis('off')
    for sign in [-1,1]:
        xx=np.linspace(.3,3,150);yy=.5*np.exp(-((xx-.3)/.35)**.5)
        b.fill_between(sign*xx,-2.4,yy,color='#d2e9eb');b.plot(sign*xx,yy,color=blue)
    b.add_patch(Rectangle((-.3,-1),.6,2.6,facecolor='#b0bdc5',edgecolor='#455b6b'));b.plot([0,0],[1.6,2.2],color='#455b6b')
    for x in [-.3,.3]:b.annotate('',xy=(x,-.65),xytext=(x,.45),arrowprops={'arrowstyle':'->','color':orange,'lw':2})
    b.annotate('',xy=(0,.15),xytext=(0,-1.5),arrowprops={'arrowstyle':'->','color':green,'lw':2});b.text(.7,-.65,tr('毛细力\n向下','Capillary force\ndownward'),fontsize=10);b.text(.4,-1.7,tr('浮力向上','Buoyancy upward'),fontsize=10);b.set_title(tr('B  Wilhelmy板：读出界面力','B  Wilhelmy plate: read interfacial force'),loc='left',fontsize=11);save(fig,'principle')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,4.8));a,b=axs
    a.scatter(depth,forces,color=blue,s=25,label=tr('构造观测','Constructed observations'));a.plot(depth,np.polyval(coeff,depth),color=orange,label=tr('线性拟合','Linear fit'));a.set_xlabel(tr('浸入深度 / mm','Immersion depth / mm'));a.set_ylabel(tr('扣除干板重量的力 / mN','Force after dry-weight tare / mN'));a.legend();a.set_title(tr('A  零深度截距分离浮力','A  Zero-depth intercept separates buoyancy'),loc='left')
    theta=np.linspace(0,70,200);b.plot(theta,50*np.cos(np.deg2rad(theta)),color=orange);b.axhline(50,color=green,ls='--',label=tr('规定真实张力50 mN/m','Specified true tension 50 mN/m'));b.set_xlabel(tr('实际接触角 / °','Actual contact angle / °'));b.set_ylabel(tr('假定完全润湿得到的张力 / mN/m','Tension inferred assuming complete wetting / mN/m'));b.legend(fontsize=9);b.set_title(tr('B  把接触角误当作零','B  Incorrectly treating contact angle as zero'),loc='left');fig.tight_layout();save(fig,'plate')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(11.5,5.5));a,b=axs
    zfull=np.linspace(0,1.8,240);rfull=pendant(zfull,gamma_fit,b_fit)
    for sign in [-1,1]:a.scatter(sign*r_obs,z,color=blue,s=13);a.plot(sign*rfull,zfull,color=orange,lw=2)
    a.set_aspect('equal');a.set_xlabel(tr('径向位置 / mm','Radial position / mm'));a.set_ylabel(tr('距底端顶点的高度 / mm','Height above bottom apex / mm'));a.set_title(tr('A  Young–Laplace：悬滴下段轮廓','A  Young–Laplace: lower pendant profile'),loc='left',fontsize=11)
    b.scatter(z,(r_obs-pred)*1000,s=20,color=blue);b.axhline(0,color='#a1abb2');b.set_xlabel(tr('距底端顶点的高度 / mm','Height above bottom apex / mm'));b.set_ylabel(tr('径向残差 / μm','Radial residual / μm'));b.set_title(tr('B  同时估计张力与顶点半径','B  Fit tension and apex radius together'),loc='left');fig.tight_layout();save(fig,'pendant')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(2,2,figsize=(11.5,8.7));a,b,d,e=axs.ravel();time=np.logspace(-2,2,200)
    a.semilogx(time,dynamic(time),color=blue);a.axhline(35,color=green,ls='--');a.set_xlabel(tr('表面年龄 / s','Surface age / s'));a.set_ylabel('γ / mN/m');a.set_title(tr('A  规定的动态吸附教学曲线','A  Prescribed dynamic teaching curve'),loc='left')
    b.semilogx(c,gamma_obs,'o',color=blue,ms=4);b.semilogx(c,bc[0]+bc[1]*np.minimum(logc-k,0),color=orange);b.axvline(10**k,color=green,ls='--');b.set_xlabel(tr('浓度 / mmol/L','Concentration / mmol/L'));b.set_ylabel('γ / mN/m');b.set_title(tr('B  转折与平台，构造数据','B  Break and plateau, constructed data'),loc='left')
    d.plot(10**knots,loss,color=orange);d.set_xlabel(tr('候选转折浓度 / mmol/L','Candidate break concentration / mmol/L'));d.set_ylabel(tr('残差平方和 / (mN/m)²','Residual sum of squares / (mN/m)²'));d.set_title(tr('C  检查转折选择的代价','C  Inspect the cost of breakpoint choices'),loc='left')
    temp=np.linspace(1,90,100);e.plot(temp,water_tension(temp),color=green);e.scatter([20],[water_tension(20)],color=orange);e.set_xlabel(tr('温度 / °C','Temperature / °C'));e.set_ylabel('γ / mN/m');e.set_title(tr('D  IAPWS纯水–水蒸气参考计算','D  IAPWS water–vapor reference calculation'),loc='left',fontsize=11);fig.tight_layout();save(fig,'dynamic')
    print(json.dumps(summary))

if __name__=='__main__':main()
```

计算中还保留了无噪声的浓度系列，用来核对转折搜索能否恢复规定的1毫摩尔每升。薄板零深度与5毫米深度的结果则可直接用排液体积手算，作为独立的单位检查。这样的核对把算法误差与观测噪声分开，也让图中的小数有可追踪的物理起点。

三种分析共同说明了测量定义的重要性。薄板曲线的截距对应接触线作用，悬滴轮廓对应密度差与曲率的静态平衡，浓度转折对应指定配方下性质变化的位置。研究一份蛋白质溶液时，可先用动态张力观察界面建立的时间过程，再在匹配年龄下比较配方；若关注蛋白质最终吸附了多少、吸附层是否含水或发生重排，则需要直接观察界面层的实验。这样，张力测量就成为连接溶液配方、界面动力学与后续吸附研究的一步，而每一条曲线都能回答一个明确的物理问题。

# Surface tension: Drops, interfaces and interfacial energy

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/p04/en/
Language: en

Measure interfacial tension through plate forces and pendant contours, then separate surface age and concentration effects.

## Why a little detergent changes a large water surface

A drop of water often beads on plastic, whereas the same volume spreads farther after a little surfactant is added. A different interfacial problem appears when a protein formulation is shaken: newly created air–liquid interfaces can adsorb protein and influence its conformation and aggregation. Uniform coatings, fine emulsion droplets and persistent foams all depend on interfaces. Surface-tension measurements connect these observations through a precise question. At specified temperature, composition and interface age, how much free energy is required to create additional liquid surface? A force instrument asks an equivalent practical question: how strongly does the interface pull along a line of contact with a probe?

Molecules inside a liquid are surrounded mainly by similar neighbours. Molecules near a boundary experience a different environment, so creating additional interface generally requires work. A small drop therefore tends toward a compact shape; a sphere has the smallest area for a given volume. Imagining a contracting film helps establish the direction of interfacial forces, provided the analogy is used carefully. A liquid interface flows and exchanges molecules with its surroundings, whereas an elastic rubber sheet has identifiable material points and a different mechanical response. Surface tension is expressed in newtons per metre, commonly millinewtons per metre. Its energetic description uses joules per square metre. These units are equivalent because work is force times distance, while the new area generated by moving a straight boundary is boundary length times distance.

The term surface tension usually refers to a liquid–gas interface. An oil–water boundary also has interfacial tension, with two liquids on opposite sides; its pendant-drop calculation uses their density difference. Viscosity describes resistance to flow inside the fluid. Honey flows slowly mainly because of its viscosity, whereas the energetic cost of enlarging its boundary is described by interfacial tension. Both properties influence drop formation, but they are different measured quantities. Similarly, low surface tension does not automatically produce complete spreading on every solid: solid–liquid and solid–gas contributions also enter the contact angle. This chapter follows two ways of reading interfacial tension, through force and through shape, before adding time and concentration to the experiment.

## Making surface cleanliness an experimental variable

In a letter published in *Nature* in 1891, Agnes Pockels described a rectangular trough approximately 70 centimetres long, 5 centimetres wide and 2 centimetres deep. It was filled to the rim, and a movable strip divided the water surface into separate regions. Moving the strip changed the area available to material at the surface. She also investigated surface forces using a small disk and a sensitive balance. The value of this arrangement was experimental control: a vague observation that one water surface behaved differently from another became a comparison of area, surface material and measuring conditions. The historical apparatus diagram reconstructs this experimental idea rather than reproducing a photograph or claiming exact mechanical dimensions for every part.

The connection with modern measurements is direct. Residues on a vessel, organic material acquired from air and traces of cleaning agent on a pipette can alter the interface that actually reaches the instrument. Pockels also revisited the relationship between cleaning and some earlier interpretations in later correspondence. A stable numerical display is therefore one part of a controlled measurement. When trace material continues to adsorb, surface tension can change with time even though the bulk solution appears unchanged. Proteins, lipids and polymers may additionally rearrange at the boundary. An experiment specifies preparation, the moment at which an interface is formed, its waiting time and the contact history of the probe or drop.

![Left: original schematic of the trough and movable-barrier idea reported by Pockels in 1891; dots represent surface material. Right: a completely wetted plate, downward capillary force and upward buoyancy; geometry and arrows are schematic.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/2faac3f432c0a14a4d7ab2fe.svg?v=2faac3f432c0)

Figure 1Left: original schematic of the trough and movable-barrier idea reported by Pockels in 1891; dots represent surface material. Right: a completely wetted plate, downward capillary force and upward buoyancy; geometry and arrows are schematic.

A modern Wilhelmy instrument suspends a thin plate from a sensitive balance. When the lower end contacts and enters the liquid, a meniscus forms around the plate. The vertical component of the force along that contact line changes the balance reading. Pendant-drop analysis observes a complementary consequence: gravity stretches a hanging drop, while interfacial tension favours a compact shape. These methods encode interface properties into different observables. Plate measurements require particular attention to wetted perimeter, contact angle and buoyancy. Shape measurements require accurate image scale, density difference and contour extraction. Understanding that distinction makes it easier to select a method for a solution that adsorbs strongly to solid probes or evolves rapidly after a fresh interface is created.

## Separating capillary force from buoyancy

The dry plate is weighed in air, and that weight is subtracted from subsequent readings. This operation is called taring. The remaining reading contains capillary force at the contact line and buoyancy acting on the submerged part of the plate. Here downward force is positive. Complete wetting produces a downward capillary contribution, while buoyancy acts upward. Consider a plate 10 millimetres wide and 0.1 millimetres thick. Its wetted perimeter includes both broad faces and both narrow edges, giving 20.2 millimetres. Using the width alone would omit most of the contact line. The narrow-edge contribution becomes small for a thin plate, but remains a defined part of the geometry.

$$
F_{\mathrm{tare}}=\gamma P\cos\theta-\Delta\rho\,gwtz,\qquad P=2(w+t)
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/b01fb8392b6a8aa7cb7333fd.svg) | Vertical force after dry-weight tare, N; downward positive. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7db9474e1e95a533a1714618.svg) | Liquid interfacial tension, N/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/1aaddf0d4be4d873ff6c0600.svg) | Wetted perimeter, m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/06e47e2878930095abe73547.svg) | Contact angle through the liquid. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/988fbc7bbcda53116494bdef.svg) | Liquid–air density contrast, kg/m³; 1000 here. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/439e3cc8d431c550923e0870.svg) | Gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s². |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/5f85a26e5089def254fee2b9.svg) | Plate width, m; 0.010 here. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/707bb132def3690d81bf1f0c.svg) | Plate thickness, m; 0.0001 here. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9032cb23a878659e74b670d3.svg) | Immersion depth, m. |

For a static plate with regular cross section and fixed contact angle, subtract buoyancy from vertical capillary force. γ=0.050 N/m, θ=0 and z=0 give 0.00101 N; z=0.005 m gives 0.00096095 N.

For a surface tension of 50 millinewtons per metre and zero contact angle, the capillary force at zero immersion is 1.01 millinewtons. Immersing the plate by 5 millimetres displaces liquid with volume equal to width times thickness times depth. With the stated density and gravity, buoyancy becomes 0.04905 millinewtons, leaving a downward tared force of 0.96095 millinewtons. Directly dividing that deeper reading by perimeter underestimates tension. A useful experiment records several depths and fits force against depth. Extrapolating the line to zero depth removes the volume-dependent buoyancy contribution. Its slope describes that contribution, while its intercept gives capillary force under the assumed wetting conditions. The noisy example yields an intercept near 1.01048 millinewtons and a tension of 50.02385 millinewtons per metre.

![Constructed observations: A separates buoyancy through the zero-depth intercept; B holds true tension at 50 mN/m and shows the consequence of incorrectly assuming zero contact angle.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/7eb3fba97f9e4ce0fa2d0cae.svg?v=7eb3fba97f9e)

Figure 2Constructed observations: A separates buoyancy through the zero-depth intercept; B holds true tension at 50 mN/m and shows the consequence of incorrectly assuming zero contact angle.

Contact angle determines the fraction of interfacial force projected vertically. If the actual angle is 30 degrees but the analysis assumes complete wetting, a true tension of 50 millinewtons per metre appears as about 43.30. The balance measures force; the angle assumption comes from the interaction between probe and liquid. Platinum plates are often used to establish favourable wetting, together with cleaning and temperature control appropriate to the instrument and solution. A protein layer adsorbing onto the plate may change its wetting during a sequence. Time-dependent force can then contain both evolution of the liquid surface and evolution of the probe surface. Independent probes or an optical shape measurement help distinguish those contributions when the research question requires it.

Preserve force, depth, time and temperature alongside the final tension. An attached bubble changes displaced volume, nearby vessel walls can disturb the meniscus, and drifting liquid level changes actual immersion. At low surfactant concentration, adsorption to the vessel and probe may also consume an appreciable fraction of dissolved material. Matching container size, liquid volume and waiting procedure makes comparisons more interpretable. Examine residuals from the force–depth line as well. A systematic curve suggests checking assumptions such as constant contact angle, stable contact line and constant plate cross section. Repeatedly obtaining the same intercept is useful precision information, while a shared error in perimeter or wetting can shift every replicate together.

## Reading interfacial tension from a drop contour

A camera initially records a contrast boundary around a hanging drop. Turning that boundary into tension requires understanding pressure across a curved interface. Tension pulls along the surface, and force directions at neighbouring positions are not parallel on a curved surface. Their combined effect is balanced by a pressure difference. The Young–Laplace relation expresses this balance using curvature in two perpendicular directions. A sphere has the same curvature radius in both directions, whereas a cylindrical surface is straight along one direction. A single visible cross-sectional radius is consequently enough only when the geometry tells us how the second curvature behaves.

$$
\Delta p=\gamma\left(\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}\right)
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/388b34d468326c8df9f49910.svg) | Pressure difference across interface, Pa; inside minus outside for a spherical drop. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7db9474e1e95a533a1714618.svg) | Interfacial tension, N/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9cac43c0b77042679a064ee0.svg) | First principal curvature radius, m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/99a0a123eddd37514ed7e5ce.svg) | Second principal curvature radius in the perpendicular direction, m. |

At mechanical equilibrium the two principal curvatures contribute additively. One spherical interface with γ=0.050 N/m and both radii 0.001 m gives 100 Pa. A pendant drop also satisfies the hydrostatic pressure variation with height.

A spherical interface with radius 1 millimetre and tension 50 millinewtons per metre has a pressure difference of 100 pascals. This example contains one liquid–gas interface. A soap film encloses a gas with two interfaces and requires accounting for both. Within a pendant drop, hydrostatic pressure decreases upward from the bottom apex. Local curvature changes accordingly. The program integrates along the surface from the nearly circular apex region, then adjusts tension and apex radius until its calculated contour matches observed coordinates. The figure shows the lower portion of the drop, where the competition between gravity and curvature is explicit; attachment near a needle introduces additional apparatus geometry.

![Lower pendant profile from an axisymmetric Young–Laplace model, with prescribed tension 50 mN/m and radial noise of standard deviation 3 μm. Left: contour and fit. Right: radial residuals.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/50ea9da6565fae40df68d8e1.svg?v=50ea9da6565f)

Figure 3Lower pendant profile from an axisymmetric Young–Laplace model, with prescribed tension 50 mN/m and radial noise of standard deviation 3 μm. Left: contour and fit. Right: radial residuals.

The constructed observation uses tension 50 millinewtons per metre and bottom-apex radius 1 millimetre, with radial coordinate noise of standard deviation 3 micrometres. Fitting gives approximately 50.955 millinewtons per metre, apex radius 1.00059 millimetres and a radial root-mean-square residual of 2.56 micrometres. Tension and apex radius influence the contour in related but distinguishable ways. Apex radius controls local curvature; tension determines how strongly gravity changes shape along height. For a very small, nearly spherical drop, gravitational deformation is weak, and a wide range of tensions can be compatible with an almost circular contour. A stable drop with appreciable, well-resolved deformation generally provides more shape information than simply selecting the smallest possible drop.

Image calibration is part of the physical model. A wrong pixel size alters both curvature and the length scale over which gravity acts. A tilted camera, an inclined drop axis or continuing oscillation can disrupt the assumed static axisymmetric shape. Calibrate against a known dimension, inspect left–right consistency, wait for motion to decay and use the density difference at the measurement temperature. A water drop in oil requires water density minus oil density; a water drop in air often permits approximating the difference by water density. Read residuals as a function of height, not just as one total error. Small scattered residuals and a persistent deviation along one side motivate different checks of lighting, contour extraction and axis placement.

A scale comparison gives an additional check on shape fitting. Curvature pressure varies approximately as tension divided by radius, while the gravitational pressure change varies as density difference times gravity times height. Increasing drop size therefore strengthens gravity relative to curvature and moves the contour away from a sphere. Pixel count alone is insufficient: physical length per pixel is required. Very large drops may approach detachment and change during imaging, so the useful range balances identifiable deformation with stable suspension. Inspect clear left and right edges, a fully visible bottom apex and unobstructed contour regions before fitting. These visual conditions have a direct effect on which part of the physical shape is available to the calculation.

## A fresh surface can belong to an old solution

Surfactant molecules commonly contain water-compatible and water-avoiding regions. Their arrangement at an air–water or oil–water boundary can lower interfacial free energy. Immediately after a fresh interface forms, its molecular population differs from that after prolonged exposure to the solution. Molecules must travel from the bulk, adsorb and sometimes reorient. Large molecules can also unfold or form networks of interactions. Surface tension therefore depends on surface age as well as formulation. Surface age begins when that particular interface is created. It is distinct from the age of the bottle of solution: a bubble blown from a solution stored overnight still presents a newly formed interface.

$$
\gamma(a)=\gamma_{\infty}+(\gamma_0-\gamma_{\infty})e^{-a/\tau_r}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/349015631ec44ef653936c85.svg) | Surface age, s. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/326221aa7409b4a62fda0814.svg) | Tension at that age, mN/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/97e4157d29a2b15aac854b6c.svg) | Initial tension, 72 mN/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/dd2b4bb24d7b7e6ed71658d9.svg) | Long-time limit, 35 mN/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7f4562fee555940b00253509.svg) | Prescribed relaxation time, 2 s. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/0be950b3e59846bc80f7e4ca.svg) | Base of natural logarithms; dimensionless. |

A prescribed teaching relaxation: the difference falls by 1/e in each τr. At age 2 s, γ=48.61154 mN/m; a particular adsorption system determines its own kinetic time law.

The example separates this time effect with a prescribed exponential curve falling from 72 to 35 millinewtons per metre, with a relaxation time of 2 seconds. At 2 seconds the tension is about 48.61 because 36.8 percent of the initial difference from the long-time value remains. This is a teaching model of relaxation, rather than an experimentally identified adsorption constant for a particular protein or detergent. Real adsorption can involve diffusion, activation barriers, occupied surface sites and molecular rearrangement, producing several time regimes. The experimentally useful relationship remains clear: changing observation age at fixed formulation and temperature can change the measured force and the shape of a newly formed drop.

Maximum bubble-pressure measurements repeatedly generate new interfaces. Gas emerges from an immersed capillary, and the developing interface passes through an approximately hemispherical state. At that stage the curvature radius equals the capillary radius and the curvature pressure reaches the relevant maximum. The measured pressure also includes the hydrostatic contribution from capillary immersion, which must be removed before interpreting tension. Changing the formation rate accesses different interface ages. The operative age is associated with growth from interface formation to the pressure maximum, rather than automatically equalling the entire bubble-detachment cycle. Comparisons with plate and pendant-drop measurements should therefore align the ages actually sampled by each method.

This distinction is especially useful for sprays and foams. A rapidly created interface may initially behave much closer to the solvent than a slowly equilibrated surface of the same formulation. A coating operation that forms fresh area in milliseconds therefore asks a different question from a drop held for minutes. For protein formulations, molecular rearrangements can continue after adsorption begins, so the time record itself carries information. Record the definition of time zero, the acquisition interval and the range over which a plateau was observed. Those details let another experiment reproduce the physical comparison rather than merely reproduce a final number.

Time curves also influence sampling. Repeatedly lifting or compressing one interface can change its area and molecular arrangement, so the next measurement may begin from a different state. Comparisons of fresh interfaces require a defined way to recreate them; ageing experiments benefit from observations that disturb the interface as little as possible. For proteins, buffer composition, salt and temperature influence charge, molecular interactions and conformational stability. An independent replicate repeats the preparation and waiting procedure with a newly established interface. Many time points from one interface instead describe the evolution of that particular interface. Both records are useful, but they answer different questions about variability.

## Connecting a concentration break to molecular aggregation

Increasing surfactant concentration often lowers surface tension through adsorption. At a certain concentration range, additional material increasingly forms aggregates such as micelles, and the tension curve may approach a flatter plateau. A micelle can be pictured as a dynamic assembly with water-avoiding portions sheltered internally and water-compatible portions exposed to water. Molecules continue exchanging between aggregates and solution. The critical micelle concentration is commonly estimated from a change in a concentration-dependent property; tension is one available property. Temperature, salt and surfactant composition influence the transition, so a concentration value belongs with its formulation and conditions.

$$
\gamma(c)=\gamma_p+k\min\!\left[\log_{10}(c/c_*),0\right]
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/482cc0189b34e0e766508729.svg) | Tension at concentration c, mN/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/b332ba26d1b8a3e4b8f817ed.svg) | Surfactant concentration, mmol/L. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/71a1a028a21bc2c5b0e55c55.svg) | Break concentration, mmol/L; one here. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4ea68d49e66db4eeec415924.svg) | Plateau tension, 35 mN/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/8dc6f7e80ecaac9fa07890ce.svg) | Slope per concentration decade below the break, −18.5 mN/m here. |

Take a logarithm of the dimensionless ratio c/c*. Below the break the curve decreases; above it a plateau is specified. c=0.1 mmol/L gives 53.5 mN/m; the noisy construction fits c*≈0.98855 mmol/L.

A logarithmic concentration axis is useful because the experiment often spans several orders of magnitude. Values of 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10 millimoles per litre are equally spaced on that axis; on a linear axis the smallest values crowd together. The constructed curve has a plateau of 35 millinewtons per metre and a break at 1 millimole per litre. Below the break, each tenfold concentration increase lowers tension by 18.5 millinewtons per metre. Thus 0.1 millimoles per litre corresponds to 53.5, while 0.01 corresponds to 72. The program tests candidate break positions, fitting the declining segment and plateau at each position. The lowest residual sum of squares gives about 0.98855 millimoles per litre for the noisy data. Plotting that fitting cost against candidate concentration reveals how strongly the data distinguish nearby choices.

![A: prescribed exponential age curve. B–C: constructed concentration series and breakpoint search. D: water temperature dependence calculated from IAPWS. The first three panels are teaching models; D is a physical reference calculation.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/experimental-methods/figures/b0274cc19a0f97d126d28539.svg?v=b0274cc19a0f)

Figure 4A: prescribed exponential age curve. B–C: constructed concentration series and breakpoint search. D: water temperature dependence calculated from IAPWS. The first three panels are teaching models; D is a physical reference calculation.

Low-concentration samples are particularly sensitive to trace impurities and adsorption onto containers. Dilution errors and stock-solution uncertainty shift the concentration axis, while unequal waiting times shift the tension axis. If concentrated samples also happen to wait longer, concentration and age become entangled. Mixed surfactants and proteins may show broad transitions, multiple processes or continuing interfacial rearrangement. A segmented line usefully describes a distinct break, while molecular interpretation benefits from independent information about aggregation, such as scattering or a suitable fluorescence probe. Keep the distinction between an observed property transition and a particular proposed aggregate structure visible in the experiment design.

$$
\gamma=B\Theta^{\mu}(1+b\Theta),\qquad\Theta=1-T/T_c
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7db9474e1e95a533a1714618.svg) | Equilibrium water–water-vapour reference tension, mN/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7533ad047439b7d799dd7afe.svg) | IAPWS coefficient, 235.8 mN/m. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/4098ceb27149a2b9e1dfa022.svg) | Dimensionless reduced temperature variable. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/75d2faaecd7646e08d872763.svg) | Exponent 1.256; dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a77a353782459b753313d802.svg) | Coefficient −0.625; dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/c15eeb9e7a3ff525fbdcd2f1.svg) | Absolute temperature, K. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/588edc03ab9f438e1d5b1f2e.svg) | Critical temperature of water, 647.096 K. |

The IAPWS reference describes equilibrium water–water-vapour tension from the triple point to the critical point. Convert 20°C to 293.15 K to obtain 72.73614 mN/m. The plot spans 1–90°C.

Even a pure-water reference requires temperature. The water curve uses the IAPWS relation for equilibrium water–water-vapour surface tension, giving approximately 72.736 millinewtons per metre at 20 degrees Celsius. It is a reference calculation used to understand temperature dependence and check units. An actual water sample also has a purity, atmosphere, surface age and instrument history. The formula requires absolute temperature: 20 degrees Celsius becomes 293.15 kelvin. Substituting 20 directly into the absolute-temperature ratio describes a completely different condition. The decreasing reference curve also explains why temperature stability matters when comparing formulations separated by a small tension difference.

For a concentration series, distribute measurements around the expected transition as well as well below and above it. Several points confined to one straight segment cannot identify where another segment begins. Replicate independently prepared solutions at selected concentrations to assess preparation variability, while repeated readings from one solution assess a different component of variation. Plot individual results before averaging. A concentration-dependent drift in waiting time, probe condition or evaporation can otherwise produce an apparently persuasive transition. Matching the experimental history makes the fitted break a clearer description of how the formulation changes.

## Interactive experiment: separate three causes of a changing force

The plate below has the same width, thickness and liquid density as the numerical example. Surface tension follows the prescribed age-dependent curve. The three controls change surface age, immersion depth and contact angle. Begin with complete wetting and zero immersion, then increase age to see how evolving tension changes the balance reading. Next hold age fixed and immerse the plate farther. The specified liquid tension remains unchanged, while buoyancy cancels part of the downward force. Finally change contact angle and compare direct division of force by perimeter with the value corrected using the known geometry. These operations isolate interface evolution, displaced volume and force projection.

## Interactive: age, buoyancy and wetting

Change one variable and compare specified tension, force and direct division by perimeter. The plate is 10 mm wide and 0.1 mm thick.

[Figure: Force versus depth](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/experimental-methods/p04/en/#P04-plot)

At age 2 seconds, zero depth and zero angle, tension is approximately 48.61 millinewtons per metre and the reading is about 0.982 millinewtons. Increasing depth to 5 millimetres reduces force by 0.04905 millinewtons without changing corrected tension. Setting angle to 30 degrees additionally multiplies the capillary contribution by about 0.866. The two geometric effects can therefore coexist. The model can display a corrected value because its input conditions are known. A laboratory establishes those conditions through probe wetting, dimensional measurements and independent checks. This gives a practical order of work: determine what can be controlled and measured, then choose the relation that converts the signal into the requested interfacial property.

The plotted force–depth line also offers a useful diagnostic exercise. Compare two ages at the same angle: their intercepts change because tension changes. Compare two angles at the same age: intercepts change again, for a different reason. The buoyancy slope remains fixed because plate cross section, liquid density and gravity are unchanged. A single force reading cannot separate all of these causes. A depth series supplies additional structure, and control of wetting supplies the remaining physical interpretation. This is why an experiment with several deliberate perturbations can teach more than many repeated readings at one setting.

## Complete analysis linking force, shape and concentration

The complete program generates three constructed observations: plate force against immersion, the lower contour of a pendant drop and tension against concentration. It applies linear extrapolation, Young–Laplace profile fitting and breakpoint search respectively, then exports observations, predictions and results as tables. A fixed random seed makes the teaching calculation reproducible while retaining visible measurement-like scatter. Read the analysis as a sequence of physical prediction, comparison with observation and adjustment of parameters. The scientific meaning of each fitted parameter can be understood before learning every mathematical detail of the numerical optimiser.

### Complete Python: force, drop profile and concentration break

Run three independent fits, retain observations and results, and calculate the IAPWS water reference.

```
"""Surface-tension measurements: plate forces, pendant shape and surface age.
All measured-looking points are constructed teaching observations.
Water reference: IAPWS R1-76(2014), https://iapws.org/technical-guidance/release/Surf-H2O
Run: python main.py --output results --language en
"""
from pathlib import Path
import argparse,json
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
from scipy.optimize import least_squares
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle,Circle

def water_tension(temperature_c):
    tau=1-(np.asarray(temperature_c)+273.15)/647.096
    return 235.8*tau**1.256*(1-.625*tau)

def plate(gamma_mNm,theta_deg,depth_mm):
    width=.010;thickness=.0001;perimeter=2*(width+thickness)
    capillary=(gamma_mNm/1000)*perimeter*np.cos(np.deg2rad(theta_deg))
    buoyancy=1000*9.81*width*thickness*(np.asarray(depth_mm)/1000)
    return (capillary-buoyancy)*1000

def pendant(z_mm,gamma_mNm=50.,apex_radius_mm=1.):
    """Axisymmetric pendant interface: z upward from bottom apex, arc length s.
    dr/ds=cos(phi), dz/ds=sin(phi). Pressure decreases upward, giving
    dphi/ds=2/b-(Delta_rho*g/gamma)*z-sin(phi)/r.
    All numerical lengths here are mm; coefficient converts SI to mm^-2.
    """
    b=apex_radius_mm;k=1000*9.81/(gamma_mNm/1000)*1e-6;eps=1e-5
    def fun(s,y):
        r,z,phi=y
        return [np.cos(phi),np.sin(phi),2/b-k*z-np.sin(phi)/max(r,1e-10)]
    zmax=float(np.max(z_mm))+.01
    def stop(s,y):return y[1]-zmax
    stop.terminal=True;stop.direction=1
    sol=solve_ivp(fun,[eps,6*b],[eps,eps*eps/(2*b),eps/b],events=stop,max_step=.01,rtol=1e-8,atol=1e-10)
    return np.interp(z_mm,sol.y[1],sol.y[0])

def dynamic(age_s):return 35+37*np.exp(-np.asarray(age_s)/2)

def breakpoint_fit(logc,y):
    knots=np.linspace(-.5,.5,401);loss=[];coeffs=[]
    for k in knots:
        X=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(logc)),np.minimum(logc-k,0)])
        coeff=np.linalg.lstsq(X,y,rcond=None)[0];loss.append(np.sum((X@coeff-y)**2));coeffs.append(coeff)
    j=int(np.argmin(loss));return knots[j],coeffs[j],knots,np.asarray(loss)

def main():
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser();p.add_argument('--output',type=Path,required=True);p.add_argument('--language',choices=['zh','en'],default='en');args=p.parse_args()
    out=args.output;out.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True);tr=lambda z,e:z if args.language=='zh' else e
    plt.rcParams.update({'font.family':['Microsoft YaHei','DejaVu Sans'],'font.size':11,'axes.spines.top':False,'axes.spines.right':False,'svg.fonttype':'none','figure.facecolor':'#fbfcfc','savefig.facecolor':'#fbfcfc','text.color':'#18344a'})
    blue='#186c94';green='#188777';orange='#d27839'
    def save(f,n):f.savefig(out/f'{n}-{args.language}.svg',bbox_inches='tight');f.savefig(out/f'{n}-{args.language}.png',bbox_inches='tight',dpi=150);plt.close(f)
    rng=np.random.default_rng(1804);depth=np.linspace(0,5,31);forces=plate(50,0,depth)+rng.normal(0,.003,len(depth));coeff=np.polyfit(depth,forces,1)
    fitted_gamma=coeff[1]/.0202
    z=np.linspace(.08,1.6,70);r=pendant(z);r_obs=r+rng.normal(0,.003,len(z))
    fit=least_squares(lambda p:pendant(z,p[0],p[1])-r_obs,[48,1.02],bounds=([20,.8],[90,1.2]),xtol=1e-10,ftol=1e-10,gtol=1e-10)
    gamma_fit,b_fit=fit.x;pred=pendant(z,gamma_fit,b_fit)
    logc=np.linspace(-2,1,45);c=10**logc;gamma_true=35-18.5*np.minimum(logc,0);gamma_obs=gamma_true+rng.normal(0,.3,len(c));k,bc,knots,loss=breakpoint_fit(logc,gamma_obs)
    noiseless_k,*_=breakpoint_fit(logc,gamma_true)
    summary={'plate_gamma_fit_mNm':float(fitted_gamma),'plate_intercept_mN':float(coeff[1]),'plate_slope_mN_per_mm':float(coeff[0]),
       'plate_force_50_zero_mN':float(plate(50,0,0)),'plate_force_50_5mm_mN':float(plate(50,0,5)),
       'plate_30deg_naive_mNm':float(50*np.cos(np.pi/6)),
       'pendant_gamma_fit_mNm':float(gamma_fit),'pendant_apex_radius_fit_mm':float(b_fit),
       'pendant_residual_rms_um':float(np.sqrt(np.mean((r_obs-pred)**2))*1000),
       'cmc_fit_mM':float(10**k),'cmc_noiseless_mM':float(10**noiseless_k),
       'surface_age_2s_mNm':float(dynamic(2)),'water20_mNm':float(water_tension(20)),
       'data_kind':'Constructed plate/drop/surfactant observations; IAPWS water reference calculation'}
    (out/'summary.json').write_text(json.dumps(summary,indent=2),encoding='utf8')
    np.savetxt(out/'data.csv',np.column_stack([depth,forces,np.polyval(coeff,depth)]),delimiter=',',header='depth_mm,force_mN,fit_mN',comments='')
    np.savetxt(out/'pendant.csv',np.column_stack([z,r_obs,pred]),delimiter=',',header='height_above_bottom_mm,observed_radius_mm,fitted_radius_mm',comments='')
    np.savetxt(out/'concentration.csv',np.column_stack([c,gamma_obs,gamma_true]),delimiter=',',header='concentration_mM,observed_tension_mNm,specified_tension_mNm',comments='')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,4.7));a,b=axs
    a.set_xlim(0,10);a.set_ylim(0,5);a.axis('off');a.add_patch(Rectangle((.5,.8),9,3,facecolor='#d2e9eb',edgecolor=blue,lw=2));a.add_patch(Rectangle((6,.8),.22,3,color=orange))
    for x in np.linspace(1,5.5,9):a.scatter(x,2.2+.45*np.sin(x*2),s=35,color=green)
    a.annotate('',xy=(4.8,4.2),xytext=(6.1,4.2),arrowprops={'arrowstyle':'->','color':orange,'lw':2});a.text(5,4.65,tr('移动隔板，压缩受限表面','Move a barrier; compress a confined surface'),ha='center',fontsize=10)
    a.plot([2.5,2.5],[2.5,4.1],color='#455b6b');a.add_patch(Circle((2.5,2.5),.25,facecolor='white',edgecolor=blue));a.text(5,.3,tr('Pockels：控制面积与表面污染','Pockels: area and surface contamination'),ha='center',fontsize=10);a.set_title(tr('A  1891年的表面研究思想','A  Surface experiments reported in 1891'),loc='left')
    b.set_xlim(-3,3);b.set_ylim(-2.4,2.3);b.axis('off')
    for sign in [-1,1]:
        xx=np.linspace(.3,3,150);yy=.5*np.exp(-((xx-.3)/.35)**.5)
        b.fill_between(sign*xx,-2.4,yy,color='#d2e9eb');b.plot(sign*xx,yy,color=blue)
    b.add_patch(Rectangle((-.3,-1),.6,2.6,facecolor='#b0bdc5',edgecolor='#455b6b'));b.plot([0,0],[1.6,2.2],color='#455b6b')
    for x in [-.3,.3]:b.annotate('',xy=(x,-.65),xytext=(x,.45),arrowprops={'arrowstyle':'->','color':orange,'lw':2})
    b.annotate('',xy=(0,.15),xytext=(0,-1.5),arrowprops={'arrowstyle':'->','color':green,'lw':2});b.text(.7,-.65,tr('毛细力\n向下','Capillary force\ndownward'),fontsize=10);b.text(.4,-1.7,tr('浮力向上','Buoyancy upward'),fontsize=10);b.set_title(tr('B  Wilhelmy板：读出界面力','B  Wilhelmy plate: read interfacial force'),loc='left',fontsize=11);save(fig,'principle')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,4.8));a,b=axs
    a.scatter(depth,forces,color=blue,s=25,label=tr('构造观测','Constructed observations'));a.plot(depth,np.polyval(coeff,depth),color=orange,label=tr('线性拟合','Linear fit'));a.set_xlabel(tr('浸入深度 / mm','Immersion depth / mm'));a.set_ylabel(tr('扣除干板重量的力 / mN','Force after dry-weight tare / mN'));a.legend();a.set_title(tr('A  零深度截距分离浮力','A  Zero-depth intercept separates buoyancy'),loc='left')
    theta=np.linspace(0,70,200);b.plot(theta,50*np.cos(np.deg2rad(theta)),color=orange);b.axhline(50,color=green,ls='--',label=tr('规定真实张力50 mN/m','Specified true tension 50 mN/m'));b.set_xlabel(tr('实际接触角 / °','Actual contact angle / °'));b.set_ylabel(tr('假定完全润湿得到的张力 / mN/m','Tension inferred assuming complete wetting / mN/m'));b.legend(fontsize=9);b.set_title(tr('B  把接触角误当作零','B  Incorrectly treating contact angle as zero'),loc='left');fig.tight_layout();save(fig,'plate')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(11.5,5.5));a,b=axs
    zfull=np.linspace(0,1.8,240);rfull=pendant(zfull,gamma_fit,b_fit)
    for sign in [-1,1]:a.scatter(sign*r_obs,z,color=blue,s=13);a.plot(sign*rfull,zfull,color=orange,lw=2)
    a.set_aspect('equal');a.set_xlabel(tr('径向位置 / mm','Radial position / mm'));a.set_ylabel(tr('距底端顶点的高度 / mm','Height above bottom apex / mm'));a.set_title(tr('A  Young–Laplace：悬滴下段轮廓','A  Young–Laplace: lower pendant profile'),loc='left',fontsize=11)
    b.scatter(z,(r_obs-pred)*1000,s=20,color=blue);b.axhline(0,color='#a1abb2');b.set_xlabel(tr('距底端顶点的高度 / mm','Height above bottom apex / mm'));b.set_ylabel(tr('径向残差 / μm','Radial residual / μm'));b.set_title(tr('B  同时估计张力与顶点半径','B  Fit tension and apex radius together'),loc='left');fig.tight_layout();save(fig,'pendant')
    fig,axs=plt.subplots(2,2,figsize=(11.5,8.7));a,b,d,e=axs.ravel();time=np.logspace(-2,2,200)
    a.semilogx(time,dynamic(time),color=blue);a.axhline(35,color=green,ls='--');a.set_xlabel(tr('表面年龄 / s','Surface age / s'));a.set_ylabel('γ / mN/m');a.set_title(tr('A  规定的动态吸附教学曲线','A  Prescribed dynamic teaching curve'),loc='left')
    b.semilogx(c,gamma_obs,'o',color=blue,ms=4);b.semilogx(c,bc[0]+bc[1]*np.minimum(logc-k,0),color=orange);b.axvline(10**k,color=green,ls='--');b.set_xlabel(tr('浓度 / mmol/L','Concentration / mmol/L'));b.set_ylabel('γ / mN/m');b.set_title(tr('B  转折与平台，构造数据','B  Break and plateau, constructed data'),loc='left')
    d.plot(10**knots,loss,color=orange);d.set_xlabel(tr('候选转折浓度 / mmol/L','Candidate break concentration / mmol/L'));d.set_ylabel(tr('残差平方和 / (mN/m)²','Residual sum of squares / (mN/m)²'));d.set_title(tr('C  检查转折选择的代价','C  Inspect the cost of breakpoint choices'),loc='left')
    temp=np.linspace(1,90,100);e.plot(temp,water_tension(temp),color=green);e.scatter([20],[water_tension(20)],color=orange);e.set_xlabel(tr('温度 / °C','Temperature / °C'));e.set_ylabel('γ / mN/m');e.set_title(tr('D  IAPWS纯水–水蒸气参考计算','D  IAPWS water–vapor reference calculation'),loc='left',fontsize=11);fig.tight_layout();save(fig,'dynamic')
    print(json.dumps(summary))

if __name__=='__main__':main()
```

The three analyses show why defining a measurement matters. The plate intercept describes contact-line force; the drop contour describes a static balance of density contrast and curvature; the concentration break locates a change in a property under a specified formulation. For a protein solution, dynamic tension can first reveal the time required for an interface to develop, followed by formulation comparisons at matched ages. Questions about how much protein remains adsorbed, how much water accompanies it and whether the layer rearranges call for experiments that observe the interfacial layer more directly. Surface tension then provides a well-defined connection between solution composition, interface dynamics and subsequent adsorption measurements.

The exported tables keep the analysis inspectable. Refit the plate over a shorter depth interval and compare intercept with slope; examine pendant residuals by height; move candidate concentration breaks and follow the cost curve. These changes have different physical meanings and should not be treated as interchangeable fitting preferences. Retaining raw coordinates and forces allows the measurement to be reinterpreted when calibration or geometry is refined. The resulting record is more useful than an isolated tension value because it preserves how that value was obtained and which controlled comparison it answers.

   Definition of age of a newly formed interface.
6. [KRÜSS — Bubble pressure tensiometer](https://www.kruss-scientific.com/en/know-how/glossary/bubble-pressure-tensiometer)

   Maximum bubble pressure and dynamic measurements.
7. [KRÜSS — Critical micelle concentration](https://www.kruss-scientific.com/en/know-how/glossary/critical-micelle-concentration-cmc-and-surfactant-concentration)

   Measurement meaning of the concentration break.
8. [IAPWS — Revised Release on Surface Tension of Ordinary Water Substance](https://iapws.org/technical-guidance/release/Surf-H2O)

   Water–vapour reference relation, coefficients and temperature range.
