# Is the Peak Still There? Signal Processing with SciPy

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p20/en/
Language: en

Connect sampling, local fitting, peak detection, and frequency response to inspect how smoothing changes a signal.

## After smoothing, is the peak still in the same place?

A sensor recording a transient process can show a slow baseline, genuine peaks, and rapid fluctuations together. A sample passing a detector may produce a voltage that rises and falls, while electrical or mechanical disturbance adds periodic interference. To identify when the peak occurs and how high it is, you may first smooth the curve. Smoothing also changes peak height, width, and sometimes position. This chapter uses SciPy with a fully specified teaching signal to examine what each processing step preserves and changes.

We create two peaks of different widths, add interference at two known frequencies, and compare a moving mean with Savitzky–Golay local polynomial smoothing. Then `find_peaks` locates maxima that satisfy explicit conditions, and a frequency view explains the effect of the window. Comparing every output with the known smooth model separates residual interference from shape distortion. The complete program exports original arrays, smoothed values, peak locations, and numerical summaries.

A signal is simply a sequence of values ordered in time. It may describe light intensity, voltage, displacement, or another instrument reading. Here amplitude is measured in mV and time in seconds. Processing routines receive arrays, while physical time enters through the sampling interval. Understanding that connection turns a “21-point window” into an interpretable time range.

## Read the sampling interval before choosing a window

Our example samples from 0 to 10 s at intervals of 0.02 s, producing 501 records. Fifty samples per second correspond to a sampling frequency of 50 Hz. Adjacent array positions represent a fixed time increment, so a filter moving by sample index also spans a fixed duration. For irregular instrument timestamps, inspect those actual times first. Treating every consecutive set of twenty-one records as the same temporal window would otherwise apply different smoothing durations at different positions.

A centered 21-point window takes ten neighbors on each side. Its earliest and latest samples are separated by 20×0.02 = 0.40 s. A five-point window spans 0.08 s and a forty-one-point window spans 0.80 s. Window length counts participating observations, whereas temporal span measures the separation between the first and last. Displaying both makes it possible to compare the processing window with the physical width of a peak.

Sampling also constrains the rates of variation that can be distinguished. With uniform 50 Hz sampling, 25 Hz is the Nyquist frequency. Faster continuous oscillations can produce the same sampled sequence as lower frequencies. A camera observing a rotating wheel provides an analogy: the observed positions alone may not reveal how many full turns occurred between frames. Our added components at 9 and 17 Hz lie below 25 Hz and appear in the later frequency plot. Faster components call for appropriate analog filtering and sampling design before acquisition.

## Build a signal whose components can be explained

The smooth model combines a rising baseline with two bell-shaped peaks. The baseline begins at 0.1 mV and rises at 0.02 mV per second. The first peak is centered at 3 s, with amplitude 1.2 mV and time scale 0.25 s; the second is centered at 7 s, with amplitude 0.8 mV and time scale 0.5 s. Peak amplitude here means the height above the baseline, while the plotted vertical value includes that baseline. The narrower first peak is more sensitive to a wide smoothing window.

$$
y_{\mathrm{clean}}(t)=b_0+b_1t+\sum_{j=1}^{2}A_j\exp\!\left[-\frac{(t-\mu_j)^2}{2w_j^2}\right]
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f54c83f4dc801bfa41bd22ff.svg) | Interference-free teaching-model voltage at time t, mV |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/707bb132def3690d81bf1f0c.svg) | Elapsed time, s |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/1786b0ad5e438341adfba90f.svg) | Baseline intercept, 0.1 mV |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/86ef2a91a3da50f97dc73bcd.svg) | Baseline slope, 0.02 mV/s |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/85c7a0c0a90e94bee07686fc.svg) | Peak index, 1 or 2; dimensionless |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/cb2c27f1e1ca2cb88caf17da.svg) | Peak amplitude above baseline, 1.2 and 0.8 mV |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7d98312b42264644b238b90b.svg) | Peak center time, 3 and 7 s |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f6264b954f8fef8d9872def7.svg) | Peak time scale, 0.25 and 0.5 s |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/64460da0d752153c52e1bd62.svg) | Natural exponential; its argument is a dimensionless ratio of squared times |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/52d4c787eb9b2a9aa747a1d4.svg) | Add the voltage contributions of both peaks |

At t=μ_j a peak’s exponent is zero and its contribution equals A_j. Increasing distance from the center makes the exponent more negative and the contribution smaller. At t=3 s, the baseline is 0.16 mV, the first peak contributes 1.2 mV, and the second contributes about 0.8 exp(−32) mV, giving approximately 1.36 mV. The time scale w describes peak width, not the standard deviation of a voltage measurement.

We add a 9 Hz sine component of amplitude 0.12 mV and a 17 Hz cosine component of amplitude 0.035 mV. These are explicitly defined periodic disturbances rather than random noise collected from an instrument. The construction gives identical data on every run and an identifiable origin for both higher-frequency components. Real measurements can combine random noise, baseline drift, and periodic disturbances, which can be investigated using instrument knowledge and repeated records.

At 3 s the smooth model is approximately 1.36 mV: the baseline contributes 0.16 mV and the first peak contributes 1.2 mV, while the second peak contributes a negligible amount. Added interference gives an observed value of approximately 1.395 mV at that instant. Neighboring high and low samples reflect both the genuine peak shape and the periodic terms. Selecting the maximum of the raw array would combine those effects in the reported peak height.

## From averaging neighbors to preserving local curvature

The simplest smoother adds a point and its neighbors and divides by their number. It pools nearby values to estimate the center, attenuating some rapid variations while also pulling a curved peak toward its lower neighbors. In 1964, Abraham Savitzky and Marcel Golay described smoothing and differentiation through local least-squares polynomials. For equally spaced observations and a fixed window, the local fit becomes a reusable set of weights. The calculation remains simple while preserving polynomial shape within the window.

![Original method diagram: five quadratic samples give a 2 mV center under a moving mean and 0 mV under a quadratic local fit. The coefficients show how local fitting becomes repeated weighting in the Savitzky–Golay method.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/63e6dbc49c375e566d99f6b7.svg?v=63e6dbc49c37)

Figure 1Original method diagram: five quadratic samples give a 2 mV center under a moving mean and 0 mV under a quadratic local fit. The coefficients show how local fitting becomes repeated weighting in the Savitzky–Golay method.

The five values 4, 1, 0, 1, and 4 occur at relative positions −2, −1, 0, 1, and 2 and lie exactly on a quadratic curve. Their moving mean is two, lifting the center from zero. Fitting a quadratic through them and evaluating it at the center returns zero. The distinction comes from the local model: an average retains one horizontal level, while a quadratic fit permits curvature. Near a peak, that curvature can be part of the feature we want to preserve.

$$
\widetilde y_i=\sum_{k=-m}^{m}c_k y_{i+k},\qquad N=2m+1
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/8985c98a921e74cb3aa7e8e1.svg) | Smoothed output at position i, mV |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/45b1400cf31b096a28adc5db.svg) | Input value k samples from the center, mV; values outside the record follow the boundary rule |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/33f73a318016d781b6ae1aa9.svg) | Current output sample index; dimensionless |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/8dc6f7e80ecaac9fa07890ce.svg) | Integer sample offset from the center; dimensionless |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/528857d51fe0ca9fb1f0a19e.svg) | Number of samples on each side of the center; nonnegative integer |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/256531b7f0ddb14dd11a59a3.svg) | Total window sample count; odd and dimensionless |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/7b0456e549b6eae9fe9ab8b6.svg) | Fixed coefficient at offset k; dimensionless |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9b9441d841a7d77652c30687.svg) | Sum the products of input values and weights across the window |

For five points, m=2 and N=5. Moving-mean weights are all 1/5, giving 2 mV from inputs 4, 1, 0, 1, and 4 mV. Quadratic Savitzky–Golay weights [−3,12,17,12,−3]/35 give 0 mV, retaining the quadratic’s center. Coefficients summing to one preserve a constant signal.

The five-point quadratic smoother has weights −3, 12, 17, 12, and −3, all divided by 35. Negative endpoint weights correct the average’s curvature bias. Their sum remains one, preserving a constant input. Substituting 4, 1, 0, 1, and 4 gives a numerator of −12+12+0+12−12 = 0. Negative weights also allow an output beyond the local input range, particularly near abrupt changes or boundaries, so its interpretation depends on local signal shape.

SciPy’s `savgol_filter` specifies this fit through window length and polynomial degree. We keep degree two fixed and investigate temporal range. The window must contain enough observations to determine the polynomial coefficients, and an odd centered window places the current sample in the middle. A higher degree retains more complicated local variation and can retain more rapid fluctuation as well. The characteristic time scale of the feature guides that choice.

Imagine moving a short ruler along the record. A moving mean compresses everything under the ruler into one horizontal level, whereas a local quadratic allows the short segment to bend. At each position, neighboring observations determine the segment and the algorithm reads its center. Equal sample spacing, a fixed window, and a fixed polynomial degree give the least-squares equations the same geometry everywhere inside the record. The corresponding weights can therefore be calculated once and reused. This is why a method described as repeated local fitting can be implemented efficiently as repeated weighted sums.

## What information does a window need at a boundary?

Inside a record, a centered window has neighbors on both sides. At the first sample, earlier observations are absent, so the calculation needs a boundary rule. We use `mode='mirror'`, reflecting interior values beyond an endpoint without repeating the endpoint itself. If a sequence begins a, b, c, the positions extending to its left correspond successively to b and c. This convention preserves output length and specifies how the first and last values are calculated.

Reflection introduces a local shape assumption. If the real signal still has a slope at an endpoint, its reflected continuation can differ from its physical continuation. Edge results should therefore be read together with the boundary rule. SciPy provides other modes, including local polynomial extrapolation. Using the same mirror rule for both smoothers here keeps the comparison focused on their weights. In an experiment, recording an extra margin around the region of interest can move the analysis away from endpoints and reduce dependence on boundary treatment.

A symmetric window uses values from both earlier and later times, making it suitable for completed records. A real-time controller does not yet have future observations and needs a causal filter or a delay before producing a centered estimate. These workflows have different timing and boundary interpretations. After choosing a useful offline smoother, connect its information requirements to the eventual application.

## Locate peaks with explicit criteria after smoothing

The figure applies a 21-point quadratic Savitzky–Golay filter. Rapid oscillations diminish while both slower peaks remain visible. The lower panel subtracts the known model from the processed result. Five points retain considerable periodic interference; forty-one points produce a more distinct shape bias near the narrow peak. Twenty-one points give a smaller overall error for these specified peak widths, interference frequencies, and sampling interval.

![Top: input with defined interference, known model, and 21-point quadratic Savitzky–Golay output. Red points meet a 0.3 mV prominence and 100-sample separation. Below: errors relative to the model at different window lengths; sampling interval 0.02 s, mirrored boundaries.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/1f6dd886740bd48e106af81a.svg?v=1f6dd886740b)

Figure 2Top: input with defined interference, known model, and 21-point quadratic Savitzky–Golay output. Red points meet a 0.3 mV prominence and 100-sample separation. Below: errors relative to the model at different window lengths; sampling interval 0.02 s, mirrored boundaries.

`find_peaks` first identifies local values higher than their neighbors and then applies the requested conditions. `distance=100` is measured in samples, corresponding to 2 s here, and requires retained peaks to be separated by at least that amount. `prominence=0.3` requires a peak to rise at least 0.3 mV relative to its surrounding contour level. Prominence is found from appropriate bases on either side and differs from absolute vertical height. A rising baseline can increase a peak’s height without increasing its prominence by the same amount.

The retained locations are 3.00 and 7.02 s, with values approximately 1.35605 and 1.04352 mV. The second selected sample lies slightly away from the specified 7 s peak center. The rising baseline and residual interference both influence the maximum of the combined curve. Returned peak positions are indices on the sampling grid; multiplying by 0.02 s converts them into time. Finer localization can use an explicitly chosen local peak model or finer acquisition sampling.

$$
\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\widetilde y_i-y_{\mathrm{clean},i})^2}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/6ffa6620282ab195b6f2fd00.svg) | Root-mean-square error relative to the known teaching model, mV |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/fb2a8560bbc7122a4dd4f1a0.svg) | Number of compared samples, 501; dimensionless |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/33f73a318016d781b6ae1aa9.svg) | Sample index; dimensionless |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/8985c98a921e74cb3aa7e8e1.svg) | Smoothed sample value, mV |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a9aa8eda074ad6c3a6f6c7a6.svg) | Interference-free model value at the same time, mV |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9b9441d841a7d77652c30687.svg) | Sum over all compared positions |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9bcc38017e1856dc949d86bd.svg) | Square root, restoring units of mV |

Squaring prevents signed errors from cancelling; averaging and taking a square root restores the original units. Errors of 0.03 and −0.04 mV give √[(0.0009+0.0016)/2]≈0.035355 mV. The 21-point quadratic filter gives about 0.005705 mV over all 501 samples, combining boundary treatment, residual interference, and shape change.

We can calculate root-mean-square error here because the teaching model without interference is known. The 21-point output gives approximately 0.005705 mV, compared with 0.075340 mV for five points and 0.012498 mV for forty-one. Measured signals generally lack a complete known reference. Independent repeats, calibration signals, established features, or held-out observations can then help evaluate processing. A before–after difference alone contains both removed interference and altered signal shape, so its meaning follows the scientific objective.

A landscape analogy helps distinguish prominence from absolute height. A summit has an elevation above sea level, but its rise above a surrounding valley describes a different feature. For a signal peak, the algorithm identifies bases on both sides and uses the higher base as its reference level. A prominence threshold therefore expresses how strongly an event must stand out locally. A distance threshold expresses how far apart retained events must lie in time. These conditions constrain different aspects of the result, and each deserves a value connected to the process being studied.

## Read a window as a selector of variation rates

A time plot shows when the signal changes. A frequency plot describes components that repeat at different rates: 9 Hz means nine oscillations per second and 17 Hz means seventeen. Both have known origins in this example. The program computes a power spectral density with `periodogram` and explicitly supplies the 50 Hz sampling frequency. Units of mV²/Hz describe squared-amplitude contribution per frequency interval. A Hann window and linear detrending help manage the finite record boundaries and slow baseline.

![Left: one-sided power spectral density using 50 Hz sampling, a Hann window, and linear detrending. Right: sinusoidal amplitude gain calculated directly from filter coefficients, with 9 Hz marked. Gain describes the filter; spectral density describes the finite records.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/a51378ffcbd433a4ef486a49.svg?v=a51378ffcbd4)

Figure 3Left: one-sided power spectral density using 50 Hz sampling, a Hann window, and linear detrending. Right: sinusoidal amplitude gain calculated directly from filter coefficients, with 9 Hz marked. Gain describes the filter; spectral density describes the finite records.

A finite-duration record spreads a frequency component across neighboring frequency positions, and the window alters the distribution of peak width and magnitude. These choices therefore belong in its interpretation. The 501-point record has a frequency spacing of approximately 50/501 = 0.0998 Hz, so 9 and 17 Hz do not fall exactly on frequency-grid locations. Local spectral peaks still identify nearby periodic components. We use the density display to compare frequency content before and after smoothing, rather than as an exact estimator of one sinusoid’s amplitude.

The companion panel calculates amplitude gain directly from the smoothing weights. Gain one retains a sinusoid’s amplitude; gain 0.1 reduces it to about one tenth. At 9 Hz, the 21-point window has gain approximately 0.04464, while the 41-point window gives approximately 0.06804. A wider window therefore does not attenuate every frequency more strongly: finite filter responses contain ripples. Considering both target shape and disturbance frequency makes parameter selection more concrete than judging smoothness by appearance.

Amplitude gain and power spectral density describe related quantities at different levels. A filter that multiplies a sinusoidal amplitude by a factor multiplies its power by the square of that factor. The gain panel describes the filter itself and can be calculated without applying it to this particular signal. The spectral panel describes the finite input and output records with the stated spectral-estimation settings. Reading them together separates an algorithm’s response from the frequency content of the data supplied to it.

## A complete program and a linked experiment

The `data` function explicitly generates the smooth model and periodic disturbance. The main loop evaluates two methods at four window lengths and stores each result’s error, value at 3 s, gain at 9 Hz, and peak information. `savgol_coeffs` supplies reusable window weights, `savgol_filter` applies local calculations to the full sequence, and `find_peaks` extracts maxima satisfying the stated conditions. Keeping the stages distinct makes the effect of a parameter change easier to locate.

### Complete Python: signal, smoothing, peaks, and frequency response

Generate an explicit signal, apply native SciPy filters and peak detection, retain numerical errors and arrays, and produce three scientific figures.

```
"""Inspect smoothing, peak finding, and frequency response on a defined teaching signal."""
from pathlib import Path
import argparse,json
import numpy as np
import scipy
from scipy import signal,ndimage
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import font_manager

DT=.02
BLUE,RED,INK,GRAY='#28658c','#b64a35','#20313e','#71808b'


def data():
    t=np.arange(501)*DT
    clean=.1+.02*t+1.2*np.exp(-.5*((t-3)/.25)**2)+.8*np.exp(-.5*((t-7)/.5)**2)
    interference=.12*np.sin(2*np.pi*9*t)+.035*np.cos(2*np.pi*17*t)
    return t,clean,clean+interference


def main():
    parser=argparse.ArgumentParser();parser.add_argument('--output',type=Path,required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--language',choices=['zh','en'],default='en');args=parser.parse_args()
    args.output.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True);zh=args.language=='zh'
    def tr(a,b):return a if zh else b
    available={font.name for font in font_manager.fontManager.ttflist}
    font_names=[name for name in ['Noto Sans CJK SC','Noto Sans SC','Microsoft YaHei','SimHei','DejaVu Sans'] if name in available]
    plt.rcParams.update({'font.family':font_names,
        'font.size':12,'svg.fonttype':'none','axes.spines.top':False,'axes.spines.right':False,'grid.alpha':.15})
    def save(fig,name):
        fig.savefig(args.output/f'{name}-{args.language}.svg');fig.savefig(args.output/f'{name}-{args.language}.png',dpi=160);plt.close(fig)
    t,clean,observed=data();results={}
    for method in ['savgol','mean']:
        for window in [5,11,21,41]:
            coefficients=signal.savgol_coeffs(window,2) if method=='savgol' else np.ones(window)/window
            smoothed=signal.savgol_filter(observed,window,2,mode='mirror') if method=='savgol' else ndimage.uniform_filter1d(observed,window,mode='mirror')
            peaks,properties=signal.find_peaks(smoothed,prominence=.3,distance=100)
            # A centered symmetric filter has a real frequency response.
            offsets=np.arange(window)-window//2
            gain9=float(abs(np.sum(coefficients*np.cos(2*np.pi*9*DT*offsets))))
            results[f'{method}_{window}']={'rmse_mV':float(np.sqrt(np.mean((smoothed-clean)**2))),
                'value_at3s_mV':float(smoothed[150]),'gain9':gain9,
                'peak_times_s':t[peaks].tolist(),'peak_values_mV':smoothed[peaks].tolist(),
                'prominences_mV':properties['prominences'].tolist(),'coefficient_sum':float(coefficients.sum())}
    smooth=signal.savgol_filter(observed,21,2,mode='mirror');peaks,properties=signal.find_peaks(smooth,prominence=.3,distance=100)
    np.savetxt(args.output/'signal.csv',np.column_stack([t,clean,observed,smooth]),delimiter=',',comments='',
        header='time_s,clean_model_mV,with_interference_mV,savgol21_mV')
    fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(12,8),layout='constrained',gridspec_kw={'height_ratios':[1.4,1]})
    axes[0].plot(t,observed,color='#bdc9d0',lw=1,label=tr('含规定干扰','Defined interference added'))
    axes[0].plot(t,clean,color=INK,lw=1.5,ls='--',label=tr('已知平滑模型','Known smooth model'))
    axes[0].plot(t,smooth,color=BLUE,lw=2,label=tr('Savitzky–Golay：21点，二次','Savitzky–Golay: 21 points, degree 2'))
    axes[0].scatter(t[peaks],smooth[peaks],color=RED,zorder=5)
    for i in peaks:axes[0].annotate(f'{t[i]:.2f} s',(t[i],smooth[i]),xytext=(8,13),textcoords='offset points',color=RED)
    axes[0].set(ylabel=tr('信号 / mV','Signal / mV'),title=tr('A  平滑与局部峰定位','A  Smoothing and local peak locations'));axes[0].legend(frameon=False,fontsize=10)
    for window,color in zip([5,21,41],[GRAY,BLUE,RED]):
        y=signal.savgol_filter(observed,window,2,mode='mirror');axes[1].plot(t,y-clean,color=color,label=tr(f'{window}点',f'{window} points'))
    axes[1].axhline(0,color=INK,lw=.8);axes[1].set(xlabel=tr('时间 / s','Time / s'),ylabel=tr('平滑结果 − 已知模型 / mV','Smoothed − known model / mV'),title=tr('B  误差同时包含残留干扰与峰形改变','B  Error includes residual interference and shape change'))
    for a in axes:a.grid();a.set_xlim(0,10)
    axes[1].legend(frameon=False,loc='lower center',bbox_to_anchor=(.5,1.02),ncol=3);axes[1].set_title(tr('B  误差同时包含残留干扰与峰形改变','B  Error includes residual interference and shape change'),pad=38);save(fig,'smoothing')
    fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,5.6),layout='constrained')
    k=np.arange(-2,3,dtype=float);values=k*k;dense=np.linspace(-2,2,200)
    axes[0].plot(dense,dense*dense,color=BLUE,lw=2,label=tr('局部二次曲线','Local quadratic'))
    axes[0].scatter(k,values,color=INK,zorder=4,label=tr('五个样本值','Five sampled values'))
    axes[0].axhline(values.mean(),color=RED,ls='--',label=tr('移动平均的中心输出 = 2','Moving-mean center output = 2'))
    axes[0].scatter([0],[0],s=80,facecolors='white',edgecolors=BLUE,zorder=5,label=tr('二次拟合的中心输出 = 0','Quadratic-fit center output = 0'))
    axes[0].set(xlabel=tr('相对样本位置 k','Relative sample offset k'),ylabel=tr('教学数值 / mV','Teaching value / mV'),title=tr('保留局部曲率','Preserve local curvature'));axes[0].legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9)
    coefficients=signal.savgol_coeffs(5,2)
    axes[1].bar(k-.14,np.ones(5)/5,width=.28,color=RED,label=tr('移动平均','Moving mean'))
    axes[1].bar(k+.14,coefficients,width=.28,color=BLUE,label='Savitzky–Golay')
    axes[1].axhline(0,color=INK,lw=1);axes[1].set(xlabel=tr('相对样本位置 k','Relative sample offset k'),ylabel=tr('权重，无量纲','Weight, dimensionless'),xticks=k,title=tr('固定权重实现局部最小二乘','Fixed weights implement local least squares'));axes[1].legend(frameon=False,fontsize=10)
    fig.suptitle(tr('Savitzky与Golay（1964）：把局部拟合变成重复加权','Savitzky and Golay (1964): local fitting as repeated weighting'),fontsize=15)
    save(fig,'history')
    fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,5.8),layout='constrained')
    for y,color,label in [(observed,GRAY,tr('含干扰','With interference')),(smooth,BLUE,'SG21')]:
        freq,psd=signal.periodogram(y,fs=1/DT,window='hann',detrend='linear',scaling='density')
        axes[0].semilogy(freq,psd,color=color,lw=1.5,label=label)
    axes[0].set(xlabel=tr('频率 / Hz','Frequency / Hz'),ylabel='PSD / mV²·Hz⁻¹',xlim=(0,25),ylim=(1e-12,1),title=tr('频域：9 Hz与17 Hz干扰','Frequency view: 9 Hz and 17 Hz interference'));axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
    freq=np.linspace(0,25,501)
    for window,color in zip([5,21,41],[GRAY,BLUE,RED]):
        c=signal.savgol_coeffs(window,2);k=np.arange(window)-window//2;gain=np.abs(np.cos(2*np.pi*freq[:,None]*DT*k[None,:])@c)
        axes[1].plot(freq,gain,color=color,label=tr(f'{window}点',f'{window} points'))
    axes[1].axvline(9,color=INK,ls=':',lw=1);axes[1].set(xlabel=tr('频率 / Hz','Frequency / Hz'),ylabel=tr('幅值增益，无量纲','Amplitude gain, dimensionless'),title=tr('窗口决定保留哪些变化速度','The window selects rates of variation'),xlim=(0,25));axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
    for a in axes:a.grid()
    save(fig,'frequency')
    summary={'versions':{'numpy':np.__version__,'scipy':scipy.__version__,'matplotlib':matplotlib.__version__},
        'sampling_interval_s':DT,'sampling_frequency_Hz':1/DT,'n':len(t),'cases':results,
        'sg5_coefficients':coefficients.tolist(),'quadratic_sg_center':float(coefficients@values),
        'quadratic_mean_center':float(values.mean())}
    (args.output/'summary.json').write_text(json.dumps(summary,indent=2),encoding='utf-8');print(json.dumps(summary))


if __name__=='__main__':main()
```

The experiment displays the complete processed signal, current window weights, and frequency response together. Select a moving mean or quadratic local fit and change its length to see different results from the same 501 records. The value at 3 s and RMSE come from the processed curve. Moving the focus changes which input neighborhood is inspected while leaving the filter result unchanged. The experiment calculates quadratic least-squares weights through a closed-form expression independently checked against the Python SciPy output.

### Link window, weights, and output

Gray is the input with defined interference, black dashed is the known smooth model, and blue is the processed output. Red neighborhood points identify mirrored boundary inputs; sampling interval is 0.02 s.

[Figure: Full signal and current window](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p20/en/#P20-signal)

[Figure: Local weights and input samples](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p20/en/#P20-weights)

[Figure: Frequency response magnitude](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p20/en/#P20-gain)

Start with a five-point quadratic fit and observe the remaining interference. Change to twenty-one points and inspect the 9 Hz gain and narrow-peak shape. At forty-one points, examine the reduced peak near 3 s. Switching to a moving mean makes every weight equal, changing both frequency response and shape bias. Move the focus to the beginning or end to examine the reflected samples that supply the centered window at a boundary.

One useful way to read the program is to follow index 150, which represents 3 s. A 21-point window takes ten neighbors on either side, spanning 2.80 to 3.20 s. The reported 1.35605 mV is the weighted sum of those 21 observed values; the known smooth model at 3 s is approximately 1.36 mV. Moving the focus displays the same kind of calculation at another position. Changing the window or method actually recomputes the trace. Keeping the viewing position separate from the processing parameters makes the interaction easier to interpret and makes individual numerical results traceable.

## Describe processing parameters as reproducible conditions

For measured signals, preserve original times and values, then record the sampling interval, smoothing method, window length, polynomial degree, and boundary mode. Peak results should also preserve detection criteria, minimum separation, prominence, and amplitude units. This lets another reader distinguish a feature in the observations from a result selected under particular processing settings. Comparing several specimens usually calls for consistent physical time scales, which can require different point counts when sampling rates differ.

A rate-of-change analysis also needs the time unit in the differentiation step. Savitzky–Golay supports polynomial derivatives; for a first derivative, supply the actual interval, such as `delta=0.02` here. The result then has units mV/s. Direct differences between neighbors emphasize rapid fluctuations, while a local fit can stabilize a rate estimate over a chosen time range. That same range also combines its internal details, so the relevant process speed still guides the window choice.

A useful processing chain keeps the relationships among observations, assumptions, parameters, and results visible. Time views check location and shape, coefficient views explain the local operation, and frequency views identify retained or attenuated rates of variation. Together they turn a smoother-looking curve into specific conclusions about weakened disturbance, preserved peak shape, and the questions the processed result can answer.

# 用积分和微分方程描述变化

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/
Language: zh-CN

从三种状态之间的转化，理解变化率、小步推进、守恒和累计面积。

## 一种物质经过中间态，什么时候最适合观察

一份样品在处理过程中，可能先从状态A变成B，再从B变成C。A可以代表尚未转化的部分，B代表暂时出现的中间态，C代表已经完成后续变化的部分。观察终点时，B也许已经很少；若研究目标恰好是B，就需要知道它什么时候最多，以及它在整个过程里持续存在了多久。这两个问题分别对应曲线的峰值与曲线下的面积，也把微分方程和积分联系到同一个具体任务。

本节采用一个明确的教学模型：总量固定，A、B、C按一对一关系依次转化，体积和环境条件保持不变，没有额外流入、流出或逆向转化。用每种状态占初始总量的分数描述组成，初始时A为1，B和C都为0。这样可以把注意力集中在变化率上。应用到真实反应时，再根据物种、化学计量关系、体积变化和测量定义建立相应方程。

SciPy的`solve_ivp`能够从初始状态和变化规则计算随时间演化的轨迹，`quad`则能够累计一段函数曲线下的面积。我们会先用纸笔能够检查的小步计算理解这两种操作，再运行完整程序。已有解析答案的简单模型提供了清楚的参照，让步长、误差、守恒和积分单位都能落到实际数字上。

## 变化率是每分钟改变多少，方程先记录流向

假设A转成B的速率与当前A的数量成正比。A越多，同样时间内能够转化的量越多；A逐渐减少，转化速度也随之降低。本例取速率常数0.8 min⁻¹。若某时刻A占0.5，A减少的瞬时速率就是每分钟0.4个分数单位。这里的“瞬时”很关键：它描述当前这一刻的方向与速度，随着A减少，后面的速度也会变化。

$$
\frac{da}{dt}=-k_1a,\qquad\frac{db}{dt}=k_1a-k_2b,\qquad\frac{dc}{dt}=k_2b
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/326d9c99fe68c4303977dd55.svg) | 分别为A、B、C占初始总量的分数，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/707bb132def3690d81bf1f0c.svg) | 经过的时间，min。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/d62ad609310d0b90a08f3cae.svg) | A→B与B→C的速率常数，本例分别为0.8和0.3 min⁻¹。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/cf7a258783fb9a082f6d20a4.svg) | 各状态分数的瞬时变化率，min⁻¹；d表示微分。 |

每项都是“当前数量×单位时间的转化速率”。若a=0.5、b=0.3、c=0.2，三个变化率为−0.4、0.4−0.09=0.31、0.09 min⁻¹，相加为0。因此总分数的变化率为0，而各状态可以持续交换数量。

三个式子可以按账本来读。A只有支出，所以带负号；B一边接收A的转化，一边向C转出，因此是收入减支出；C只接收B的转化。把三个变化率相加，成对的流入与流出刚好抵消，说明总分数保持不变。第二个速率常数取0.3 min⁻¹，使B向C的转出相对较慢，B在早期能够积累，后期又随着A来源减少而下降。

符号中的导数可以从平均速度理解。用两个临近时刻的分数差除以时间差，得到这小段时间里的平均变化率；把时间间隔逐渐缩短，就走向某一时刻的变化率。它与位置—速度关系相似：知道现在的位置和速度，可以估计很短时间后的新位置。对这里的样品，位置换成三个分数，速度换成三个流向相互关联的变化率。

把初始总量归一为1，相当于把样品分成许多相同的计数单位，记录每个单位目前在哪个状态。这里的一对一转化保证单位总数保持不变。对于有多个反应物、产物数量不同的化学反应，应按化学计量关系选择浓度或物质量方程，再检查元素或质量守恒。分数方便教学，具体实验中的守恒对象则由实际过程决定。

## 从当前斜率向前走：把连续变化变成可计算的小步

十八世纪，Euler将积分和微分方程系统地组织为研究变化的数学工具。他的《积分学基础》第一卷于1768年出版。今天写一段数值程序时，仍然要处理同一个基本关系：已知变化规则，怎样恢复随时间变化的量。欧拉方法给出一种容易画出来的做法——先沿当前斜率走一小步，再在新位置重新计算斜率。

$$
\mathbf y_{n+1}=\mathbf y_n+h\,\mathbf f(t_n,\mathbf y_n)
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f9863792b3128c856f71d728.svg) | 第n个计算节点的状态向量，包含a、b、c三个无量纲分数。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/794309c181b5d3eef90282ba.svg) | 当前和下一个计算节点的整数编号，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/994427fe929fdf538d7c1be7.svg) | 向前推进的时间步长，min。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a588fc41a723666b153cc137.svg) | 第n个节点的时间，min。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a06debad6e153cb789c38ba5.svg) | 由前述三个方程组成的变化率向量，各分量单位min⁻¹。 |

速度乘时间给出这一步的近似变化量，再加到当前状态上。初值(1,0,0)、步长0.5 min和变化率(−0.8,0.8,0) min⁻¹给出下一步(0.6,0.4,0)。三个分数合计1，但这一粗步尚未计入步内新生成B的进一步转化。

从A=1、B=0、C=0出发，当前变化率依次为−0.8、0.8、0 min⁻¹。如果一步取0.5 min，就把这些速度分别乘以0.5，加回原值，得到A=0.6、B=0.4、C=0。这一步把最初的速度保持了半分钟，所以它是一种近似。在真实连续模型里，A一开始减少，速度就随之减慢，而B刚出现就开始向C转化；分步计算到下一点才更新这些影响。

![欧拉方法以当前斜率连接相邻节点，细化步长后接近解析曲线。右图独立计算三个分数相对解析解的最大绝对误差，参考线表示与步长成正比的趋势。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/f04647f595c40c336922f754.svg?v=f04647f595c4)

图 1欧拉方法以当前斜率连接相邻节点，细化步长后接近解析曲线。右图独立计算三个分数相对解析解的最大绝对误差，参考线表示与步长成正比的趋势。

图中较粗的折线偏离解析曲线，缩短步长后逐渐靠近。右图把不同步长的最大绝对误差放在双对数坐标下，细步长区间大致沿着与步长成正比的方向变化。这种比较比单看一条光滑曲线更有解释力：绘图可以把少数点连接得很顺，真正的数值精度要通过步长变化、独立答案或更严格的求解设置来判断。

## 让求解器选择小步，自己明确初值和输出时刻

完整程序将变化规则写进`rhs(t, y)`。参数`t`是当前时间，`y`按A、B、C的顺序保存当前三个分数，返回值也按相同顺序给出三个导数。顺序就像表格的列名，一旦约定，后续初值、图例和误差检查都要一致。虽然本例的速率常数不随时间改变，接口仍保留时间参数，便于描述升温、外部输入或其他随时间变化的条件。

`solve_ivp`接收时间范围0到10 min和初值[1, 0, 0]，默认使用RK45方法。它在一个步长内利用多个位置的变化率，并依据误差估计调整内部步长。本例用`t_eval`要求在501个均匀时间点保存结果，便于比较与绘图；这些保存点并不意味着求解器内部始终采用0.02 min的步长。输出网格与算法实际走过的小步承担不同任务。

程序设置相对容差`rtol=1e-9`和绝对容差`atol=1e-11`。相对容差随分数大小缩放，绝对容差在数值接近零时仍提供误差控制尺度。它们约束的是求解器的局部误差估计，最终整条曲线的偏差还要通过结果检查。本例同时计算解析解，得到三种分数在全部保存点上的最大绝对差约7.21×10⁻¹¹，直接说明这次运行的数值吻合程度。

![同一串联模型的三个分数与B积分。左图为RK45数值解，右图用解析B曲线填出面积；时间单位min，总量初始归一为1。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/229f29c5e5b658545e3bc67f.svg?v=229f29c5e5b6)

图 2同一串联模型的三个分数与B积分。左图为RK45数值解，右图用解析B曲线填出面积；时间单位min，总量初始归一为1。

程序还把B的变化率设为事件函数，寻找它从正变负的位置。这个零点表示B从增加转为减少，也就是本模型的峰顶时刻，约为1.96166 min。事件定位在连续数值解上寻找零点，比直接挑出501个保存值中的最大值更细。实际使用时需要让事件函数对应清楚的科学条件，例如某个浓度达到阈值，或某种净流量改变方向。

解析解也可以从变化规律读懂：A每经过相同时间都会按相同比例减少，因此具有指数衰减形式。B不断接收不同时间由A转入的部分，而每一批转入的部分又按自己的停留时间向C衰减；把这些贡献相加，会得到两条指数曲线之差。C再由总分数减去A和B获得。程序中的解析表达式采用两个速率常数不同的形式，本节所有可选速率均满足这个条件。

$$
a(t)=e^{-k_1t},\qquad b(t)=\frac{k_1}{k_2-k_1}\left(e^{-k_1t}-e^{-k_2t}\right),\qquad c(t)=1-a(t)-b(t)
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/db3924ef96d9ef424c4cfc5d.svg) | 初值(1,0,0)下，时间t时的三个分数，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/dec0f7dc61f0e9a546cd9d6d.svg) | t为时间(min)，两个速率常数单位min⁻¹，且本式要求两者不相等。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/0be950b3e59846bc80f7e4ca.svg) | 自然指数函数的底数，约2.71828；指数中的速率常数乘时间为无量纲量。 |

代入t=0，两个指数均为1，因此a=1、b=0、c=0。代入t=2 min、速率0.8和0.3 min⁻¹，可得a≈0.201897、b≈0.555064、c≈0.243039，总和为1。该表达式提供独立于逐步求解的核对答案。

## 总量正确以后，还要看每个分数是否合理

守恒检查很有用，因为它把三个输出通过一个关系联系起来。若代码里把B的转出写成正号，或者忘记C的流入，总量就会出现明显漂移。然而，守恒本身只检验流量账是否对得上。欧拉步同时减去A转出的量、加给B，再把B转出的量加给C，所以即使步长很大，它仍然可能保持总分数为1。

![2 min欧拉步出现负A分数，却仍保持三个分数之和为1。上图虚线为连续解析模型，实线与圆点为粗步结果，下图单独检查总量。](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/fcf207372151633a1539dfc5.svg?v=fcf207372151)

图 32 min欧拉步出现负A分数，却仍保持三个分数之和为1。上图虚线为连续解析模型，实线与圆点为粗步结果，下图单独检查总量。

把步长改为2 min，第一步就得到A=−0.6、B=1.6、C=0。总和确实还是1，但分数已经超出了这个物理模型的含义。原因是程序把初始每分钟0.8的转出速度保持了两分钟，搬走了1.6份，而起初只有1份。这个例子清楚地区分了三个问题：总量是否守恒，每个状态是否保持非负，以及数值轨迹是否接近连续方程的解。

对A单独的更新式，新的分数是原分数乘以“1减去速率常数乘步长”。要使非负的A在这一步之后仍非负，速率常数与步长的乘积就应不超过1。更大的步长还可能产生正负交替的振荡；当放大因子的绝对值超过1，振荡会增长。这个具体推导说明，选步长需要结合变化的快慢，不能只根据一张图上想显示多少个点决定。

遇到一个过程变化很快、另一个过程变化很慢的模型，显式算法可能被最快的时间尺度限制，这也是刚性问题常见的来源。SciPy提供Radau和BDF等方法处理此类方程。判断时先看时间尺度、求解器状态、函数求值次数和收紧容差后的变化，再选择适合模型的方法；更换算法之后，守恒、非负和关键输出仍然值得一起检查。

误差比较还需要明确“在哪些位置比较”。本节欧拉曲线的误差在每个欧拉节点上计算，每个节点先分别求A、B、C的绝对差，再取其中最大的一个；全程最大误差再从这些节点值中取最大。它回答的是最差的已计算分量偏了多少，和平均误差承担不同作用。由于所有分量都是分数，三者可以直接比较；单位或量级差别很大的状态变量需要先确定合适的缩放方式。

## 曲线下的面积，把数量和持续时间一起累计

B在某一时刻有多少，与B在整个过程里出现了多久，是两个不同的问题。若B分数在一段0.5 min时间内近似为0.4，这一小段的“分数乘时间”就是0.2 min。把整段过程分成很多这样的小条，再把它们相加，就得到B曲线下的面积。由于分数无量纲，面积的单位是min；若纵轴换成浓度mmol/L，面积的单位就会变成mmol·min/L。

$$
I_B(T)=\int_0^T b(t)\,dt\;\approx\;\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} b(t_n)h,\qquad T=Nh
$$

| 符号 | 含义与单位 |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a11305f0a6beaa6b17d10d0f.svg) | 从0到T的B分数积分，min。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/ea3059ae9f52fe6b926fbbba.svg) | 时间t时B的分数，无量纲。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f9815edca06dc233accaf513.svg) | 积分中的时间与终止时间，min。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f31d38e9354f49723c5bb666.svg) | dt表示极短时间增量；积分号表示连续累计，单位由被积函数乘min确定。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a23a4935fef8a0becb8f51d8.svg) | h为均匀步长(min)，N为总步数，n为0至N−1的整数编号，t_n=nh为各小条左端时间(min)。 |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9b9441d841a7d77652c30687.svg) | 将N个左端矩形的面积相加。 |

若两段各0.5 min的B分数近似为0.4和0.5，两块矩形的面积为0.2和0.25 min，合计0.45 min。缩短小条可更细地描述曲线。完整模型在0–10 min上的积分为3.068473 min；公式右边的有限和是指定左端矩形规则下的近似。

从0到10 min，本模型B的积分约为3.068473 min。它可以解释为所有初始单位在这一观察窗口中处于B状态的平均累计时间；如果只有少部分进入B，或很快离开B，面积都会减小。这样的量适合比较暂态的持续程度。对于具体实验，应再把该积分与实际研究目标对应起来，例如中间态暴露量、累计释放量或反应贡献，并保留正确的单位。

`quad`接收一个能够在任意指定时间求值的函数，本例把解析B函数交给它积分。返回的第二个数是数值积分误差的估计，本次约3.41×10⁻¹⁴ min。它描述计算方法对给定函数的积分误差；速率常数的实验误差需要通过参数变化或不确定度传播另行评估。明确这两类误差的对象，才能正确使用程序返回的精细数字。

如果手里只有离散测量点，可以用`trapezoid`把相邻两点之间的区域视为梯形，再将各梯形面积相加。本例对501个解析值作梯形积分得到3.068446 min，与直接函数积分略有差别。这一区别来自有限采样和插值形状。时间间隔不均匀时，应把实际时间数组一同传入，而不能把行号当成等间隔时间。

对完整无限时长的过程，还可以从账本得到一个简洁检验：C最后接收全部初始单位，累计的B→C转移为1。因为该流量在每一刻等于0.3 min⁻¹乘B分数，B在无限时间上的积分就是1除以0.3 min⁻¹，即约3.333333 min。本节只积分到10 min，所以得到较小的3.068473 min；剩余差值对应10 min之后B仍会持续存在的尾部。

## 完整程序：把模型、数值算法与核对答案放在一起

下面的程序保留了三条清楚的计算路径。`rhs`提供变化率，`solve_ivp`据此推进状态；`exact`给出同一模型的解析解，用来比较数值输出；`euler`显式执行简单小步，展示步长为何影响结果。解析函数只用于这个有闭式答案的案例，数值求解的接口则可以继续用于更复杂的模型。

### 完整示例：串联转化、峰顶事件、积分与步长比较

运行后生成三幅图、fractions.csv和summary.json。所有输入与解析核对函数包含在程序内。

```
"""Follow a conserved three-state conversion with integration and an ODE solver."""
from pathlib import Path
import argparse,json
import numpy as np
import scipy
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp,quad,trapezoid
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import font_manager

COLORS=['#28658c','#c26835','#477f67']
K1,K2=.8,.3


def exact(t,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    t=np.asarray(t);a=np.exp(-k1*t)
    b=k1/(k2-k1)*(np.exp(-k1*t)-np.exp(-k2*t))
    return np.array([a,b,1-a-b])


def rhs(t,y,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    a,b,c=y
    return np.array([-k1*a,k1*a-k2*b,k2*b])


def euler(h,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    t=np.linspace(0,10,round(10/h)+1);y=np.zeros((3,len(t)));y[:,0]=[1,0,0]
    for i in range(len(t)-1):y[:,i+1]=y[:,i]+h*rhs(t[i],y[:,i],k1,k2)
    return t,y


def b_integral(end,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    return k1/(k2-k1)*((1-np.exp(-k1*end))/k1-(1-np.exp(-k2*end))/k2)


def main():
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser();p.add_argument('--output',type=Path,required=True);p.add_argument('--language',choices=['zh','en'],default='en');args=p.parse_args()
    args.output.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True);zh=args.language=='zh'
    def tr(a,b):return a if zh else b
    available={f.name for f in font_manager.fontManager.ttflist}
    plt.rcParams.update({'font.family':[f for f in ['Noto Sans CJK SC','Noto Sans SC','Microsoft YaHei','SimHei','DejaVu Sans'] if f in available],'font.size':12,'svg.fonttype':'none','axes.spines.top':False,'axes.spines.right':False,'grid.alpha':.15})
    def save(fig,name):
        fig.savefig(args.output/f'{name}-{args.language}.svg');fig.savefig(args.output/f'{name}-{args.language}.png',dpi=160);plt.close(fig)
    t=np.linspace(0,10,501)
    def peak_b(t,y):return K1*y[0]-K2*y[1]
    peak_b.direction=-1
    solution=solve_ivp(rhs,(0,10),[1.,0.,0.],t_eval=t,rtol=1e-9,atol=1e-11,events=peak_b)
    if not solution.success:raise RuntimeError(solution.message)
    reference=exact(t);area,area_error=quad(lambda time:float(exact(time)[1]),0,10,epsabs=1e-11)
    comparisons={}
    for h in [.1,.5,1.,2.]:
        te,ye=euler(h);comparisons[str(h)]={'max_error':float(np.max(np.abs(ye-exact(te)))),'min_fraction':float(ye.min()),'sum_error':float(np.max(np.abs(ye.sum(axis=0)-1))),
            'first_step':ye[:,1].tolist(),'final':ye[:,-1].tolist(),'left_integral_B_min':float(h*ye[1,:-1].sum())}
    np.savetxt(args.output/'fractions.csv',np.column_stack([t,solution.y.T,reference.T]),delimiter=',',comments='',header='time_min,A_numeric,B_numeric,C_numeric,A_exact,B_exact,C_exact')
    fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,5.8),layout='constrained',gridspec_kw={'width_ratios':[1.5,1]})
    for i,name in enumerate('ABC'):ax[0].plot(t,solution.y[i],color=COLORS[i],lw=2.3,label=name)
    ax[0].set(xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('状态分数，无量纲','State fraction, dimensionless'),title=tr('A → B → C：中间态先升后降','A → B → C: an intermediate rises and falls'),xlim=(0,10),ylim=(0,1));ax[0].legend(frameon=False);ax[0].grid()
    ax[1].fill_between(t,0,reference[1],color=COLORS[1],alpha=.2);ax[1].plot(t,reference[1],color=COLORS[1],lw=2)
    ax[1].text(.96,.92,tr(f'0–10 min的面积\n{area:.6f} min',f'Area over 0–10 min\n{area:.6f} min'),ha='right',va='top',transform=ax[1].transAxes)
    ax[1].set(xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('B的分数，无量纲','Fraction in B, dimensionless'),title=tr('面积累计“数量 × 持续时间”','Area accumulates fraction × time'),xlim=(0,10),ylim=(0,.65));ax[1].grid();save(fig,'conversion')
    fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,5.8),layout='constrained')
    for h,color in zip([1.,.5,.1],['#b64a35','#8f8990',COLORS[0]]):
        te,ye=euler(h);ax[0].plot(te,ye[0],'.-',color=color,lw=1.4,label=f'h = {h:g} min')
    ax[0].plot(t,reference[0],'--',color='#20313e',lw=1.8,label=tr('解析曲线','Analytic curve'))
    ax[0].set(xlim=(0,3),ylim=(0,1.02),xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('A的分数，无量纲','Fraction in A, dimensionless'),title=tr('欧拉步：沿当前斜率向前走','Euler steps: advance along the current slope'));ax[0].legend(frameon=False,fontsize=10);ax[0].grid()
    hvals=np.array([.025,.05,.1,.2,.5,1.]);errors=[]
    for h in hvals:
        te,ye=euler(h);errors.append(np.max(np.abs(ye-exact(te))))
    ax[1].loglog(hvals,errors,'o-',color=COLORS[1],label=tr('三种分数的最大绝对误差','Maximum absolute error across A, B, C'))
    ax[1].loglog(hvals,errors[0]*hvals/hvals[0],':',color='#71808b',label=tr('与步长成正比的参考线','Reference proportional to step size'))
    ax[1].set(xlabel=tr('步长 h / min','Step size h / min'),ylabel=tr('最大绝对误差，无量纲','Maximum absolute error, dimensionless'),title=tr('缩短步长，检验逐步逼近','Reduce the step and inspect convergence'));ax[1].legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9);ax[1].grid(which='both');save(fig,'history')
    fig,ax=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(12,7.5),layout='constrained',gridspec_kw={'height_ratios':[1.5,1]})
    te,ye=euler(2.)
    for i,name in enumerate('ABC'):
        ax[0].plot(t,reference[i],color=COLORS[i],alpha=.5,ls='--');ax[0].plot(te,ye[i],'o-',color=COLORS[i],label=name)
    ax[0].axhline(0,color='#20313e',lw=1);ax[0].set(ylabel=tr('状态分数，无量纲','State fraction, dimensionless'),title=tr('h = 2 min：总量保持，个别分数却变成负值','h = 2 min: total is conserved while a fraction becomes negative'));ax[0].legend(frameon=False,ncol=3);ax[0].grid()
    ax[1].plot(te,ye.sum(axis=0),'o-',color='#20313e');ax[1].set(ylim=(.95,1.05),xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('A + B + C，无量纲','A + B + C, dimensionless'),title=tr('守恒、非负与准确性是三项不同检查','Conservation, positivity, and accuracy are separate checks'));ax[1].grid();save(fig,'checks')
    summary={'versions':{'numpy':np.__version__,'scipy':scipy.__version__,'matplotlib':matplotlib.__version__},'rates_per_min':[K1,K2],
        'solver_success':bool(solution.success),'solver_max_error':float(np.max(np.abs(solution.y-reference))),
        'solver_sum_error':float(np.max(np.abs(solution.y.sum(axis=0)-1))),
        'B_peak_time_min':float(solution.t_events[0][0]),'B_peak_time_exact_min':float(np.log(K1/K2)/(K1-K2)),
        'integral_B_min':area,'integral_B_exact_min':float(b_integral(10)),'quad_error_estimate_min':area_error,
        'trapezoid_B_min':float(trapezoid(reference[1],x=t)),'euler':comparisons}
    (args.output/'summary.json').write_text(json.dumps(summary,indent=2),encoding='utf-8');print(json.dumps(summary))


if __name__=='__main__':main()
```

读完代码后，可以先检查输出文件中的第一行：时间为0，三种数值分数和解析分数都应是1、0、0。再检查最后一行，确认A已经很少、C占主要部分。摘要同时记录求解器是否成功、与解析解的最大差、总量偏差、B的峰顶时刻和积分值。每项记录对应前文的一个科学或计算问题，而不是把所有返回值都堆进表格。

程序中的峰顶定位和积分各自使用适合的问题形式。峰顶是变化率的零点，所以交给事件检测；面积是函数在区间上的累计，所以交给积分。若以后只拿到实验采样数据，可以先明确要保留怎样的插值或局部模型，再选相应工具。把问题形式说清楚，通常比记住更多函数名更能帮助选择算法。

## 联动实验：改变速度和步长，观察三项检查怎样分开

实验同时显示三种状态的连续解析曲线与欧拉折线、当前时刻的组成，以及各数值节点相对于解析解的最大误差。改变第一步转化速率，会改变整个过程的物理时间尺度；改变欧拉步长，则改变对同一连续过程的数值近似。把这两个控制放在一起，能够看到模型参数与算法参数各自改变了什么。

### 过程速度与计算步长

[Figure: 三个分数的连续解和欧拉近似](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/#P21-trajectory)

[Figure: 当前组成比较](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/#P21-composition)

[Figure: 各节点的最大分数误差](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/#P21-error)

颜色依次对应A、B、C。主图实线为解析解，带圆点折线为欧拉结果；组成图浅色柱为解析值，深色柱为欧拉插值。

先保持0.8 min⁻¹的转化速率，将步长从0.1 min改到0.5 min、1 min和2 min。总量仍接近1，但最大误差逐渐变大，2 min时出现负分数。再把速率降到0.4 min⁻¹，观察同样步长怎样对应不同的转化比例。当前时刻的数值分数通过欧拉节点间的直线插值得到，节点误差则始终在算法实际计算的位置上比较。

读数中的B积分采用欧拉左端矩形累计，因而同时受状态近似和面积近似影响；解析积分提供独立参照。移动观察时刻只改变组成图的截面，整段0到10 min的最大误差与积分不会随观察位置改变。这样可以把“曲线的哪个位置”与“整次计算有多准确”分开阅读。

## 把变化问题交给计算机前，先把量和条件放稳

准备自己的模型时，可以从一张流向图开始：哪些量需要随时间保存，哪些过程增加它们，哪些过程减少它们，初始值和单位分别是什么。先让每条流向在方程中成对出现，再检查相加后应该保持什么。若系统存在输入输出，总量变化也应与这些边界流量对应。这个步骤往往比立即调节求解器参数更能发现模型中的遗漏。

运行之后，把关键科学量与数值设置一起保存，例如峰顶时间、累计面积、初值、速率参数、求解方法和容差。选取几组更严格的设置比较关键量是否稳定，再把主要变化与实验参数联系起来。数值积分和微分方程求解由此成为一条完整的研究链：从流向解释变化，从曲线读取过程，再把过程浓缩成有单位、有含义的结果。

# Describing Change with Integrals and Differential Equations

Source: https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/en/
Language: en

Use a three-state conversion to understand rates, numerical steps, conservation, and accumulated area.

## When should an intermediate state be observed?

A sample may change from state A to B and then from B to C. A could represent material before conversion, B a temporary intermediate, and C material after a subsequent change. By the end of an experiment, little B may remain. If B is the feature of interest, two useful questions are when it reaches its largest fraction and how long it remains present during the process. These questions concern a curve's peak and its area, bringing differential equations and integration into the same practical problem.

We use a defined teaching model: a fixed total passes through A, B, and C in a one-to-one sequence, with constant volume and conditions, no additional input or output, and no reverse conversion. Each state is described as a fraction of the initial total. Initially A is 1 and both B and C are 0. This setup keeps attention on rates of change. For an actual reaction, the corresponding equations would be built from the species, stoichiometry, volume changes, and measurement definitions.

SciPy's `solve_ivp` computes a trajectory from an initial state and a rule for how that state changes. Its `quad` function accumulates the area beneath a supplied function. We first examine short calculations that can be checked by hand, then run the complete program. A simple model with a known analytic answer makes step size, error, conservation, and integral units concrete rather than leaving them as abstract solver options.

## Rates describe change per minute; the equations record the flows

Suppose the rate at which A becomes B is proportional to the amount of A currently present. More A allows more conversion in the same short interval; as A decreases, its conversion rate also decreases. The first rate constant is 0.8 min⁻¹. When A has a fraction of 0.5, its instantaneous loss rate is 0.4 fraction units per minute. “Instantaneous” matters: this is the direction and speed at that moment, and the speed changes as the state changes.

$$
\frac{da}{dt}=-k_1a,\qquad\frac{db}{dt}=k_1a-k_2b,\qquad\frac{dc}{dt}=k_2b
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/326d9c99fe68c4303977dd55.svg) | Fractions of the initial total in A, B, and C; dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/707bb132def3690d81bf1f0c.svg) | Elapsed time, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/d62ad609310d0b90a08f3cae.svg) | Rate constants for A→B and B→C, respectively 0.8 and 0.3 min⁻¹. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/cf7a258783fb9a082f6d20a4.svg) | Instantaneous rates of change in the fractions, min⁻¹; d denotes differentiation. |

Each transfer is a current fraction multiplied by a rate constant. For a = 0.5, b = 0.3, and c = 0.2, the rates are −0.4, 0.4 − 0.09 = 0.31, and 0.09 min⁻¹. They sum to zero, so the total stays constant while its composition changes.

The three equations can be read as accounts of incoming and outgoing material. A only loses material, so its rate is negative. B receives material from A and loses material to C, giving an inflow minus an outflow. C receives the second flow. Adding the three rates cancels each transfer against its counterpart, leaving a constant total fraction. The second rate constant is 0.3 min⁻¹. Because removal from B is relatively slow, B accumulates early and later declines as its supply from A becomes smaller.

A derivative can be approached through an average rate. Subtract the fractions at two nearby times and divide by the elapsed time to obtain the average change over that interval. Shrinking the interval leads toward the rate at one time. This resembles the relation between position and velocity: a present position and velocity predict a position a short time later. Here the position is replaced by three fractions, and the velocities are replaced by three coupled rates of transfer.

Normalizing the initial total to 1 amounts to dividing the sample into equal counting units and tracking which state each occupies. The one-to-one conversion preserves their total number. For a chemical reaction with multiple reactants or different stoichiometric coefficients, construct equations for concentrations or amounts and then check the appropriate element or mass balance. Fractions make this example convenient, while the physical process determines what must actually be conserved.

## Advance along the current slope, then calculate it again

In the eighteenth century, Euler organized integration and differential equations into systematic tools for studying change. The first volume of his *Foundations of Integral Calculus* appeared in 1768. A numerical program still addresses the same basic relationship: given a rule for change, recover the quantity that changes with time. The Euler method provides an especially clear geometric construction. Move a short distance along the current slope, then recalculate the slope at the new position.

$$
\mathbf y_{n+1}=\mathbf y_n+h\,\mathbf f(t_n,\mathbf y_n)
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f9863792b3128c856f71d728.svg) | State vector at node n, containing dimensionless fractions a, b, and c. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/794309c181b5d3eef90282ba.svg) | Integer labels of the current and next numerical nodes, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/994427fe929fdf538d7c1be7.svg) | Time step, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a588fc41a723666b153cc137.svg) | Time at node n, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a06debad6e153cb789c38ba5.svg) | Rate vector defined by the three preceding equations; each component has units min⁻¹. |

Rate multiplied by time gives the approximate change over one step. Initial state (1, 0, 0), step 0.5 min, and rate (−0.8, 0.8, 0) min⁻¹ produce (0.6, 0.4, 0). The total is 1, while conversion of newly formed B within this coarse step enters only through later updates.

Starting from A = 1, B = 0, and C = 0, the current rates are −0.8, 0.8, and 0 min⁻¹. For a 0.5 min step, multiply each rate by 0.5 and add it to the corresponding starting value. The result is A = 0.6, B = 0.4, and C = 0. This holds the initial rates constant for half a minute. In the continuous model, A begins slowing immediately as it decreases, and newly formed B immediately starts converting to C. The discrete calculation updates these effects at the next node.

![Euler steps connect nodes using their current slopes. Refinement approaches the analytic curve. The right panel independently measures maximum absolute error across all three fractions; the reference line is proportional to step size.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/55a7342979f7dcd42434114e.svg?v=55a7342979f7)

Figure 1Euler steps connect nodes using their current slopes. Refinement approaches the analytic curve. The right panel independently measures maximum absolute error across all three fractions; the reference line is proportional to step size.

The coarse polygonal curves depart from the analytic curve, whereas shorter steps approach it. The right panel plots maximum absolute error against step size on logarithmic axes. At small steps, the trend roughly follows a line proportional to step size. This comparison is more informative than the smooth appearance of a single plot. A plotting program can smoothly connect a few points; numerical accuracy is assessed through refinement, an independent answer, or a more stringent solution procedure.

## Let the solver choose its steps; specify the initial state and output times

The program expresses the rate rule in `rhs(t, y)`. Its argument `t` is the current time, while `y` contains the fractions in the order A, B, C. The returned derivatives use the same order. This ordering plays the role of table column names: the initial values, plot labels, and checks must follow it consistently. Although the present rate constants do not depend on time, the interface keeps the time argument so that heating, external inputs, or other time-dependent conditions can be represented.

`solve_ivp` receives the interval from 0 to 10 min and the initial state [1, 0, 0]. Its default RK45 method evaluates rates at several positions during a step and adjusts its internal step size using an error estimate. Here `t_eval` requests results at 501 evenly spaced times for plotting and comparison. These saved times do not require the solver to use a fixed internal step of 0.02 min. An output grid and the algorithm's internal steps serve different purposes.

The settings are `rtol=1e-9` and `atol=1e-11`. Relative tolerance scales with the magnitude of a fraction, whereas absolute tolerance supplies a scale even when a fraction is close to zero. They control estimates of local error, so the final trajectory is also checked directly. Comparing all three computed fractions with their analytic values at every saved time gives a maximum absolute difference of approximately 7.21 × 10⁻¹¹ in this run.

![Three fractions and the B integral for the same sequential model. RK45 produces the left trajectories; the analytic B curve defines the shaded area on the right. Time is in minutes and the initial total is normalized to 1.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/414bbb94b67f0f074da41f76.svg?v=414bbb94b67f)

Figure 2Three fractions and the B integral for the same sequential model. RK45 produces the left trajectories; the analytic B curve defines the shaded area on the right. Time is in minutes and the initial total is normalized to 1.

The program also uses the rate of B as an event function, locating where it changes from positive to negative. That zero marks the transition from increasing B to decreasing B, giving a peak time of approximately 1.96166 min. Event detection finds a zero on the continuous numerical solution rather than simply choosing the largest of the 501 stored values. In a new application, an event should correspond to a precise condition, such as a concentration crossing a threshold or a net flow reversing direction.

The analytic solution can also be understood from the flow rules. A loses the same proportion over equal time intervals, giving exponential decay. B receives contributions from A at many different times, and each contribution subsequently decays toward C according to how long it has been in B. Adding these contributions gives a difference of two exponentials. C follows by subtracting A and B from the total. The expression used in the program assumes distinct rate constants, a condition satisfied by every selectable rate in this chapter.

$$
a(t)=e^{-k_1t},\qquad b(t)=\frac{k_1}{k_2-k_1}\left(e^{-k_1t}-e^{-k_2t}\right),\qquad c(t)=1-a(t)-b(t)
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/db3924ef96d9ef424c4cfc5d.svg) | Three dimensionless fractions at time t for initial state (1, 0, 0). |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/dec0f7dc61f0e9a546cd9d6d.svg) | t is time in min; both rate constants have units min⁻¹ and must be distinct for this expression. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/0be950b3e59846bc80f7e4ca.svg) | Base of the natural exponential, approximately 2.71828. Rate multiplied by time in each exponent is dimensionless. |

At t = 0 both exponentials equal 1, giving a = 1, b = 0, c = 0. At t = 2 min with rates 0.8 and 0.3 min⁻¹, the fractions are approximately 0.201897, 0.555064, and 0.243039. Their total is 1. This expression supplies a check independent of time stepping.

## A correct total is one check; each fraction also has a meaning

Conservation is useful because it connects three outputs through one relationship. A mistaken positive sign on the loss from B, or an omitted gain by C, would produce a visible drift in the total. Conservation checks whether transfers balance. An Euler step subtracts material from A and adds the same amount to B, then subtracts another amount from B and adds it to C. It can therefore preserve a total of 1 even when the step is very large.

![A 2 min Euler step produces a negative A fraction while preserving a total of 1. Dashed curves show the analytic model, and solid curves with circles show the coarse numerical result. The lower panel checks the total separately.](https://ml-biomat.com/static/tutorials/python-scientific/figures/dfb20e6198e1b48fceb4acb6.svg?v=dfb20e6198e1)

Figure 3A 2 min Euler step produces a negative A fraction while preserving a total of 1. Dashed curves show the analytic model, and solid curves with circles show the coarse numerical result. The lower panel checks the total separately.

With a 2 min step, the first update gives A = −0.6, B = 1.6, and C = 0. Their sum is still 1, but the fractions have left the range implied by the physical model. The update has maintained the initial transfer rate of 0.8 per minute for two whole minutes, moving 1.6 units when only 1 unit was present. This separates three questions: whether the total is conserved, whether all states remain nonnegative, and whether the trajectory closely approximates the continuous equations.

For A alone, an Euler update multiplies its current fraction by one minus the rate constant times the step size. To preserve a nonnegative A during that update, the product of rate constant and step size must be no greater than 1. Larger steps can introduce alternating signs; when the magnitude of the multiplier exceeds 1, those oscillations grow. This calculation connects step size to the speed of the process, rather than to the desired number of plotted points.

When one process evolves much faster than another, the fastest time scale can restrict an explicit method. This is a common source of stiffness. SciPy provides methods such as Radau and BDF for stiff systems. Examine the time scales, solver status, function evaluation count, and changes under tighter settings when choosing a method. After a change of algorithm, conservation, positivity, and the scientific outputs remain useful complementary checks.

An error comparison also needs a precise set of locations. At each Euler node, the program computes the absolute differences for A, B, and C, then selects the largest component difference. The full-run maximum is the largest of those node values. It describes the worst calculated component discrepancy, which answers a different question from an average error. All components here are dimensionless fractions and can be compared directly. State variables with different units or very different scales require an explicit scaling choice.

## Area accumulates an amount together with its duration

The amount of B at one instant differs from its cumulative presence during the process. If B stays near 0.4 for an interval of 0.5 min, that interval contributes approximately 0.2 min of fraction multiplied by time. Divide the entire process into many such strips and add their contributions to obtain the area beneath the B curve. Because a fraction is dimensionless, the area has units of minutes. With concentration in mmol/L on the vertical axis, the corresponding integral would instead have units of mmol·min/L.

$$
I_B(T)=\int_0^T b(t)\,dt\;\approx\;\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} b(t_n)h,\qquad T=Nh
$$

| Symbol | Meaning and units |
| --- | --- |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a11305f0a6beaa6b17d10d0f.svg) | Integral of the B fraction from 0 to T, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/ea3059ae9f52fe6b926fbbba.svg) | Fraction in B at time t, dimensionless. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f9815edca06dc233accaf513.svg) | Integration time and final time, min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/f31d38e9354f49723c5bb666.svg) | dt is an infinitesimal time increment; the integral accumulates the function over time, giving its units multiplied by min. |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/a23a4935fef8a0becb8f51d8.svg) | h is the uniform step (min), N the number of intervals, n an integer from 0 to N−1, and t_n = nh the left-end time (min). |
| ![Formula](https://ml-biomat.com/static/agent-math/9b9441d841a7d77652c30687.svg) | Sum the areas of N left-end rectangles. |

If two half-minute intervals have approximate B fractions of 0.4 and 0.5, their areas are 0.2 and 0.25 min, totaling 0.45 min. Shorter strips describe the curve more closely. The complete model integrates to 3.068473 min over 0–10 min; the finite sum on the right is specifically a left-rectangle approximation.

Over 0–10 min, the integral for B is approximately 3.068473 min. It describes the average accumulated time spent in B during this observation window per initial unit. The area decreases if fewer units enter B or if they leave it quickly. Such an integral compares the persistence of an intermediate. In a particular experiment, connect the quantity to the actual question, such as intermediate exposure, accumulated release, or reaction contribution, while retaining its physical units.

`quad` takes a callable function that can be evaluated at any requested time. Here it integrates the analytic expression for B. Its second return value estimates numerical integration error, approximately 3.41 × 10⁻¹⁴ min in this calculation. This estimate concerns the integration of the specified function. Experimental uncertainty in the rate constants is assessed through parameter variation or uncertainty propagation. Distinguishing these quantities gives the many reported decimal places their proper meaning.

If only sampled measurements are available, `trapezoid` approximates the region between adjacent points by a trapezoid and adds the areas. Applying it to the 501 analytic samples gives 3.068446 min, slightly different from direct function integration because of finite sampling and the implied interpolation. For uneven sampling, supply the actual time array. Row numbers would otherwise assign an artificial and generally incorrect duration to each interval.

The flow account provides another compact check over an infinitely long observation period. Eventually C receives all initial units, so the accumulated B→C transfer is 1. At every time that transfer rate equals 0.3 min⁻¹ multiplied by the B fraction. The integral of B over infinite time is therefore 1 divided by 0.3 min⁻¹, or approximately 3.333333 min. Stopping at 10 min gives the smaller value 3.068473 min; the difference belongs to the tail of B that remains after the observation window.

## A complete program with a model, an algorithm, and an independent answer

The program keeps three calculation paths visible. `rhs` supplies rates and `solve_ivp` evolves the state. `exact` supplies the analytic solution of the same model for comparison. `euler` explicitly implements simple steps so that their effect can be inspected. The analytic function is specific to this closed-form example, whereas the numerical solver interface also supports more complicated models with additional processes.

### Complete example: sequential conversion, peak events, integrals, and step-size comparison

Running the program creates three figures, fractions.csv, and summary.json. All inputs and analytic comparison functions are included.

```
"""Follow a conserved three-state conversion with integration and an ODE solver."""
from pathlib import Path
import argparse,json
import numpy as np
import scipy
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp,quad,trapezoid
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import font_manager

COLORS=['#28658c','#c26835','#477f67']
K1,K2=.8,.3


def exact(t,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    t=np.asarray(t);a=np.exp(-k1*t)
    b=k1/(k2-k1)*(np.exp(-k1*t)-np.exp(-k2*t))
    return np.array([a,b,1-a-b])


def rhs(t,y,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    a,b,c=y
    return np.array([-k1*a,k1*a-k2*b,k2*b])


def euler(h,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    t=np.linspace(0,10,round(10/h)+1);y=np.zeros((3,len(t)));y[:,0]=[1,0,0]
    for i in range(len(t)-1):y[:,i+1]=y[:,i]+h*rhs(t[i],y[:,i],k1,k2)
    return t,y


def b_integral(end,k1=K1,k2=K2):
    return k1/(k2-k1)*((1-np.exp(-k1*end))/k1-(1-np.exp(-k2*end))/k2)


def main():
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser();p.add_argument('--output',type=Path,required=True);p.add_argument('--language',choices=['zh','en'],default='en');args=p.parse_args()
    args.output.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True);zh=args.language=='zh'
    def tr(a,b):return a if zh else b
    available={f.name for f in font_manager.fontManager.ttflist}
    plt.rcParams.update({'font.family':[f for f in ['Noto Sans CJK SC','Noto Sans SC','Microsoft YaHei','SimHei','DejaVu Sans'] if f in available],'font.size':12,'svg.fonttype':'none','axes.spines.top':False,'axes.spines.right':False,'grid.alpha':.15})
    def save(fig,name):
        fig.savefig(args.output/f'{name}-{args.language}.svg');fig.savefig(args.output/f'{name}-{args.language}.png',dpi=160);plt.close(fig)
    t=np.linspace(0,10,501)
    def peak_b(t,y):return K1*y[0]-K2*y[1]
    peak_b.direction=-1
    solution=solve_ivp(rhs,(0,10),[1.,0.,0.],t_eval=t,rtol=1e-9,atol=1e-11,events=peak_b)
    if not solution.success:raise RuntimeError(solution.message)
    reference=exact(t);area,area_error=quad(lambda time:float(exact(time)[1]),0,10,epsabs=1e-11)
    comparisons={}
    for h in [.1,.5,1.,2.]:
        te,ye=euler(h);comparisons[str(h)]={'max_error':float(np.max(np.abs(ye-exact(te)))),'min_fraction':float(ye.min()),'sum_error':float(np.max(np.abs(ye.sum(axis=0)-1))),
            'first_step':ye[:,1].tolist(),'final':ye[:,-1].tolist(),'left_integral_B_min':float(h*ye[1,:-1].sum())}
    np.savetxt(args.output/'fractions.csv',np.column_stack([t,solution.y.T,reference.T]),delimiter=',',comments='',header='time_min,A_numeric,B_numeric,C_numeric,A_exact,B_exact,C_exact')
    fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,5.8),layout='constrained',gridspec_kw={'width_ratios':[1.5,1]})
    for i,name in enumerate('ABC'):ax[0].plot(t,solution.y[i],color=COLORS[i],lw=2.3,label=name)
    ax[0].set(xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('状态分数，无量纲','State fraction, dimensionless'),title=tr('A → B → C：中间态先升后降','A → B → C: an intermediate rises and falls'),xlim=(0,10),ylim=(0,1));ax[0].legend(frameon=False);ax[0].grid()
    ax[1].fill_between(t,0,reference[1],color=COLORS[1],alpha=.2);ax[1].plot(t,reference[1],color=COLORS[1],lw=2)
    ax[1].text(.96,.92,tr(f'0–10 min的面积\n{area:.6f} min',f'Area over 0–10 min\n{area:.6f} min'),ha='right',va='top',transform=ax[1].transAxes)
    ax[1].set(xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('B的分数，无量纲','Fraction in B, dimensionless'),title=tr('面积累计“数量 × 持续时间”','Area accumulates fraction × time'),xlim=(0,10),ylim=(0,.65));ax[1].grid();save(fig,'conversion')
    fig,ax=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(12,5.8),layout='constrained')
    for h,color in zip([1.,.5,.1],['#b64a35','#8f8990',COLORS[0]]):
        te,ye=euler(h);ax[0].plot(te,ye[0],'.-',color=color,lw=1.4,label=f'h = {h:g} min')
    ax[0].plot(t,reference[0],'--',color='#20313e',lw=1.8,label=tr('解析曲线','Analytic curve'))
    ax[0].set(xlim=(0,3),ylim=(0,1.02),xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('A的分数，无量纲','Fraction in A, dimensionless'),title=tr('欧拉步：沿当前斜率向前走','Euler steps: advance along the current slope'));ax[0].legend(frameon=False,fontsize=10);ax[0].grid()
    hvals=np.array([.025,.05,.1,.2,.5,1.]);errors=[]
    for h in hvals:
        te,ye=euler(h);errors.append(np.max(np.abs(ye-exact(te))))
    ax[1].loglog(hvals,errors,'o-',color=COLORS[1],label=tr('三种分数的最大绝对误差','Maximum absolute error across A, B, C'))
    ax[1].loglog(hvals,errors[0]*hvals/hvals[0],':',color='#71808b',label=tr('与步长成正比的参考线','Reference proportional to step size'))
    ax[1].set(xlabel=tr('步长 h / min','Step size h / min'),ylabel=tr('最大绝对误差，无量纲','Maximum absolute error, dimensionless'),title=tr('缩短步长，检验逐步逼近','Reduce the step and inspect convergence'));ax[1].legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9);ax[1].grid(which='both');save(fig,'history')
    fig,ax=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(12,7.5),layout='constrained',gridspec_kw={'height_ratios':[1.5,1]})
    te,ye=euler(2.)
    for i,name in enumerate('ABC'):
        ax[0].plot(t,reference[i],color=COLORS[i],alpha=.5,ls='--');ax[0].plot(te,ye[i],'o-',color=COLORS[i],label=name)
    ax[0].axhline(0,color='#20313e',lw=1);ax[0].set(ylabel=tr('状态分数，无量纲','State fraction, dimensionless'),title=tr('h = 2 min：总量保持，个别分数却变成负值','h = 2 min: total is conserved while a fraction becomes negative'));ax[0].legend(frameon=False,ncol=3);ax[0].grid()
    ax[1].plot(te,ye.sum(axis=0),'o-',color='#20313e');ax[1].set(ylim=(.95,1.05),xlabel=tr('时间 / min','Time / min'),ylabel=tr('A + B + C，无量纲','A + B + C, dimensionless'),title=tr('守恒、非负与准确性是三项不同检查','Conservation, positivity, and accuracy are separate checks'));ax[1].grid();save(fig,'checks')
    summary={'versions':{'numpy':np.__version__,'scipy':scipy.__version__,'matplotlib':matplotlib.__version__},'rates_per_min':[K1,K2],
        'solver_success':bool(solution.success),'solver_max_error':float(np.max(np.abs(solution.y-reference))),
        'solver_sum_error':float(np.max(np.abs(solution.y.sum(axis=0)-1))),
        'B_peak_time_min':float(solution.t_events[0][0]),'B_peak_time_exact_min':float(np.log(K1/K2)/(K1-K2)),
        'integral_B_min':area,'integral_B_exact_min':float(b_integral(10)),'quad_error_estimate_min':area_error,
        'trapezoid_B_min':float(trapezoid(reference[1],x=t)),'euler':comparisons}
    (args.output/'summary.json').write_text(json.dumps(summary,indent=2),encoding='utf-8');print(json.dumps(summary))


if __name__=='__main__':main()
```

Start checking the output with its first row: at time zero, both the numerical and analytic fractions should be 1, 0, 0. Then inspect the last row, where little A remains and C is the dominant state. The summary records solver success, maximum analytic difference, total-fraction error, the peak time of B, and its integral. Each entry answers one of the scientific or computational questions developed above.

Peak localization and integration use different mathematical forms of the problem. A peak is found where a rate vanishes, so it is handled by event detection. An area is an accumulation over an interval, so it is handled by quadrature. With experimental samples, first decide what interpolation or local model is justified, then choose the corresponding tool. Specifying the question clearly is often more useful than memorizing additional function names.

## Change the rate and step size, then compare the checks

The experiment links continuous analytic curves and Euler trajectories, the composition at the selected time, and the maximum component error at each numerical node. Changing the first conversion rate changes a physical time scale. Changing the Euler step changes the numerical approximation to the same continuous process. Viewing these controls together makes their different roles visible.

### Process rate and numerical step

[Figure: Continuous and Euler trajectories for three fractions](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/en/#P21-trajectory)

[Figure: Current composition comparison](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/en/#P21-composition)

[Figure: Maximum fraction error at each node](https://ml-biomat.com/tutorials/python-scientific/p21/en/#P21-error)

Colors identify A, B, and C. Main-panel solid curves are analytic; lines with circles are Euler results. Pale composition bars are analytic and darker bars are Euler interpolations.

Keep the first rate at 0.8 min⁻¹ and increase the step from 0.1 min to 0.5, 1, and 2 min. The total stays near 1 while maximum error increases; the 2 min step also produces negative fractions. Then lower the rate to 0.4 min⁻¹ and inspect the effect of the same step sizes. The selected numerical composition uses straight-line interpolation between Euler nodes. Node errors are always evaluated at the positions actually calculated by the algorithm.

The displayed B integral uses left-end rectangles along the Euler trajectory, so it includes effects from both state approximation and area approximation. An analytic integral provides an independent reference. Moving the observation time only changes the displayed composition. It does not change the maximum error or integral over the full 0–10 min calculation. This separates a location on the trajectory from a property of the complete computation.

## Establish quantities and conditions before choosing solver settings

For a new model, begin with a flow diagram. Identify the quantities to track, the processes that increase or decrease each one, their initial values, and their units. Represent internal transfers in matching pairs, then check what adding the equations should preserve. If the system has inputs or outputs, the total change should match those boundary flows. This step often reveals omissions more effectively than immediate adjustment of solver settings.

Save the key scientific results together with the numerical setup: peak times, accumulated areas, initial states, rate parameters, solver method, and tolerances. Compare important outputs under stricter settings before relating their variation to experimental parameters. Integration and differential-equation solving then form a coherent analysis: use flows to explain change, trajectories to inspect the process, and carefully defined quantities to summarize what happened.

   Initial-value problems, RK45, tolerances, and events.

   BSD-3-Clause; technical reference
